title: Regarding the standardised uptake value (SUV) in FDG PET imaging:

stems.label: A
stems.text: It is a simplified index of glucose utilisation.
stems.explanation: This is the definition. SUV = tissue concentration (kBq/ml) divided by (injected activity / body mass) — in words, how much hotter this voxel is than if the tracer had spread uniformly through the body. FDG is a glucose analogue that is phosphorylated and then trapped, so its distribution maps glucose metabolism, and the SUV is the simplified, semi-quantitative number attached to that map.

stems.label: B
stems.text: It assumes that plasma FDG concentration is proportional to the injected activity and inversely proportional to body mass.
stems.explanation: That assumption is precisely what the normalisation term in the formula is: injected activity divided by body mass. Read the formula rather than the sentence and the statement answers itself — this is the SUV statement most often marked False by mistake.

stems.label: C
stems.text: It is independent of the PET scanner used and of the uptake time.
stems.explanation: Both halves are false. The scanner, the reconstruction algorithm, the uptake time and the patient's blood glucose all move the SUV — plasma FDG concentration changes with time, and the reconstruction affects every quantitative index. The rule that fixes the whole cluster: the SUV is standardised, not absolute.

stems.label: D
stems.text: An SUVmax of 3.5 is the threshold for malignancy.
stems.explanation: The conventionally quoted (and crude) threshold the banks expect is 2.5, not 3.5 — that is the mark-scoring detail. No threshold is truly universal in any case: the SUV varies with everything in statement c, and benign inflammation can be avid.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The SUV cannot be used to distinguish benign from malignant disease.
stems.explanation: This is the same fact asked from the other side, and it is False too. The SUV does contribute to separating benign from malignant — it simply is not a binary rule, because it moves with scanner, reconstruction, uptake time and glucose, and inflammatory lesions can be avid.

stems.label: A
stems.text: It should be corrected for the patient's blood glucose level.
stems.explanation: Blood glucose competes with FDG and moves the SUV, so it must be taken into account when the number is interpreted — one of the several measurement conditions that shift a supposedly standardised index.

stems.label: B
stems.text: It is a simplified index of glucose utilisation.
stems.explanation: That is the definition: FDG enters cells and is phosphorylated like glucose, but the charged phosphorylated form cannot be metabolised further and is trapped, so uptake maps glucose metabolism. The SUV is a semi-quantitative index of it, not an absolute measurement.

stems.label: C
stems.text: It assumes plasma FDG concentration is proportional to injected activity and inversely proportional to body mass.
stems.explanation: SUV = tissue concentration in kBq/ml divided by (injected activity / body mass). The normalisation term is exactly that assumption — how much hotter this voxel is than if the tracer had spread uniformly.

stems.label: D
stems.text: It is independent of the uptake time between injection and scanning.
stems.explanation: Plasma FDG concentration changes with time, so the SUV moves with uptake time — which is why the 60-minute period is standardised. Scanner and reconstruction algorithm shift it too. SUV is standardised, not absolute.

stems.label: E
stems.text: An SUVmax of 3.5 is the threshold for malignancy.
stems.explanation: The conventionally quoted crude threshold is 2.5. Even that is not universal: SUV varies with scanner, reconstruction, uptake time and glucose, and benign inflammation can be avid. Note the flip side — 'SUV cannot distinguish benign from malignant' is also False; it contributes, it is simply not a binary rule.

title: Regarding the Doppler shift in ultrasound

stems.label: A
stems.text: It is proportional to the transmitted frequency.
stems.explanation: fD = 2f0v·cosθ/c. The transmitted frequency sits in the numerator, so doubling f0 doubles the shift.

stems.label: B
stems.text: It increases as the velocity of blood in the vessel increases.
stems.explanation: Velocity is in the numerator of fD = 2f0v·cosθ/c. Frequency, velocity and angle are the variables in the equation.

stems.label: C
stems.text: It increases as the intensity of the transmitted beam is increased.
stems.explanation: Intensity is not in the equation. Raising output alters echo amplitude, never the frequency difference.

stems.label: D
stems.text: It increases as the propagation velocity of ultrasound in the medium increases.
stems.explanation: c is in the denominator. A faster medium gives a smaller fractional shift. Re-asked in the March 2026 paper.

stems.label: E
stems.text: It is greatest when the beam is perpendicular to the direction of flow.
stems.explanation: The shift goes with cosθ: maximal with the beam along the flow, and zero at 90 degrees.

title: Regarding the Doppler frequency shift in ultrasound

stems.label: A
stems.text: The Doppler shift is proportional to the transmitted frequency.
stems.explanation: fD = 2.f0.v.cos(theta)/c - linear in f0. This term is also why a higher operating frequency makes aliasing more likely: a bigger shift against the same Nyquist ceiling.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The Doppler shift is proportional to the velocity of blood flow.
stems.explanation: Linear in v. That is the entire point of the measurement.

stems.label: C
stems.text: The Doppler shift increases as the angle between the beam and the direction of flow increases.
stems.explanation: It follows cos(theta): maximal at 0 degrees with the beam parallel to flow, and zero at 90 degrees. So the effect is least, not greatest, for structures moving at right angles to the beam - the reverse of the X-ray habit.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The Doppler shift increases with the diameter of the vessel insonated.
stems.explanation: Vessel size is not in the equation. Neither are beam intensity, pulse repetition frequency or tissue density - intensity changes signal amplitude, not frequency.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The Doppler shift increases with the propagation speed of ultrasound in the tissue.
stems.explanation: c sits in the denominator, so the relation is inverse. In a faster medium the same blood velocity is a smaller fraction of the wave speed, so the fractional frequency change is smaller.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Pitch is the table feed per rotation divided by the total collimated beam width.
stems.explanation: That is the MDCT definition, and pitch is a ratio, so it carries no units — 'the unit of pitch is mm/s' is false. The older single-slice wording (table feed divided by slice thickness) passes only because collimation and slice thickness were then the same thing.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Increasing pitch from 1.0 to 1.5 reduces patient dose, other factors being fixed.
stems.explanation: CTDIvol = CTDIw / pitch, so dose falls inversely with pitch.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Increasing pitch shortens the scan time and reduces motion artefact.
stems.explanation: Faster coverage of the same length, and less time in which the patient can move. Dose, time and motion artefact all fall together.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Increasing pitch reduces image noise.
stems.explanation: Noise rises — fewer projections contribute to each reconstructed slice. Raising pitch trades everything at once: dose and time down, noise and partial volume up.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Partial volume artefact is reduced by increasing the pitch.
stems.explanation: The reverse — more averaging between rotations, and the interpolation broadens the slice profile. Partial volume is reduced by thinner slices, and is never eliminated.

title: Regarding chemical shift artefact in MRI

stems.label: A
stems.text: It appears along the frequency-encoding direction.
stems.explanation: Position along the readout axis is encoded by frequency, and fat resonates 3.5 ppm from water, so fat is mapped to the wrong pixel.

stems.label: B
stems.text: It appears along the phase-encoding direction.
stems.explanation: Frequency-encode direction, not phase. EPI is the single licensed exception; motion and truncation are the phase-encode artefacts.

stems.label: C
stems.text: It becomes more prominent as the static field strength is increased.
stems.explanation: The separation is fixed at 3.5 ppm, so in absolute terms it grows with B0: 220 Hz at 1.5 T, 440 Hz at 3 T.

stems.label: D
stems.text: It is reduced by increasing the receiver bandwidth.
stems.explanation: Wider bandwidth means more Hz per pixel, so a fixed frequency offset displaces fat by fewer pixels. The price is SNR, which falls as 1/√BW.

stems.label: E
stems.text: It is reduced by intravenous gadolinium.
stems.explanation: Gadolinium shortens T1 and T2. It cannot touch the fat-water resonant frequency separation, which is what causes the artefact. Asked in at least four recall years, always false.

title: Regarding metallic implants in the MR environment

stems.label: A
stems.text: Titanium implants align with the static magnetic field.
stems.explanation: Titanium is weakly paramagnetic, experiences negligible torque and does not align with B0, which is why many titanium implants are MR conditional.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Ferromagnetic objects experience a rotational force as well as attraction.
stems.explanation: They try to align with the field lines. Torque on a ferromagnetic aneurysm clip has caused at least one patient death, which is why implant screening is absolute.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Any metal object presents a projectile hazard in the fringe field.
stems.explanation: Only ferromagnetic materials - iron, nickel, cobalt - are strongly attracted. Diamagnetic materials, including most tissue, are weakly repelled.

stems.label: D
stems.text: An implant may be affected by both the static field and the RF pulses.
stems.explanation: Two mechanisms: B0 moves or rotates a ferromagnetic implant, while RF absorption heats the metal and burns adjacent tissue. Gradient switching adds vibration and heating by Lenz's law.

stems.label: E
stems.text: All cochlear implants are an absolute contraindication to MRI.
stems.explanation: Many modern cochlear implants are MR conditional and may be scanned under specified conditions. The word 'all' is what makes it false.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Decreasing the window width reduces the displayed contrast between small density differences.
stems.explanation: Backwards. A narrow window maps a small HU range across all the available grey levels, so small differences become visible — narrow window means high contrast.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The window width is the range of Hounsfield units covered by a structure.
stems.explanation: It is the range of HU displayed across the grey scale — an operator choice, with nothing to do with any structure's intrinsic range.

stems.label: C
stems.text: A narrow window is used when the density differences of interest are small.
stems.explanation: Small HU range spread over the whole grey scale, so small differences separate. Width is contrast; level is brightness.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Decreasing the display window width increases the noise recorded in the image.
stems.explanation: Display settings change nothing recorded. Noise may look more apparent in a narrow window, but the data are untouched — SNR is unaffected by display window width.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The window level determines the brightness of the displayed image.
stems.explanation: Level shifts brightness and tissue selection; it does not change contrast. Width = contrast, level = brightness.

title: Regarding scatter and photoelectric interactions at diagnostic photon energies

stems.label: A
stems.text: Raising the tube voltage from 80 to 120 kVp increases the proportion of interactions in the patient that are Compton rather than photoelectric.
stems.explanation: P(photoelectric) is proportional to Z³/E³ and collapses as mean photon energy rises, so the scatter share grows; more scatter is produced overall and the scatter fraction reaching the receptor rises with kVp. Note the sheets speak of relative dominance and of scatter rising — the bank's older wording, that Compton is simply less likely at 120 kV, is not supported.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Compton photons cannot be scattered through angles greater than 90°.
stems.explanation: Scatter certainly runs beyond 90°. File 17 §3 gives the direction as energy-dependent: at high kVp scatter is more forward-directed, so a greater proportion reaches the receptor; at low kV it is more back-directed, which is exactly why less of it reaches the receptor and contrast rises. Backscatter is not excluded — it is the low-kV norm.

title: Regarding Compton effect happens when energy is lower than electron binding energy

stems.label: A
stems.text: Compton effect happens when energy is lower than electron binding energy.
stems.explanation: Compton scatter involves a loosely bound outer-shell electron and is the dominant interaction in soft tissue at diagnostic energies.

title: Regarding scattered radiation in radiography and fluoroscopy

stems.label: A
stems.text: Scattered radiation deposits energy in the patient and staff, and is the dominant source of staff dose in fluoroscopy.
stems.explanation: Staff dose in fluoroscopy comes mostly from stray radiation: scatter off the patient — not the primary beam — is the dominant contribution. Hence lead aprons, thyroid collars, leaded glasses, table drapes, ceiling-suspended screens, and distance.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Scattered radiation reaching the receptor can be about ten times the primary in large-field trunk radiography.
stems.explanation: Contrast is degraded by the factor [1 + S/P], quoted 'up to 10 times', so S/P can approach 9–10:1. It is a 'can be', not a constant.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Scatter is reduced by collimating the beam.
stems.explanation: A smaller field irradiates a smaller volume, so less scatter is generated. The cheapest scatter control there is.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Scatter in abdominal radiography is reduced by increasing the tube current.
stems.explanation: More mA gives more primary and proportionally more scatter — the scatter fraction is unchanged.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Increasing the patient-to-receptor distance reduces the scatter reaching the receptor.
stems.explanation: The air gap technique: obliquely travelling scatter misses the receptor. The cost is a magnified image and more output.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Water has a CT number of 0 and air −1000.
stems.explanation: The two fixed points of the scale, by definition: CT number = 1000 × (μ − μwater) / μwater. 'Water is 100' and 'air is −100' are recycled falses — −100 is fat territory.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The CT number of fat is about −100.
stems.explanation: Fat sits conventionally at −50 to −100 HU. The ladder to hold: air −1000, lung −300 to −800, fat −50 to −100, water 0, white matter 20–30, grey matter 35–45, liver 40–50, muscle 40–60, bone >1000.

stems.label: C
stems.text: A pixel represents the average linear attenuation coefficient of its voxel, expressed relative to water.
stems.explanation: True as written. Include 'relative to water' when you answer — a strict examiner marks 'the CT number is the amount of attenuation' false for omitting the reference.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The CT number of a tissue is independent of the tube voltage.
stems.explanation: The attenuation coefficients of tissue and of water change differently with energy, so HU shifts with kVp — iodine most of all, K-edge 33 keV. It IS independent of mA, which changes photon number and never energy.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The CT number of a pixel is affected by slice thickness, surrounding anatomy and the reconstruction algorithm.
stems.explanation: All three. Slice thickness through partial volume averaging inside the voxel; surrounding anatomy through beam hardening along the ray from adjacent bone; the kernel because it changes the computed numbers. 'Determined only by physical density' is false — Z and energy matter too.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Beam hardening decreases CT numbers.
stems.explanation: The hardened beam is attenuated less than the reconstruction assumes, so HU is depressed — cupping centrally and along rays through bone. Dark bands or streaks between two dense objects are the paired appearance, and rib hardening can mimic a hepatic lesion.

stems.label: B
stems.text: CT artefacts increase at the edges of bone.
stems.explanation: Beam hardening, partial volume and streak all peak at abrupt high-attenuation boundaries; the posterior fossa between the petrous bones is the textbook example.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Ring artefact is caused by patient motion.
stems.explanation: It is caused by a faulty or miscalibrated detector element, which traces a circle as the gantry rotates in third-generation geometry. It occurs in multislice and in helical scanning — both denials are recycled falses.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Cone beam artefact is greatest at the centre of the rotation axis.
stems.explanation: On-axis structures are imaged correctly; the misregistration grows towards the periphery, where the wide beam crosses detector rows obliquely. Wide-detector scanners need cone-beam reconstruction algorithms for exactly this.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Dental fillings cause streak artefact.
stems.explanation: Dense metal creates inconsistent projections — beam hardening plus photon starvation, where some rays lose essentially all their photons. Fixes are metal-artefact-reduction algorithms, iterative reconstruction and higher kV.

title: Regarding radiation dose from CT examinations

stems.label: A
stems.text: The entrance surface dose from CT is higher than from plain radiography.
stems.explanation: CT's entrance dose is far above radiography's — a verified recall true.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Dose is distributed more uniformly around the patient in CT than in plain radiography.
stems.explanation: The tube irradiates from every angle through the rotation, so the dose is spread circumferentially rather than concentrated at one entrance surface.

stems.label: C
stems.text: A non-contrast CT head delivers a typical effective dose of 1–3 mSv.
stems.explanation: Head 1–3 mSv, brain alone often quoted 1–2.

stems.label: D
stems.text: A typical CT abdomen delivers an effective dose of 5–10 mSv.
stems.explanation: The set to memorise: head 1–3, abdomen 5–10, chest–abdomen–pelvis 12–15 mSv.

stems.label: E
stems.text: A CT abdomen–pelvis typically delivers about 4 mSv.
stems.explanation: 8 mSv is nearer. Fetal dose from a pelvic CT is ~20–30 mGy.

stems.label: A
stems.text: The effective dose from 1 g of bone is greater than the effective dose from 1 g of soft tissue.
stems.explanation: Effective dose is a whole-body construct — the sum of organ equivalent doses multiplied by their tissue weighting factors — so it is not defined per gram of tissue. Bone does absorb more energy per gram than soft tissue, but that is absorbed dose, not effective dose.

stems.label: B
stems.text: A controlled area must be designated wherever staff are likely to receive more than 1 mSv effective dose in a year.
stems.explanation: The designation threshold is 6 mSv effective dose, or 3/10 of any dose limit, or the need for special procedures to restrict exposure. The 1 mSv-likely tier is the supervised area, kept under review.

stems.label: C
stems.text: A controlled area must be designated wherever staff are likely to receive more than 3 mSv effective dose in a year.
stems.explanation: 3 mSv is a recycled distractor, as is 1 mSv. The trigger is 6 mSv effective, 3/10 of any dose limit, the need for special procedures, or a dose rate above 7.5 µSv/h averaged over the working day.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Dose records for classified workers must be kept until the worker dies.
stems.explanation: They are kept for 30 years from the last entry, and until the person is (or would be) 75. 'Kept until death' is the recall bank's False. Unclassified records are kept 2 years.

stems.label: E
stems.text: A worker must be classified if likely to exceed 6 mSv effective dose in a year.
stems.explanation: Classification is triggered at 6 mSv effective dose or 3/10 of any dose limit: 6 mSv effective, 15 mSv lens, 150 mSv skin and extremities. Note that 15 mSv for the lens is a statutory holdover, not 3/10 of the current 20 mSv limit.

title: Regarding the CT scanner and its beam

stems.label: A
stems.text: Pre-patient collimation is primarily employed to remove scattered radiation.
stems.explanation: The word 'primarily' settles it. Pre-patient collimation defines the z-axis beam width and limits the irradiated volume; scatter is removed post-patient by the anti-scatter septa standing on the detector array — the same logic as the gamma camera.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The primary function of the bow-tie filter is to reduce streak artefact from metal implants.
stems.explanation: The bow-tie has two real functions and metal streak is neither. Primarily it equalises transmitted intensity across the patient, controlling peripheral dose and matching the detector signal range; secondarily its thicker edges pre-harden the outer rays, reducing beam-hardening artefact.

stems.label: C
stems.text: The CT beam is more heavily filtered than that used in plain radiography.
stems.explanation: Heavy flat filtration pre-hardens the beam, plus the bow-tie; some modern scanners add a tin spectral filter as well.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The transmitted intensity is measured by an array of solid-state scintillation detectors.
stems.explanation: Scintillator (gadolinium oxysulphide, rare-earth ceramic or cadmium tungstate) glued to a photodiode, elements around 0.5 mm², QDE 80–90%, with negligible afterglow. Xenon gas detectors are obsolete.

stems.label: E
stems.text: A topogram is acquired with the tube stationary and is used to plan the scan.
stems.explanation: Tube parked at 12 o'clock for a frontal view or 3/9 o'clock for a lateral, table moving, narrowest collimation. It sets the scan range and drives tube-current modulation, which is why a poorly acquired topogram costs dose accuracy for the whole scan.

stems.label: A
stems.text: The main role of the collimator is to reject scatter.
stems.explanation: The collimator provides spatial localisation — it is the image-forming component, a lead honeycomb admitting only photons travelling along the hole axis. Scatter rejection is electronic, done by the pulse height analyser on energy. Collimator = where; PHA = whether.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Each crystal is viewed by more than one photomultiplier tube.
stems.explanation: One large NaI(Tl) crystal sits behind an array of 30–100 PMTs, optically coupled by light guide or grease; the scintillation's position is computed by weighting their outputs, the closer tube seeing more light. The same holds in PET, where each detector block is read by about four PMTs with position decoded from the light-sharing pattern.

stems.label: C
stems.text: More than one event can be detected by a gamma camera.
stems.explanation: Read as in rapid succession: dead time per event is short enough that high count rates and dynamic studies (renal, lymphatic, GI) are routine. Two photons arriving simultaneously are a different matter — their light sums to a false energy (pile-up) and the PHA rejects the event. Successive yes, simultaneous no.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The pulse height analyser window is typically set at plus or minus 10 per cent around the 140 keV photopeak.
stems.explanation: Approximately 126–154 keV. A wider window gains counts (sensitivity up) but accepts more scatter (contrast down); a narrower window is cleaner but slower. The window width therefore moves both sensitivity and contrast.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The field of view of a gamma camera is determined by the size of the collimator holes.
stems.explanation: Field of view is set by the crystal area, about 60 x 50 cm in a modern rectangular camera. Hole size sets resolution and sensitivity, nothing else.

title: Regarding patient dose in nuclear medicine

stems.label: A
stems.text: Rapid clearance of the radionuclide from an organ reduces the patient dose.
stems.explanation: Dose is committed by the activity resident in the body over time, and physical decay and biological clearance are the only exits — the effective half-life again, always shorter than either parent value. The faster an organ clears the tracer, the fewer transformations occur while it is still in the patient.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Beta emission increases the dose from a radionuclide.
stems.explanation: Particulate emission deposits its energy locally, in the patient, with zero imaging value. That is precisely why the ideal imaging radionuclide is a pure gamma emitter, and why Tc-99m's 140 keV gamma with no associated beta is the model.

stems.label: C
stems.text: A longer physical half-life increases patient dose.
stems.explanation: More nuclear transformations occur while the activity is still in the patient. The same logic makes an ideal half-life 4–6 hours: shorter than or equal to 1 hour is too short to stock or to image the biodistribution, and 12 or 24 hours is too long — dose rises.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Extending the acquisition time increases the dose to the patient.
stems.explanation: Scan duration changes nothing. The dose was determined at injection and is committed by the activity resident in the body; a longer acquisition only collects more of the photons already being emitted, which improves SNR.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Collimators with wider holes reduce patient dose.
stems.explanation: The collimator sits downstream of the patient — it only decides what you catch. Wider holes raise sensitivity and worsen resolution; the dose does not move.

stems.label: A
stems.text: PET detects positron annihilation occurring within the nucleus.
stems.explanation: The positron is emitted from the nucleus, travels a few millimetres through tissue losing energy by collisions, then annihilates with an electron outside it. The scanner detects the two 511 keV annihilation photons — never the positron itself. 'Both positrons and gamma radiation are detected' is likewise False.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Two-dimensional PET acquisition uses parallel-hole collimators.
stems.explanation: Coincidence detection is electronic collimation — no lead in the way, which is the source of PET's sensitivity advantage over SPECT. Old-style 2D PET did use thin annular septa between rings (that statement is True), but never gamma-camera-style parallel-hole collimators. Modern scanners are 3D, with septa retracted or absent.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Bismuth germanate is used in PET because its decay time is superior to that of sodium iodide.
stems.explanation: BGO wins on stopping power — dense and cheap, where NaI stops too little at 511 keV. Its decay time is its weakness: 300 ns against NaI's 230 ns, the slowest of the three. LSO/LYSO are the fast crystals at 40 ns, which is why time-of-flight is feasible with them and not with BGO.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Each annihilation yields two 511 keV photons emitted at approximately 180 degrees to one another.
stems.explanation: 511 keV is the electron rest mass, fixed by physics whatever the radionuclide — which is why gamma-camera crystals and collimators are the wrong tools at PET energies. Detecting both within a coincidence window of about 6–12 ns places the event on the line joining the two detectors.

stems.label: E
stems.text: PET spatial resolution is typically 4–6 mm and is limited by positron range.
stems.explanation: The image forms where the positron annihilates, not where it was emitted — a physical floor no detector can beat, with slight photon non-collinearity added. About 4 mm for PET against about 10 mm for SPECT. Resolution is best at the centre of the ring and degrades peripherally, so 'resolution is uniform across the image' is False.

stems.label: A
stems.text: F-18 has a half-life of approximately 110 minutes.
stems.explanation: 109–110 minutes, and that figure is the whole reason regional cyclotrons can supply hospitals off site. Most other PET nuclides — C-11, N-13, O-15 — live only minutes and need the cyclotron on site.

stems.label: B
stems.text: F-18 is produced in a generator.
stems.explanation: Cyclotron-produced, by proton bombardment making proton-rich nuclides. This is the standard half-right trap: the 110-minute half-life in the same stem is correct, the production route is not.

stems.label: C
stems.text: PET and CT data are acquired sequentially.
stems.explanation: The gantries are in series and the CT — used for attenuation correction and localisation — is acquired first, then the PET bed positions. Reverse this only on an emphatic 'always'.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The injected activity of FDG for an adult is typically 100 MBq.
stems.explanation: 250–350 MBq, given weight-based at 3–4 MBq/kg, with an ARSAC DRL of 400 MBq. Anchor it against the resulting dose: about 5–7 mSv from the FDG, 8 mSv at the DRL.

stems.label: E
stems.text: An uptake period of 60 minutes is allowed after injection.
stems.explanation: Sixty minutes, with the patient resting quietly to suppress muscle uptake, allows optimum lesion uptake — not 30 minutes, and not 'to prevent decay of F-18', since nothing meaningful decays between 30 and 60 minutes at a 110-minute half-life.

title: Regarding mr safety expert is usually a medical physicist

stems.label: A
stems.text: MR safety expert is usually a medical physicist.
stems.explanation: The MR Safety Expert is usually a medical physicist providing technical MR safety advice.

stems.label: A
stems.text: The MR controlled area is bounded by the 50 mT field contour.
stems.explanation: The controlled contour is 0.5 mT, the 5 gauss line — a factor of 100 out. 50 mT is not a recognised boundary.

stems.label: B
stems.text: An inner controlled area is defined by the 3 mT contour.
stems.explanation: Two contours are used: 0.5 mT (5 gauss) for the controlled area and 3 mT for the inner controlled area.

stems.label: C
stems.text: A whole-body SAR of 2 W/kg corresponds to a core temperature rise of about 0.5 °C.
stems.explanation: The paired SAR limits are 2 W/kg for 0.5 °C and 4 W/kg for 1.0 °C.

stems.label: D
stems.text: A whole-body SAR of 4 W/kg corresponds to a core temperature rise of about 1.0 °C.
stems.explanation: The upper limb of the same pair — twice the specific absorption rate, twice the temperature rise.

stems.label: E
stems.text: A magnet quench carries a risk of asphyxiation.
stems.explanation: The boiled-off cryogen displaces oxygen from the scan room — asphyxiation is the hazard of a quench.

title: Regarding radiofrequency shielding and cryogens in the MR scanner room

stems.label: A
stems.text: The Faraday cage limits the extent of the fringe field.
stems.explanation: The cage is an RF shield. The fringe field is limited by magnetic shielding coils, an entirely different thing.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The Faraday cage reduces the MR signal obtained from the patient.
stems.explanation: It keeps external radiofrequency out so it cannot corrupt the image. It does nothing to the signal generated inside it.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Failure of the Faraday cage produces zipper artefact.
stems.explanation: RF interference from room equipment or a failed cage appears as a line of alternating dark and light signal.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The main magnet is surrounded by cryogenic liquids.
stems.explanation: Clinical scanners are superconducting and held near absolute zero, at which the coils have no resistance and can carry the currents that make 1.5 or 3 T.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Liquid helium is a flammable hazard.
stems.explanation: Helium is inert and non-flammable. Its hazards are cold burns, pressure, and asphyxiation by oxygen displacement during a quench.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Molybdenum-68 is the parent radionuclide of technetium-99m.
stems.explanation: The parent is Mo-99, half-life 66 hours, itself a reactor fission product; 'Mo-68' is a corrupted distractor. Tc-99m (6 hours) is eluted from the Mo-99/alumina column, the parent outliving the daughter so it is continuously replenished in transient equilibrium.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Technetium-99m is produced in a cyclotron.
stems.explanation: It is generator-produced — washed off the Mo-99/alumina column with saline, typically each morning. Cyclotrons make the proton-rich nuclides: F-18 and I-123. Generator supply, cheap and on site, is much of why Tc-99m dominates.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Technetium-99m emits a gamma ray of 0.14 MeV.
stems.explanation: 0.14 MeV = 140 keV. It sits mid-range in the ideal window of 0.1–0.2 MeV: below that, photons are absorbed in the patient (dose, no signal); above it, they are hard to collimate and inefficiently detected. Watch the units — and note that '150 keV' is False.

stems.label: D
stems.text: It decays to a stable daughter.
stems.explanation: The exam-level answer is True. Tc-99m decays to Tc-99, which has a half-life of about 2 x 10^5 years — Farr's criterion is 'stable, or half-life far longer than a human lifespan', so effectively stable. A radioactive daughter would keep irradiating the patient after the picture is taken, which is why a stable daughter is on the ideal-agent list.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Technetium-99m decays by isomeric transition.
stems.explanation: A metastable nucleus drops to its ground state emitting a pure gamma ray: no particle, no change in Z or A — that is what 'isomeric' means. It does not decay by electron capture, and isomeric transition does not reduce the atomic number.

title: Regarding the specific absorption rate (SAR) in MRI

stems.label: A
stems.text: SAR increases approximately with the square of the flip angle.
stems.explanation: Larger RF pulses deposit more energy; SAR goes as (flip angle)². This is why FSE with a long echo train is a high-SAR sequence.

stems.label: B
stems.text: SAR is proportional to the square of the Larmor frequency.
stems.explanation: SAR goes as B0², and the Larmor frequency is proportional to B0, so 3 T scanning is far more SAR-limited than 1.5 T.

stems.label: C
stems.text: SAR is reduced by increasing the TR.
stems.explanation: Longer TR means fewer RF pulses per unit time, a lower duty cycle and therefore lower time-averaged SAR.

stems.label: D
stems.text: SAR is reduced by increasing the number of phase-encoding steps.
stems.explanation: Nor by thicker slices or a larger FOV. None of these change the RF power deposited per kilogram.

stems.label: E
stems.text: In normal operating mode the whole-body SAR limit is 2 W/kg.
stems.explanation: Normal mode 2 W/kg for a 0.5 °C rise; first level (controlled) mode 4 W/kg for 1.0 °C.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Spatial resolution is limited by the size of the detector elements.
stems.explanation: Resolution is set by detector element size and sampling, together with focal spot and kernel — smaller detector elements improve it.

stems.label: B
stems.text: A high-resolution CT technique raises in-plane resolution to 15 lp/mm.
stems.explanation: 15 lp/mm is film-screen mammography and is always false in CT. The sources split between 0.7 lp/mm and Farr's 10–16 lp/cm, with an accepted envelope of 0.5–2 lp/mm; never stray outside it. CT resolution is coarse next to radiography — its win is contrast.

stems.label: C
stems.text: A smaller focal spot improves spatial resolution.
stems.explanation: Geometric unsharpness, the plain-radiography rule applied inside the gantry.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Reducing the scan time improves spatial resolution.
stems.explanation: It reduces motion artefact — a different currency. Increasing slice thickness, by contrast, worsens z-resolution through partial volume.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Interpolating a 512×512 image to 1024×1024 improves spatial resolution.
stems.explanation: Interpolation happens after acquisition; resolution was fixed by detector sampling. Smaller-looking pixels, the same information.

stems.label: A
stems.text: The reconstructed slice width can never exceed the width of one detector row.
stems.explanation: Detector row width sets the MINIMUM attainable slice thickness in MDCT, not the maximum — adjacent rows are combined to give thicker slices, and the collimator sets the total beam width covering the whole detector bank.

stems.label: B
stems.text: In MDCT, slice thickness is determined by the collimator width.
stems.explanation: It is set by the detector element width along z. The collimator defines the total beam width across the whole detector bank. Single-slice CT was the era in which the collimator set slice width.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Quarter-detector offset is used to increase transaxial resolution.
stems.explanation: The detector array is offset from the focal-spot axis by a quarter of a detector width, so opposing 180° projections interleave and the effective sampling frequency doubles.

stems.label: D
stems.text: MDCT inherently delivers a lower dose than single-slice CT.
stems.explanation: MDCT suffers overbeaming (penumbra wasted beyond the outer detector rows) and overranging (extra half-rotations at each end of a helical run), so it is not inherently lower-dose. Dose is also not proportional to the number of detector rows.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Helical scanning permits single-breath-hold acquisition and multiphase contrast studies.
stems.explanation: The two clinical wins: no slice misregistration from breathing, and pre-contrast, arterial, venous and delayed phases from one setup. Note that acquisition is not started simultaneously with the injection — a delay lets the bolus reach the target phase.

title: Regarding attenuation of ultrasound in tissue

stems.label: A
stems.text: The attenuation coefficient of soft tissue is approximately 15 dB/cm/MHz.
stems.explanation: Soft tissue is 0.5-1.0 dB/cm/MHz, average about 0.7. 15 dB/cm at 1 MHz is bone - the quoted figure is out by an order of magnitude.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The attenuation coefficient of lung exceeds 30 dB/cm at 1 MHz.
stems.explanation: Lung is about 40 dB/cm at 1 MHz, the highest in the body. Water at about 0.002 is the other extreme, which is why a full bladder makes an acoustic window.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Attenuation is mainly due to reflection and scattering at boundaries.
stems.explanation: Mainly absorption - frictional, viscous and molecular relaxation processes converting the beam to heat. That is why most transmitted energy ends up as heat in the patient and why absorption dominates thermal safety.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The intensity of the beam falls exponentially with depth.
stems.explanation: A fixed fraction is removed per cm, which is exactly why attenuation is quoted in dB - logarithmic and additive.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Attenuation is proportional to the acoustic impedance of the tissue.
stems.explanation: No link between the two. Bone happens to be high in both, but lung has low impedance and the highest attenuation of all - lung breaks any assumed correlation.

title: Regarding acoustic impedance and reflection at tissue interfaces

stems.label: A
stems.text: Acoustic impedance is the product of tissue density and the speed of sound in that tissue.
stems.explanation: Z = rho.c, measured in Rayls. It is an intrinsic tissue property: nothing about the probe, the frequency or tissue motion changes it.

stems.label: B
stems.text: A large difference in acoustic impedance between two tissues produces more reflection.
stems.explanation: R = [(Z1-Z2)/(Z1+Z2)]^2. Soft tissue to soft tissue reflects about 1%, muscle to bone about 30%, tissue to air about 99.9%.

stems.label: C
stems.text: More energy is reflected at a bone-muscle interface than at a muscle-fluid interface.
stems.explanation: Muscle-bone reflects about 30%; a soft tissue to fluid interface is well under 1%. A stem claiming 15% reflects at a tissue-fluid interface is false.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Reflection occurs wherever there is a difference in tissue density.
stems.explanation: Precision trap: reflection needs a difference in impedance (rho.c), not density alone. Two tissues of different density but matched Z reflect nothing.

stems.label: E
stems.text: At least 5% of the incident energy must be reflected for a boundary to be detected.
stems.explanation: Reflected intensities of 1% or less produce perfectly detectable signals - nearly the whole image is made of them.

title: Regarding the speed of ultrasound in tissue

stems.label: A
stems.text: The scanner assumes a propagation speed of 1540 m/s in soft tissue.
stems.explanation: 1540 m/s is the average the scanner assumes for every depth calculation. Real soft tissue spans about 1300-1800 m/s, so figures such as 150 m/s or 1240 m/s are false.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Ultrasound travels faster in muscle than in bone.
stems.explanation: Bone is about 3000-4000 m/s against muscle at about 1580 m/s - more than double. Speed rises with stiffness, and bone is by far the stiffer.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Ultrasound travels faster in muscle than in fat.
stems.explanation: Muscle about 1580 m/s, fat about 1450 m/s. Muscle is denser and stiffer, and stiffness wins.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The speed of sound is inversely proportional to the compressibility of the medium.
stems.explanation: Close but not exact, and the exam wants the exactness: c = 1/sqrt(k.rho), an inverse square-root relation, not inverse proportionality. More compressible means slower, which is why fat is slow and bone fast.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The velocity of ultrasound depends on its frequency.
stems.explanation: c is a property of the medium, c = sqrt(stiffness/density), essentially frequency-independent in tissue. The medium sets c and the probe sets f, so raising the operating frequency changes wavelength, not speed.

title: Regarding the mechanical index in ultrasound

stems.label: A
stems.text: The mechanical index estimates the risk of cavitation.
stems.explanation: Cavitation - bubble oscillation and collapse driven by the peak rarefaction pressure - is the non-thermal harm mechanism, and MI is the index that tracks it.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The mechanical index is the peak rarefactional pressure divided by the square root of the frequency.
stems.explanation: MI = peak negative pressure / sqrt(f), so MI falls as frequency rises. Low frequency is the dangerous end for cavitation.

stems.label: C
stems.text: The mechanical index warns the operator about non-thermal effects rather than heating.
stems.explanation: MI has nothing to do with heating - a stem saying MI is calculated from tissue heating is false. Two harm mechanisms, two indices: thermal is TI, mechanical is MI.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The mechanical index is influenced by tissue perfusion.
stems.explanation: Perfusion belongs to the thermal side of safety - blood flow carries heat away. MI is not perfusion-related.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The thermal index is derived from the mechanical index.
stems.explanation: They are independent. TI is emitted power divided by the power needed to raise temperature by 1 degree C; MI is peak rarefactional pressure over the square root of frequency.

title: Regarding filtration of the diagnostic X-ray beam

stems.label: A
stems.text: Added filtration reduces the intensity of the beam.
stems.explanation: Photons are removed, so intensity falls — but the half-value layer rises, because what is removed is the low-energy end. Splitting that pair is the whole point of the question.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Filtration reduces patient skin dose.
stems.explanation: The soft photons it removes would have been absorbed in skin without ever reaching the receptor.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Beam filtration improves image contrast.
stems.explanation: Hardening the beam cuts the photoelectric fraction and therefore differential attenuation, so subject contrast falls: filtration trades contrast for dose. Do not confuse this with K-edge filtration in mammography, which narrows the spectrum and does improve contrast.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Added filtration of 0.5 mm Al is sufficient for a general radiographic tube.
stems.explanation: Total filtration must exceed 2.5 mm Al equivalent above 70 kVp (1.5 mm Al below 70 kVp); inherent filtration alone is only ~0.5–1.0 mm Al equivalent, so 0.5 mm added is nowhere near sufficient.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Filtration is used to limit the dynamic range of the detector.
stems.explanation: Filtration shapes beam quality and cuts dose. The one shaped-filter exception — the CT bow-tie, which does equalise detector signal — is not what this statement describes.

title: Regarding beam quality and added filtration

stems.label: A
stems.text: A beryllium tube window is used when the kVp is less than 50.
stems.explanation: Mammography runs at 25–35 kVp, and beryllium barely attenuates the low-energy photons that carry glandular–adipose contrast.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Added filtration reduces the maximum photon energy in the beam.
stems.explanation: Maximum photon energy equals the tube voltage, full stop. Filtration raises the mean energy by cutting the low end; it cannot touch the top end.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Inherent filtration is typically equivalent to 2 mm Al.
stems.explanation: Inherent filtration — tube window, oil, housing — is ~0.5–1.0 mm Al equivalent. 2.5 mm Al is the figure that total filtration must exceed.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Increasing amounts of aluminium filtration are required at higher tube voltages.
stems.explanation: Higher kVp widens the energy range, so more filtration is needed to lift the minimum energy: 1.5 mm Al below 70 kVp, 2.5 mm Al above.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Increasing added filtration improves spatial resolution.
stems.explanation: Filtration alters the spectrum only. Contrast and dose change; resolution is set by focal spot, geometry and detector.

stems.label: A
stems.text: The imaging plate is made of caesium iodide.
stems.explanation: CR uses a photostimulable storage phosphor — europium-doped barium fluorohalide (BaFX:Eu / BaFBr:Eu). Caesium iodide is the scintillator of indirect DR and the input phosphor of an image intensifier, and sodium iodide is the gamma-camera crystal. Three materials, three modalities: keep them apart and this whole family of stems falls.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The plate is read with a red laser and the phosphor emits blue light.
stems.explanation: A rotating mirror scans a red laser across the plate; the trapped electrons are released and emit blue photostimulated luminescence, which a light guide collects into a photomultiplier tube. Red in, blue out — Farr's is explicit, and the reversed version ('scanned with a blue laser') is a classic direction-reversal trap.

stems.label: C
stems.text: The imaging plate consists of a matrix of individual detector elements.
stems.explanation: The phosphor is a continuous, unstructured layer. Pixels exist only because the laser samples the plate discretely at readout. That is also why CR needs no per-element gain calibration, unlike DR — correcting for non-uniformity of the detector is a DR requirement, not a CR one.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Any residual latent image is removed by exposure to high-intensity white light.
stems.explanation: That is the erasure step after readout. Skip it or let it fail and the previous image persists as the ghost artefact. Note too that the plate is sensitive to any ionising radiation, so plates left unused accumulate background fog and should be erased before use.

stems.label: E
stems.text: CR spatial resolution of about 4 lp/mm is better than film-screen.
stems.explanation: The number is right and the comparison is wrong. CR gives about 3.5–5.5 lp/mm (90 micron pixels on small plates give 5.5 lp/mm, 140 micron on large plates 3.5 lp/mm, so smaller plates resolve better), while film-screen manages 8–12 lp/mm. Digital wins on dynamic range, processing and dose — never on limiting spatial resolution.

title: Regarding digital radiography: matrix, pixel and image quality

stems.label: A
stems.text: Changing from a 512 × 512 to a 1024 × 1024 matrix doubles the storage required.
stems.explanation: It quadruples it — pixel count scales with area, not with the side of the matrix.

stems.label: B
stems.text: For a fixed field of view, a larger matrix improves spatial resolution.
stems.explanation: More pixels across the same field of view means smaller pixels and finer sampling. Enlarge the matrix and the FOV together and pixel size — and resolution — are unchanged, so check the stem for a stated FOV.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Spatial resolution increases with pixel depth.
stems.explanation: Pixel depth is the number of grey levels a pixel can record — contrast resolution. Only pixel size affects spatial resolution.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Structures smaller than the pixel size cannot be detected.
stems.explanation: A high-contrast structure smaller than a pixel is still visible; it occupies one pixel with reduced contrast (partial volume averaging). Detection is not resolution.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Increasing the number of photons recorded per pixel improves the signal-to-noise ratio.
stems.explanation: Quantum noise falls as 1/√N: more detected photons, less mottle.

stems.label: A
stems.text: The imaging plate is read by scanning it with a laser.
stems.explanation: A rotating mirror sweeps a red laser across the plate; trapped electrons are released and emit blue photostimulated luminescence, collected by a light guide into a photomultiplier tube.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The imaging plate consists of a matrix of individual detector elements.
stems.explanation: The photostimulable phosphor (BaFX:Eu) is a continuous, unstructured layer. Pixels exist only because the laser samples the plate discretely at readout — which is also why CR, unlike DR, needs no per-element gain calibration.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Automatic exposure control is still used with CR despite its wide dynamic range.
stems.explanation: That wide range hides overexposure — dose creep — because the image still looks fine. Detector dose indicators exist for the same reason.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The plate is scanned with a blue laser to release the stored energy.
stems.explanation: Backwards: red laser in, blue light out, because most phosphors release blue light. A classic direction-reversal trap.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Any residual latent image is removed by exposure to high-intensity white light.
stems.explanation: The erasure step after readout. Skip or fail it and the next exposure carries a ghost artefact.

title: Regarding effective dose and radiation risk

stems.label: A
stems.text: An effective dose of 1 mSv corresponds to a fatal cancer risk of approximately 1 in 20,000.
stems.explanation: The master risk conversion, scaled linearly: 6 mSv gives roughly 1 in 3,300 and 10 mSv roughly 1 in 2,000.

stems.label: B
stems.text: An effective dose of 1 mSv corresponds to a risk of hereditary effects of approximately 1 in 10,000.
stems.explanation: A recycled False. Hereditary risk is much lower than the fatal cancer risk, which is the 1 in 20,000 per mSv figure.

stems.label: C
stems.text: An effective dose of 1 mSv corresponds to a fatal cancer risk of approximately 1 in 300.
stems.explanation: Another recycled False from the same stem family. The figure is 1 in 20,000 per mSv.

stems.label: D
stems.text: An effective dose of 10 mSv corresponds to a fatal cancer risk of approximately 1 in 2,000.
stems.explanation: Straight arithmetic on the 1 in 20,000 per mSv conversion.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Effective dose is a reliable indicator of the fetal dose in a pregnant patient.
stems.explanation: Effective dose is the mother's whole-body stochastic risk. Fetal dose is the equivalent dose to the uterus. Two different questions wearing one stem — one of the nine statements missed on both attempts at the same mock.

title: Regarding SAR is proptional to square of larmor frequency

stems.label: A
stems.text: SAR is proptional to square of larmor frequency.
stems.explanation: SAR ∝ (Larmor frequency)² and (flip angle)². True: Larmor frequency is proportional to B0, and SAR rises strongly with field strength.

title: Regarding susceptibility ('lens' or metal) artefact in MRI

stems.label: A
stems.text: It becomes worse as the static field strength increases.
stems.explanation: Field distortions scale with B0, so metal artefact is worse at 3 T than at 1.5 T.

stems.label: B
stems.text: It makes the affected region appear brighter.
stems.explanation: The appearance is signal loss, blooming and geometric distortion, not brightening. The recall bank asks the field-strength half and the brightness half as separate statements.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Signal void around a metallic implant is more likely with gradient echo than with spin echo.
stems.explanation: GRE has no 180 degree pulse to undo static dephasing, so susceptibility is expressed in full. Farr's advises avoiding GRE and EPI where metal sits in the FOV.

stems.label: D
stems.text: It is reduced by increasing the receiver bandwidth.
stems.explanation: The listed fixes are reduce TE, increase receiver bandwidth, use a lower field strength, and use STIR near metal.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Spectral fat saturation is preferred to STIR for fat suppression near metal.
stems.explanation: The reverse. STIR nulls by T1 and tolerates field inhomogeneity; spectral fat sat depends on clean separation of the fat and water peaks and fails near metal.

title: Regarding Doppler modes and duplex scanning

stems.label: A
stems.text: Duplex scanning combines B-mode imaging with pulsed Doppler.
stems.explanation: B-mode plus pulsed Doppler is duplex; adding colour makes it triplex.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Duplex scanning combines M-mode with Doppler.
stems.explanation: The pairing is with B-mode. M-mode is one line sampled at very high rate and displayed against time - the highest temporal resolution, used for valves and the fetal heart.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Continuous wave Doppler has no depth discrimination.
stems.explanation: One element always transmits and another always receives, so echoes from every depth along the line superimpose. Pulsed wave adds a range gate, opening the receive window at 2 x depth / c, and inherits aliasing in exchange.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Both the amplitude and the direction of flow can be assessed with power Doppler.
stems.explanation: Power Doppler shows amplitude only - no speed and no direction - but is more sensitive to slow flow and nearly angle-independent. Colour Doppler is the one carrying mean velocity and direction.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Doppler requires a higher transmitted frequency than B-mode imaging.
stems.explanation: The same 2-15 MHz range serves both, with continuous wave Doppler probes typically 2-10 MHz according to vessel depth.

stems.label: A
stems.text: A 90 degree RF excitation pulse is used.
stems.explanation: 90 degree excitation, then refocusing. Both halves have been asked separately and repeatedly in the recall bank.

stems.label: B
stems.text: A 180 degree refocusing pulse is applied at TE/2.
stems.explanation: The 180 degree pulse reverses dephasing caused by static field inhomogeneity, so spin echo contrast is governed by true T2.

stems.label: C
stems.text: T2* effects can be obtained with conventional spin echo.
stems.explanation: The 180 degree pulse cancels the static-inhomogeneity dephasing that T2* consists of. For T2* contrast - susceptibility, blood products, iron, calcium - you need gradient echo.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The echo appears at a time TE after the 180 degree pulse.
stems.explanation: TE is measured from the 90 degree pulse. Since the 180 sits at TE/2, the echo forms TE/2 after it.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Increasing the number of phase-encoding steps increases the TE.
stems.explanation: More phase steps lengthen the scan time and improve resolution along the phase axis. TE is set independently.

title: Regarding the ultrasound transducer and its coupling to tissue

stems.label: A
stems.text: The probe transmits ultrasound into air more efficiently than into soft tissue.
stems.explanation: The tissue-air mismatch reflects about 99.9%, which is why coupling gel is essential and why bowel gas shadows.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The probe surface reaches a higher temperature when the transducer is run in air than when it is in contact with tissue.
stems.explanation: The energy has nowhere to go, so it stays in the probe. The IEC surface limits reflect this: 50 degrees C in air against 43 degrees C on tissue.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Approximately 99.9% of the beam is reflected at a tissue-air interface.
stems.explanation: The benchmark set to memorise: tissue to tissue about 1%, muscle to bone about 30%, tissue to air about 99.9%.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The matching layer has an acoustic impedance intermediate between the crystal and tissue.
stems.explanation: PZT's impedance is so high that fired straight into tissue about 80% would reflect. The layer is chosen at Z = sqrt(Zcrystal x Ztissue) and its thickness tuned to a quarter wavelength to maximise transmission.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The backing block lengthens the emitted pulse.
stems.explanation: It damps the ringing, so the pulse dies quickly - a shorter pulse, broader bandwidth, lower Q and better axial resolution, at the cost of output. Continuous wave probes, wanting a single pure frequency, are air-backed instead.

title: Regarding pulsed Doppler ultrasound and aliasing

stems.label: A
stems.text: The Nyquist limit is equal to half the pulse repetition frequency.
stems.explanation: PRF is the sampling rate, and the maximum frequency that can be sampled unambiguously is PRF/2.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Increasing the PRF raises the maximum Doppler shift that can be displayed without aliasing.
stems.explanation: Raise the sampling rate and the Nyquist limit, PRF/2, rises with it.

stems.label: C
stems.text: The magnitude of the Doppler shift depends on the PRF.
stems.explanation: PRF samples the shift; it never creates it. This one beat you on both mock attempts and was re-asked in the March 2026 paper.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The Doppler shift depends on the diameter of the vessel insonated.
stems.explanation: Vessel size is not in fD = 2f0v·cosθ/c, alongside intensity and PRF.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Pulsed Doppler produces the highest acoustic output of the ultrasound modes.
stems.explanation: Beam dwell, long pulses and high PRF together give the highest ISPTA. Answer this TRUE even where memory of the recall says otherwise.

title: Regarding frequency and wavelength in diagnostic ultrasound

stems.label: A
stems.text: Diagnostic imaging uses ultrasound frequencies of 2-15 MHz.
stems.explanation: Sound above 20 kHz is ultrasound; the diagnostic band is 2-15 MHz, with continuous wave Doppler probes typically 2-10 MHz.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Ultrasound wavelengths in soft tissue across the diagnostic range are about 0.1-1.5 mm.
stems.explanation: Lambda = c/f = 1540/f: 1.5 mm at 1 MHz falling to 0.1 mm at 15 MHz. A stem quoting 1-5 mm is false - do the division in your head.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Raising the transmitted frequency improves spatial resolution.
stems.explanation: Shorter wavelength shortens the pulse, improving axial resolution, and narrows the beam, improving lateral resolution. Spatial resolution improves with frequency across the board.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Raising the transmitted frequency increases the depth of penetration.
stems.explanation: The trade-off runs the other way. Attenuation rises with frequency, so penetration falls; the rule of thumb is penetration of about 40/f cm.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Attenuation of ultrasound in soft tissue is independent of frequency.
stems.explanation: It rises roughly linearly with frequency - the defining trade-off of the whole modality. Higher frequency means better resolution, less penetration and more heating.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Flip angles of less than 90 degrees are frequently used.
stems.explanation: A small flip leaves residual longitudinal magnetisation, so less recovery time is needed and TR can be very short.

stems.label: B
stems.text: A 180 degree RF pulse is applied to produce the echo.
stems.explanation: A bipolar readout gradient does the job: a negative lobe to dephase, a positive lobe to rephase, along the frequency-encode axis.

stems.label: C
stems.text: They generate T2-weighted images.
stems.explanation: They generate T2*-weighted images. Gradient reversal cannot undo dephasing from main-field inhomogeneity and susceptibility, so those contribute to the decay by design.

stems.label: D
stems.text: They show more artefact than spin echo in the presence of main field inhomogeneity.
stems.explanation: Same cause, no refocusing pulse. Susceptibility and metal artefacts are markedly worse on GRE.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Field inhomogeneities affect T2 more than T2*.
stems.explanation: Backwards. T2* is defined as including inhomogeneity dephasing; true T2 is a tissue property unaffected by it.

title: Regarding TR, TE and weighting in MRI

stems.label: A
stems.text: TR is shorter than TE.
stems.explanation: Every weighting pair on the numbers page has TR far longer than TE: T1w TE <30 ms with TR 300–800 ms; T2w TE >80 ms with TR >2000 ms. The echo has to happen before the next excitation.

stems.label: B
stems.text: A TE of 120 ms with a long TR gives a T2-weighted image.
stems.explanation: Long TE with a long TR is the classic T2-weighted regime. The verified parameters: T1w TE <30 ms, TR 300–800 ms; T2w TE >80 ms, TR >2000 ms. TE 120 ms sits well inside the T2w band.

title: Regarding the bow-tie filter in CT

stems.label: A
stems.text: Its primary function is to equalise the transmitted intensity across the patient.
stems.explanation: The periphery attenuates less than the centre, so the shaped filter evens out the transmitted intensity across the patient. It is also the one shaped-filter exception that does equalise detector signal.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Its primary function is to harden the beam.
stems.explanation: Two functions, one primary. The thicker edges do pre-harden the outer rays, but the primary purpose is to equalise intensity across the patient — this is the statement the owner got right first time and talked himself out of on the retest.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Its progressively thicker edges pre-harden the peripheral rays.
stems.explanation: The second of the bow-tie's two real functions: 'it also pre-hardens the outer rays — two functions, one primary'. File 17 §2 says the same, that CT uses heavier filtration plus a shaped bow-tie to pre-harden the beam and equalise transmitted intensity. Learn both, not a letter.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Lower filtration is used for CT than for general radiography.
stems.explanation: CT uses heavier flat filtration plus the shaped bow-tie, to pre-harden the beam and equalise transmitted intensity across the patient.

title: Regarding CT number and photoelectric attenuation

stems.label: A
stems.text: The CT number of a tissue is independent of the tube voltage.
stems.explanation: The sorting rule is flat: HU moves with kVp, never with mA. Iodine shifts most — K-edge 33 keV — which is why low-kV scanning boosts iodine contrast.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The CT number of a tissue is independent of the tube current.
stems.explanation: The other half of the same rule: HU moves with kVp, never with mA. More mA buys photons — SNR rises as √mAs — so it changes noise, not the measured attenuation.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Photoelectric attenuation is strongly dependent on atomic number and photon energy.
stems.explanation: Photoelectric probability ∝ ρZ³/E³ — it collapses as mean photon energy rises, which is why raising kVp cuts the photoelectric share, and why K-edge effects matter (iodine 33 keV, low kV boosts iodine).

stems.label: A
stems.text: The subtraction process increases the random noise content of the image.
stems.explanation: The noise variances of mask and live image add, so noise rises by about √2 while vessel signal is unchanged: SNR falls and quantum mottle increases. Both bank wordings — 'SNR is increased after subtraction' and 'quantum mottle decreases in the subtracted image' — are therefore false.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The subtracted image has better spatial resolution than the unsubtracted image.
stems.explanation: Subtraction improves contrast and the conspicuity of contrast-filled vessels. It cannot exceed the intrinsic detector resolution, and misregistration can make it worse.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Patient dose in DSA is higher than in conventional angiography.
stems.explanation: Acquisition frames are high-dose and the runs are added on top of screening time, so total dose is high.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The mask image is subtracted from the contrast-filled image.
stems.explanation: That direction, not the reverse. The mask is the pre-contrast image, histogram-normalised and stored; several masks can be held for different table positions.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Logarithmic subtraction is used to eliminate the effect of overlying and underlying tissues.
stems.explanation: Attenuation is exponential with depth; the log transform makes it additive, so subtraction cancels background independent of tissue thickness.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Iterative reconstruction permits a reduction in patient dose.
stems.explanation: The accepted exam reading: iterative reconstruction suppresses noise so well that the same image quality arrives from lower acquisition parameters. Pedantically the reconstruction happens after the exposure — the saving is in what the protocol can get away with. 'Iterative is used exclusively' is false; FBP remains in routine use.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Filtered back-projection is faster than iterative reconstruction and gives sharper edges.
stems.explanation: FBP is computationally simple and fast, and classic iterative reconstruction smooths slightly in exchange for its noise suppression. Answer it this way for a classic-IR framing; modern model-based IR can match or beat FBP resolution.

stems.label: C
stems.text: A bone (sharp) reconstruction kernel increases image noise.
stems.explanation: Sharp kernels preserve high spatial frequencies, and noise lives there. One dial, two readouts — the kernel changes both SNR and transaxial resolution.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The filter in filtered back-projection removes low-energy photons from the beam.
stems.explanation: The FBP filter is a mathematical convolution kernel applied to the projection data. Physical filtration happened at the tube, before the patient.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Filtered back-projection handles metal and beam-hardening artefacts better than iterative reconstruction.
stems.explanation: The other way round — iterative reconstruction can build corrections for those effects into the loop. Both techniques remain equally vulnerable to patient motion.

title: Regarding aliasing in pulsed Doppler ultrasound

stems.label: A
stems.text: Aliasing can occur at physiological blood velocities.
stems.explanation: Farr's worked example: 30 cm/s at 10 MHz gives a shift of about 4 kHz, needing a PRF of at least 8 kHz - unattainable beyond about 9.6 cm depth. Normal arteries alias routinely at depth, stenotic jets more so.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The maximum detectable frequency shift is half the pulse repetition frequency.
stems.explanation: The Nyquist limit. You must sample at least twice per cycle of the shift being measured, so the sampling frequency must be at least twice the Doppler shift.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Increasing the pulse repetition frequency raises the Nyquist limit.
stems.explanation: Nyquist = PRF/2, so raising PRF - the scale control - is the first fix for aliasing. Maximum PRF is itself capped by depth: PRFmax = c/2d, about 13 microseconds per cm of round trip.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Aliasing occurs in continuous wave Doppler.
stems.explanation: No pulses, no sampling, no Nyquist limit. Aliasing belongs exclusively to pulsed and colour Doppler; continuous wave is the escape route for high velocities.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Increasing the angle of insonation makes aliasing more likely.
stems.explanation: A larger angle gives a smaller cos(theta) and so a smaller measured shift - it reduces aliasing. The other fixes are a higher PRF, a lower transmit frequency, shifting the baseline, or switching to continuous wave.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Image sharpness improves as the focal spot is made smaller.
stems.explanation: Penumbra = focal spot size × (OID / FOD). The penumbra is the projection of the finite focal spot, so a smaller spot gives a smaller penumbra.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Reducing the object-to-receptor distance reduces unsharpness.
stems.explanation: A smaller OID means less magnification and a smaller penumbra, which is why the receptor is placed as close to the patient as possible in routine radiography.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Increasing the focus-to-patient distance improves sharpness.
stems.explanation: A longer focus-to-patient distance lowers the ratio OID/FOD and so shrinks the penumbra. The ideal set-up minimises focal spot, maximises focus-detector distance and minimises object-detector distance.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Inserting a grid between patient and receptor improves sharpness.
stems.explanation: Grids act on scatter: they buy contrast and pay for it in dose. They never change spatial resolution.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Increasing the tube voltage improves sharpness.
stems.explanation: kVp changes which interactions occur — contrast and dose — but has no effect on spatial resolution.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Increasing the tube current (mA) improves spatial resolution.
stems.explanation: Not in isolation. Geometric unsharpness is nothing more than the penumbra cast by a finite focal spot: penumbra = focal spot size x (OID/FOD), and mA appears nowhere in that equation. A higher mA could permit a shorter exposure and so less motion blur, but only if the stem says exposure time changes.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Image sharpness is improved by increasing the focus-to-patient distance.
stems.explanation: Increasing FSD reduces the penumbra, because the ratio OID/FOD falls.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Image sharpness is improved by increasing the focal spot size.
stems.explanation: The penumbra is the projection of the finite focal spot: bigger spot, bigger penumbra. The ideal set-up minimises focal spot size, maximises focus-detector distance and minimises object-detector distance.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Decreasing the patient-to-receptor distance improves spatial resolution.
stems.explanation: A smaller OID means less magnification and a smaller penumbra, which is why the receptor is placed as close to the patient as possible in routine radiography.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Image sharpness is improved by inserting a grid between the patient and the receptor.
stems.explanation: Grids act on scatter, so they change contrast, not spatial resolution. Grids never touch resolution.

stems.label: A
stems.text: In-plane (X-Y) spatial resolution is better than that of full-field digital mammography.
stems.explanation: Farr's gives X-Y resolution as comparable to full-field digital mammography, 100-280 micrometres. The gain is in the z-axis, not in the plane, so under the usual 'spatial resolution' reading the statement is false.

stems.label: B
stems.text: It can separate structures lying above and below a lesion.
stems.explanation: Z-axis resolution is increased, which is precisely what allows depth separation of overlying from underlying tissue. The tube sweeps an arc to obtain the projections that make this possible.

stems.label: C
stems.text: The reconstructed voxels are isotropic.
stems.explanation: Farr's describes anisotropic voxels: X-Y resolution matches FFDM at 100-280 micrometres while the depth information comes from a limited-angle sweep. Isotropic resolution would require equal dimensions in all three axes.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The tube sweeps through an arc of 15-50 degrees.
stems.explanation: That is the quoted sweep angle; the limited arc is why depth resolution improves but in-plane resolution does not.

stems.label: E
stems.text: High-density objects such as surgical clips produce a blurring ripple artefact.
stems.explanation: Few projections are acquired, so high-density objects appear wider with ripples equal in number to the projections, running perpendicular to the tube sweep. Iterative reconstruction makes it less marked.

title: Regarding mammography and digital breast tomosynthesis:

stems.label: A
stems.text: Compression reduces the amount of scattered radiation.
stems.explanation: Compression thins the tissue, so fewer scattering events occur — the same principle whether the part compressed is the breast or the abdomen. It also cuts dose and geometric unsharpness. Compare this with the other scatter levers: collimation reduces scatter (smaller irradiated volume), an air gap keeps obliquely travelling scatter off the receptor, and raising mA does not change the scatter fraction at all.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Breast compression improves both contrast and spatial resolution.
stems.explanation: Compression at 100–150 N equalises breast thickness, brings lesions closer to the receptor (less geometric unsharpness), reduces scatter, and reduces both dose and movement unsharpness. It does everything — which is why it is worth the discomfort.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Tomosynthesis improves spatial resolution in the X-Y plane compared with full-field digital mammography.
stems.explanation: In-plane (X-Y) resolution is comparable to full-field digital mammography at 100–280 microns. Under the usual 'spatial resolution' reading the statement is marked False — but read which axis the stem means, because the Z axis is a different answer.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Tomosynthesis increases resolution along the Z axis, allowing structures at different depths to be separated.
stems.explanation: This is what the technique buys. A series of low-dose projections acquired across the tube sweep is reconstructed into anisotropic voxels with increased Z-axis resolution, so overlapping tissues at different depths can be separated — quasi-three-dimensional data rather than one superimposed projection. The price is a set of characteristic artefacts: blurring ripple around high-density objects such as clips and markers, with as many ripples as there were projections, perpendicular to the tube sweep.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The tube sweep angle in tomosynthesis is typically 15-50 degrees.
stems.explanation: 15-50 degrees is the quoted range. It is a limited-angle technique, which is exactly why the depth resolution is coarse compared with the in-plane resolution and why only a few projections are available to reconstruct from.

title: Regarding increasing radius of conductive area increases current

stems.label: A
stems.text: Increasing radius of conductive area increases current.
stems.explanation: For a conductor of fixed length and resistivity, resistance falls as cross sectional area increases, so current rises for a fixed voltage.

stems.label: A
stems.text: 1 cGy*cm2 = 1 µGy*m2.
stems.explanation: Because 1 cGy equals 10,000 µGy and 1 m squared equals 10,000 cm squared, 1 cGy cm squared equals 1 µGy m squared.

title: Regarding the quantities used to estimate patient dose

stems.label: A
stems.text: Dose–area product is expressed in Gy·cm².
stems.explanation: DAP is a product of dose and the area irradiated, hence gray times square centimetres.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Effective dose can be estimated from the dose–area product.
stems.explanation: DAP (Gy·cm²) multiplied by a conversion factor gives effective dose in mSv — exactly as the dose–length product does for CT.

stems.label: C
stems.text: The conversion factor from dose–area product to effective dose is higher for an AP chest radiograph than for a PA.
stems.explanation: AP delivers more dose to the anterior radiosensitive organs, which is why chest radiographs are performed PA.

stems.label: D
stems.text: CTDIvol is a measure of the dose received by the patient.
stems.explanation: CTDI is a phantom quantity (16 or 32 cm phantoms). The chain runs CTDI ÷ pitch = CTDIvol, × scan length = DLP (mGy·cm), × k = mSv. CTDI is not patient dose.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Adult body CT is typically performed at 120 kVp or above.
stems.explanation: 120 kV is the working adult default; the tube range is 80–140 kV.

stems.label: B
stems.text: 80–100 kVp is the typical range for adult thorax–abdomen–pelvis scanning.
stems.explanation: 80–100 kV belongs to paediatrics, slim patients and iodine-boosting angiography, not to the adult body default of 120 kV.

stems.label: C
stems.text: The CT number of iodine rises as the tube potential is lowered.
stems.explanation: Lower the kV and the spectrum sits nearer iodine's K-edge, photoelectric capture soars and iodine HU rises — the basis of low-kV CT angiography and reduced-contrast-dose protocols.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The K-edge of iodine is 33 keV.
stems.explanation: Iodine 33 keV, barium 37 keV, gadolinium 50 keV. The GGC paper's '53 keV' for iodine is false.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Increasing kV in CT reduces image noise.
stems.explanation: CT protocols fix the mAs, so raising kV puts more photons in each voxel and noise falls — flatly true in CT, unlike fluoroscopy under automatic brightness control. Noise rises with lower kVp, lower mA, thinner slices, faster rotation, a larger matrix and larger patients.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Gadolinium affects T2 more than T1.
stems.explanation: It is paramagnetic and shortens both, but the T1 effect dominates at clinical doses, which is why enhancement is bright on T1-weighted images.

stems.label: B
stems.text: It has an elimination half-life of about 2 minutes.
stems.explanation: About 90 minutes with normal renal function. Extracellular gadolinium chelates distribute much like iodinated contrast.

stems.label: C
stems.text: It cannot be used if the eGFR is below 30.
stems.explanation: A caution, not an absolute bar. High-risk linear agents are contraindicated; macrocyclic group II agents may be used with care where clinically necessary. The word 'cannot' is the giveaway.

stems.label: D
stems.text: It should not be used in cardiac impairment.
stems.explanation: Not a recognised contraindication. What matters is renal function, agent class, pregnancy and previous reactions.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Its use in pregnancy is associated with an increased risk of stillbirth and neonatal death.
stems.explanation: MRI in pregnancy may proceed where justified, but it should not be contrast-enhanced. The risk attaches to gadolinium-enhanced MRI at any stage.

title: Regarding the thermal index in ultrasound

stems.label: A
