stems.text: The thermal index is the ratio of emitted power to the power needed to raise tissue temperature by 1 degree C.
stems.explanation: One degree, not two - a stem quoting a 2 degree rise is false.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The thermal index is affected by attenuation along the beam path.
stems.explanation: TI is a calculated estimate that depends on how much energy the intervening path absorbs before the target, so path attenuation moves it.

stems.label: C
stems.text: The thermal index is highest when the probe lies on skin directly overlying bone.
stems.explanation: Bone is by far the strongest absorber, hence the dedicated cranial index TIC and the fact that thermal effects are greater in bone than in soft tissue.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The thermal index underestimates the temperature rise in highly perfused tissue.
stems.explanation: The opposite: blood flow carries heat away, so in high perfusion TI overestimates the real temperature rise. The underestimation scenarios are fluid paths, poorly perfused tissue such as the lens, and probe self-heating.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The thermal index is unaffected by the transmitted frequency.
stems.explanation: Attenuation and absorption both rise with frequency, and temperature rise increases with operating frequency. TI follows path attenuation, so frequency moves it.

title: Regarding if used I123 with iodine CT contrast will affect the count

stems.label: A
stems.text: if used I123 with iodine CT contrast will affect the count.
stems.explanation: Iodinated CT contrast can saturate thyroid iodine handling and reduce subsequent I-123 uptake/counts, so timing matters for thyroid nuclear medicine studies.

title: Regarding the specific absorption rate (SAR) in MRI:

stems.label: A
stems.text: SAR is reduced by increasing the slice thickness.
stems.explanation: SAR is the RF power deposited per kilogram of tissue, in W/kg. A thicker slice changes the volume imaged, not the RF power deposited per kilogram, so the SAR does not fall. The dial that genuinely lowers time-averaged SAR is a longer TR.

stems.label: B
stems.text: SAR is reduced by increasing the field of view.
stems.explanation: Same trap as the slice thickness. Enlarging the field of view alters the geometry that is sampled; it does not change how much RF energy each kilogram of tissue absorbs, so SAR is unchanged.

stems.label: C
stems.text: SAR is reduced by increasing the number of phase-encoding steps.
stems.explanation: More phase-encoding steps means more RF pulses in total and a longer scan, but no reduction in the power deposited per kilogram. Sampling parameters do not lower SAR.

stems.label: D
stems.text: SAR is reduced by increasing the repetition time (TR).
stems.explanation: This is the one that works. A longer TR means fewer RF pulses per unit time — a lower duty cycle — so the time-averaged RF power deposited per kilogram falls.

stems.label: E
stems.text: SAR rises approximately with the square of the flip angle.
stems.explanation: SAR goes roughly as the square of the flip angle and as the square of B0 (hence the square of the Larmor frequency). This is why 3 T scanning is more SAR-limited than 1.5 T, and why fast spin echo with a long train of large refocusing pulses is a high-SAR sequence. Farr's operating modes: normal 2 W/kg (0.5 degrees C rise), first level controlled 4 W/kg (1.0 degrees C).

title: Regarding the signal-to-noise ratio of an MR image

stems.label: A
stems.text: SNR is increased by increasing the TR.
stems.explanation: Longer TR allows more longitudinal recovery before the next excitation, so more signal is available, with diminishing returns as recovery completes.

stems.label: B
stems.text: SNR is increased by increasing the number of phase-encoding steps at a fixed field of view.
stems.explanation: More phase steps means smaller voxels and less signal from each, so SNR falls. It buys resolution along the phase axis and costs scan time.

stems.label: C
stems.text: SNR is increased by increasing the static field strength.
stems.explanation: M0 is proportional to B0, so a bigger field creates a bigger spin excess and more signal. The costs are SAR, susceptibility and chemical shift.

stems.label: D
stems.text: SNR is increased by increasing the slice thickness.
stems.explanation: More spins per voxel. A larger FOV at fixed matrix and a larger pixel do the same, and all three cost spatial resolution.

stems.label: E
stems.text: SNR is increased by increasing the receiver bandwidth.
stems.explanation: Signal occupies a narrow band, noise is broadband. Widen the bandwidth and you admit proportionally more noise: SNR goes as 1/√BW.

title: Regarding SNR increase in MRI with

stems.label: A
stems.text: increase signal averaging.
stems.explanation: Increasing signal averages improves SNR by the square root of the number of averages, at the cost of scan time.

stems.label: B
stems.text: increase strength of MRI.
stems.explanation: Higher field strength generally increases SNR, although artefacts and SAR also increase.

title: Regarding the effective focal spot of a diagnostic X-ray tube

stems.label: A
stems.text: It is equal in size to the area of the target from which X-rays are emitted.
stems.explanation: That area is the actual focal spot. The effective focal spot is its projection towards the receptor and is smaller, by the line-focus principle: effective = actual x sin(theta).

stems.label: B
stems.text: It becomes smaller as the target (anode) angle is increased.
stems.explanation: effective = actual x sin(theta), so a larger anode angle gives a larger effective spot. Steep (small) target angles give small effective spots, and a narrower field.

stems.label: C
stems.text: It depends on the dimensions of the cathode filament.
stems.explanation: Filament dimensions and the focusing cup define the electron footprint on the anode. Dual-focus tubes carry two filaments to give the broad 1.2 mm and fine 0.6 mm spots.

stems.label: D
stems.text: It increases with tube current (mA).
stems.explanation: Focal-spot blooming: at high mA, mutual repulsion (space charge) in the denser electron beam spreads the spot, worst at low kV.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Increasing the tube voltage (kV) increases the focal spot size.
stems.explanation: Blooming is a tube-current effect. Higher kV slightly reduces it, by accelerating electrons through the space charge faster. Focal spot geometry is set by the filament, focusing cup and target angle.

title: Regarding CT dose indices and the factors that alter patient dose

stems.label: A
stems.text: A wide-bore scanner gives a higher dose than a narrow-bore scanner.
stems.explanation: Bore diameter is not a dose determinant. The real levers are kV, mAs, pitch, collimation, scan length, filtration, tube-current modulation and iterative reconstruction.

stems.label: B
stems.text: CTDI estimates the dose delivered to the patient's organs.
stems.explanation: CTDI is the average dose in a standard Perspex phantom (16 cm head, 32 cm body), measured with a 100 mm pencil ionisation chamber. It describes the scanner protocol, not the patient — patient-facing estimates go through DLP × k-factor.

stems.label: C
stems.text: CTDI is measured in mGy/cm.
stems.explanation: CTDI is in mGy; DLP is in mGy·cm. The units alone answer several stems.

stems.label: D
stems.text: DLP is CTDIvol multiplied by the scan length, and effective dose is proportional to DLP.
stems.explanation: CTDIw = ⅓ centre + ⅔ periphery; CTDIvol = CTDIw / pitch; DLP = CTDIvol × scan length in mGy·cm; region-specific k-factors convert DLP to effective dose in mSv.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Patient effective dose increases with the number of slices acquired.
stems.explanation: More slices means a longer scan length, more tissue irradiated and a larger DLP. It feels like a display parameter; it is a coverage parameter — DLP has 'length' in its name.

title: Regarding contrast media and X-ray attenuation

stems.label: A
stems.text: Iodine has a K-edge at approximately 33 keV.
stems.explanation: One of the three K-edge figures that recur across years: iodine 33 keV, barium 37 keV, gadolinium 50 keV.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Barium has a K-edge at approximately 37 keV.
stems.explanation: Barium sits just above iodine in the same recurring K-edge set.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Gadolinium has a K-edge at approximately 50 keV.
stems.explanation: Gadolinium's higher atomic number puts its K-edge well above iodine's.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Air acts as a positive contrast agent because it attenuates more than soft tissue.
stems.explanation: Air is about -1000 HU against water at 0. It attenuates far less than tissue, so it is negative contrast; only iodine, barium and gadolinium raise attenuation through high atomic number.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Lowering the tube kV increases the attenuation of iodinated contrast.
stems.explanation: Low kV pulls the beam spectrum towards the 33 keV K-edge, so iodine absorbs more: low kV boosts iodine.

title: Regarding l123 is better> i 125 in imaging because

stems.label: A
stems.text: it’s energy is matching to gamma energy.
stems.explanation: Iodine 123 emits a 159 keV photon well suited to gamma camera imaging.

stems.label: B
stems.text: it’s half life is short.
stems.explanation: Compared with iodine 125, iodine 123 has a shorter half life and more suitable photon energy, giving better images and lower patient dose.

stems.label: C
stems.text: easly excreted.
stems.explanation: As a reason that iodine 123 is preferable to iodine 125. Isotopes of iodine have essentially the same chemical and biological behaviour, so easy excretion is not an intrinsic advantage of iodine 123. Iodine 123 is better suited to imaging because its approximately 13 hour physical half life and 159 keV gamma emission provide lower dose and better gamma camera imaging than iodine 125.

stems.label: D
stems.text: lower radiation dose.
stems.explanation: I-123 has a shorter half-life and more suitable gamma energy than I-125, so it generally gives better imaging with lower patient dose.

stems.label: E
stems.text: better image quality.
stems.explanation: I-123 emits photons more suitable for gamma-camera imaging, whereas I-125 has low-energy emissions that are less suitable and give poorer images.

title: Regarding the effect of decreasing the tube voltage (kVp), with mAs held constant

stems.label: A
stems.text: Dose to the patient falls.
stems.explanation: At constant mAs, HVL, output, patient dose and receptor dose all move together with kVp. Output and dose vary roughly as kVp squared, so lowering kV lowers entrance dose.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Dose to the image receptor falls.
stems.explanation: Same line of the table: at fixed mAs the beam is both weaker and less penetrating, so less energy reaches the receptor. Receptor dose in fact falls faster than kVp squared (the clinical 15% rule).

stems.label: C
stems.text: More scatter is produced within the patient.
stems.explanation: Photoelectric probability goes as Z cubed over E cubed, so as photon energy falls the photoelectric fraction rises and relatively fewer Compton events occur. Less scatter is produced, not more.

stems.label: D
stems.text: More scatter reaches the image receptor.
stems.explanation: Lower kV means photoelectric absorption takes over, output falls and the scatter that is produced is more back-directed, so less of it reaches the receptor.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Subject contrast increases.
stems.explanation: Differential attenuation is made by photoelectric events, and there are relatively more of them at low kVp; less scatter fog reaches the receptor as well. Contrast and scatter fraction are the only frame-proof answers in the kV family - they move the same way whether mAs or receptor dose is held constant.

title: Regarding microbubble contrast agents in ultrasound

stems.label: A
stems.text: The diameter of a microbubble equals the thickness of the transducer crystal.
stems.explanation: Microbubbles are gas-filled and under 4 micrometres, capillary-sized, and bear no relation to any probe dimension. Crystal thickness is set by the resonant frequency, lambda = 2t.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Microbubble contrast agents are less than 4 micrometres in diameter.
stems.explanation: Small enough to pass through capillaries, which is what makes them a true intravascular agent.

stems.label: C
stems.text: The diameter of a microbubble equals the ultrasound wavelength.
stems.explanation: Far smaller. Wavelength in the diagnostic range is 0.1-1.5 mm, tens to hundreds of times larger than a 4 micrometre bubble.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Microbubbles are imaged using harmonic or pulse-inversion techniques.
stems.explanation: They work by resonant, non-linear oscillation, which generates harmonics - so the scanner listens at twice the transmitted frequency and separates the signal by filtering or pulse inversion.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Microbubbles lower the threshold for cavitation.
stems.explanation: Gas is the seed. Injected microbubbles, like existing gas bodies in lung and bowel, make cavitation more likely - it is more likely above MI 0.7, with microbubble contrast, and in lung or bowel.

title: Regarding patient dose quantities in radiography and fluoroscopy:

stems.label: A
stems.text: Patient dose can be monitored using a dose-area product meter.
stems.explanation: The DAP meter sits at the tube exit and integrates Gy per square centimetre over the whole beam — dose multiplied by the irradiated area. Note what it does and does not measure: it measures patient dose, not the dose rate arriving at the detector, which needs a dosemeter at the detector face. This is the quantity that carries the irradiated area in it; entrance surface dose is simply the dose at the skin where the beam enters.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Effective dose can be estimated from the dose-area product.
stems.explanation: DAP in Gy per square centimetre multiplied by a conversion factor gives effective dose in mSv — exactly as DLP does for CT. The conversion factor is projection-specific: AP has a higher factor than PA for a chest radiograph, because more dose reaches the anterior radiosensitive organs, which is why chest radiographs are taken PA.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Increasing kVp reduces the entrance surface dose for the same receptor dose.
stems.explanation: A more penetrating beam needs far less mAs to deliver the same dose to the receptor, so the dose at the skin falls. This is the whole basis of high-kV dose-saving technique. The chain matters: output goes as kVp squared, but receptor dose rises faster than that (clinically, the 15% rule — a 15% kV rise doubles receptor exposure), so mAs drops by more than output rose.

stems.label: D
stems.text: At a fixed mAs, entrance skin dose increases in direct proportion to tube voltage.
stems.explanation: At fixed mAs, ESD rises roughly as the square of kVp, not linearly — output (air kerma) goes as kVp squared. Notice how the answer flips with the frame: at fixed mAs the skin dose rises with kV, but at constant receptor dose (statement c) it falls. Read the stem for what is being held constant before answering.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Skin dose in interventional radiology is reduced by increasing the tube-to-patient distance.
stems.explanation: Inverse square law, with the detector dose held constant by automatic brightness control: move the tube further from the skin and the entrance dose falls. The converse is the one that catches people out — increasing the patient-to-detector distance brings the patient closer to the tube and raises skin dose, as well as magnifying. Angling the beam and using several projections also lowers peak skin dose by spreading it, which is what prevents deterministic skin injury in long procedures.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Intensity.
stems.explanation: If saying filtration increases intensity: filtration removes photons, although it increases mean beam energy.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Amount of scatter reaching film.
stems.explanation: Filtration removes low-energy photons, reducing skin dose and increasing beam quality/HVL.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Dose.
stems.explanation: If saying filtration increases patient dose: added filtration generally lowers entrance skin dose.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Surface area of filament increases amount of x-rays produced.
stems.explanation: Filament/focal spot size affects heat loading and focal spot geometry; tube current/mA primarily controls the number of X-rays produced.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Contains xenon gas.
stems.explanation: An X-ray tube contains a vacuum, not xenon gas.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Heat is regulated by conduction.
stems.explanation: Most anode heat is dissipated by radiation to the tube housing and then conduction/convection through cooling systems, not simply by conduction within the vacuum.

stems.label: A
stems.text: High contrast.
stems.explanation: High kV reduces subject contrast because the beam is more penetrating and Compton scatter dominates.

stems.label: B
stems.text: High beam intensity.
stems.explanation: Tube output increases strongly with kVp, approximately proportional to kVp squared.

stems.label: A
stems.text: The imaging plate is coated with caesium iodide.
stems.explanation: CR uses a photostimulable storage phosphor, europium-doped barium fluorohalide (BaFX:Eu / BaFBr:Eu). CsI is the scintillator of indirect DR and the input phosphor of an image intensifier; NaI is the gamma-camera crystal.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The size of the phosphor crystals and the thickness of the phosphor layer affect the sensitivity of the plate.
stems.explanation: Layer thickness and crystal or grain size set X-ray absorption efficiency, and are traded directly against resolution: a thicker phosphor absorbs more X-rays but scatters the readout laser more.

stems.label: C
stems.text: The plate is scanned with a blue laser to release the stored signal.
stems.explanation: Backwards, and a classic direction-reversal trap. Farr's is explicit: red laser light is used because most phosphors release blue light. Red in, blue out, collected by a light guide into a photomultiplier tube.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Any residual latent image is removed by exposure to high-intensity white light.
stems.explanation: This is the erasure step after readout. Skip or fail it and the next image carries a ghost artefact.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The plate consists of a matrix of discrete detector elements.
stems.explanation: The phosphor is a continuous, unstructured layer. Pixels exist only because the laser samples the plate discretely at readout, which is also why CR needs no per-element gain calibration, unlike DR.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Typical matrix size is 256x256.
stems.explanation: A conventional CT image matrix is typically 512 x 512, although other matrices can be selected.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Increasing matrix size from 512x512 to 1024x1024 doubles the amount of storage required.
stems.explanation: Quadruples. False if it says doubles: 512 x 512 to 1024 x 1024 quadruples the pixel count and storage.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Tissue in the centre may have a lower HU than actual value.
stems.explanation: Preferential removal of low energy photons causes beam hardening. In a uniform object this can produce cupping, with spuriously low central CT numbers, and streaks near dense structures.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Uses a thicker filter.
stems.explanation: CT uses substantial shaped filtration, including a bow tie filter, to harden and shape the beam across the patient.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Filtered backprojection refers to a technique involving using a filter to remove low energy beams.
stems.explanation: The filter in filtered backprojection is a mathematical convolution filter applied to projection data before backprojection. It is not physical x ray filtration.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Slice thickness affects dose.
stems.explanation: As a direct setting: slice thickness mainly affects noise and z-resolution unless mAs is changed.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Adjusting window width can improve contrast.
stems.explanation: Narrowing window width increases displayed contrast by spreading a smaller HU range across the grey scale.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Metal can cause photon starvation occurs in the centre.
stems.explanation: Dense metal can attenuate nearly all photons along some paths, producing photon starvation and streak artefact.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Multislice detectors don’t get ring artifact.
stems.explanation: A faulty or miscalibrated detector element can still create ring artefact in multidetector CT.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Water has HU of 0.
stems.explanation: Water is defined as 0 HU.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Air has HU of -100.
stems.explanation: Air is around -1000 HU; -100 HU is closer to fat.

stems.label: B
stems.text: MPR of isotropic image can produce an oblique image without loss of quality.
stems.explanation: Near isotropic voxels allow multiplanar reconstruction in oblique planes with little or no loss of spatial resolution relative to the source data.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Objects at periphery may appear brighter than at the centre.
stems.explanation: Vignetting causes reduced brightness at the image intensifier periphery, not increased brightness.

title: Regarding CT dose indices and typical CT doses:

stems.label: A
stems.text: CTDI is measured in mGy/cm.
stems.explanation: CTDI is in mGy; it is DLP that is in mGy.cm. The units alone answer several stems in this family — CTDI is the dose from one rotation, DLP carries the scan length in its name and therefore in its units.

stems.label: B
stems.text: DLP equals CTDIvol multiplied by the scan length.
stems.explanation: Farr's verbatim: DLP (mGy.cm) = CTDIvol x L. The full chain is worth holding as one object — CTDI is the dose from one rotation, measured with a 100 mm pencil ionisation chamber in Perspex phantoms (16 cm head, 32 cm body); CTDIw = one third centre plus two thirds periphery; CTDIvol = CTDIw / pitch; DLP = CTDIvol x length; and effective dose = DLP x a region-specific k factor.

stems.label: C
stems.text: CTDI estimates the dose delivered to the patient's organs.
stems.explanation: CTDI is the average dose in a standard Perspex phantom — a protocol-comparison index describing the scanner, not the patient. Farr's says outright it is less useful for comparing doses to individual patients. Patient-facing estimates go through DLP multiplied by a k factor.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Patient effective dose increases with the number of slices acquired.
stems.explanation: More slices means a longer scan length, more tissue irradiated and a larger DLP. It feels like a display parameter, which is the trap; it is a coverage parameter. Anchor it on the fact that DLP has 'length' in its name. Contrast this with the genuine non-levers, which change nothing: display FOV, reconstructed slice thickness, matrix, pixel size, detector-row count and bore size.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The typical effective dose from a CT head examination is 1-3 mSv.
stems.explanation: 1-3 mSv is the figure to give (brain alone is often quoted as 1-2). The companion set to memorise: abdomen 5-10 mSv, chest-abdomen-pelvis 12-15 mSv, chest radiograph about 0.1 mSv, against a UK background of 2.7 mSv per year.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Referrer must justify the examination.
stems.explanation: The referrer supplies clinical information; the practitioner justifies the exposure.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Practitioners must be doctor/dentists.
stems.explanation: An IR(ME)R practitioner must be adequately trained and entitled by the employer. The role is not restricted solely to registered doctors or dentists.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Operator is responsible for optimising dose.
stems.explanation: Under IR(ME)R, the operator optimises the practical exposure within their assigned duties, while the practitioner justifies the exposure.

stems.label: A
stems.text: RPA must design local rules.
stems.explanation: The employer establishes local rules after consulting the Radiation Protection Adviser. The Radiation Protection Supervisor helps implement them.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Employer is responsible to ensure employees are compliant.
stems.explanation: The employer must provide arrangements, training and supervision to ensure compliance with radiation safety requirements.

stems.label: C
stems.text: All employees entering the area must be immediately classified.
stems.explanation: Entering a controlled area does not automatically make a worker classified; classification depends on likely occupational dose and work pattern.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Objects 3mm apart can be resolved.
stems.explanation: Routine gamma camera spatial resolution is closer to about 10 mm clinically, so objects only 3 mm apart are not usually resolved.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Collimator’s primary function is to remove scatter.
stems.explanation: The gamma-camera collimator primarily provides spatial information by accepting photons from selected directions; energy-windowing is the main scatter rejection method.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Higher resolution than planar imaging.
stems.explanation: If saying superior spatial resolution: SPECT has better localisation/contrast but not necessarily better spatial resolution than planar imaging.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Higher contrast than planar imaging.
stems.explanation: SPECT improves contrast by separating overlying/underlying activity with tomographic reconstruction.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Higher dose than planar imaging.
stems.explanation: SPECT reconstructs a 3D activity distribution from rotating gamma camera projections.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Better attenuation correction.
stems.explanation: SPECT can use attenuation correction, especially with CT-based correction.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Detects positron annihilation within the nucleus.
stems.explanation: Positron annihilation occurs after the positron leaves the nucleus and meets an electron.

stems.label: B
stems.text: 2D acquisition is done with collimators.
stems.explanation: PET detects paired 511 keV annihilation photons in coincidence.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Minimum coincidence timing window depends on distance between detectors and speed of light.
stems.explanation: Coincidence timing requirements are related to photon travel time and detector timing resolution. Time of flight localisation uses the arrival time difference between opposing detectors.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Have a high chemical purity.
stems.explanation: High chemical and radiochemical purity ensures the activity is in the intended compound and limits unwanted biodistribution.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Long half life.
stems.explanation: An ideal diagnostic radiopharmaceutical should have a half-life long enough for imaging but short enough to minimise dose; a long half-life is undesirable.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Emit energy 100-250keV.
stems.explanation: Ideal diagnostic gamma photon energy is roughly 100-250 keV, balancing tissue escape with collimator and detector efficiency.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Emit some beta particles.
stems.explanation: Beta emission adds absorbed dose without helping external gamma-camera imaging; an ideal imaging radionuclide is a gamma emitter with little particulate emission.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Acoustic impedence directly proportional with density.
stems.explanation: Acoustic impedance is Z = rho c, so it is directly proportional to tissue density.

stems.label: B
stems.text: 99% of ultrasound reflected at air-soft tissue interface.
stems.explanation: The air-soft tissue impedance mismatch reflects almost all ultrasound; gel removes the air interface.

stems.label: C
stems.text: 15% of ultrasound reflected at soft tissue-fluid interface.
stems.explanation: Reflection at a soft tissue fluid interface is usually very small because their acoustic impedances are similar, generally well below 15 percent.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Maximum when beam is parallel to blood flow.
stems.explanation: Doppler shift increases with blood velocity.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Change in ultrasound velocity when it is reflected.
stems.explanation: Doppler effect is the change in frequency of the ultrasound echoes when reflected by a moving object. True: Doppler shift increases with blood velocity.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Increase in ultrasound frequency when reflected by blood moving towards probe.
stems.explanation: Doppler shift is directly proportional to transmitted frequency.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Susceptibility is taken advantage of in T2* weighted imaging.
stems.explanation: Susceptibility artefact arises from local magnetic field distortion and spin dephasing.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Turbulent flow is bright on GRE.
stems.explanation: GRE is fast but more susceptible to T2* and magnetic field inhomogeneity because it lacks a 180 degree pulse.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Chemical shift can occur in the frequency-encoding direction.
stems.explanation: Fat-water frequency differences are mapped as displacement along the frequency-encoding axis.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Voxel size.
stems.explanation: Increasing voxel volume includes more spins in each voxel and increases signal. For fixed matrix size, a larger field of view or thicker slice therefore increases SNR.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Matrix size.
stems.explanation: Increasing matrix size at fixed FOV makes pixels smaller, so each pixel contains less signal and SNR falls.

stems.label: C
stems.text: TR.
stems.explanation: A longer TR allows more longitudinal recovery before the next excitation, increasing signal and SNR, although scan time increases.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Receiver bandwidth.
stems.explanation: Increasing receiver bandwidth increases noise admitted per pixel, so SNR decreases; narrower bandwidth improves SNR but increases chemical shift artefact.

stems.label: E
stems.text: TE.
stems.explanation: A longer TE allows more T2/T2* decay before signal sampling, so SNR decreases rather than increases.

stems.label: A
stems.text: STIR is used with gadolinium contrast to produce a useful image.
stems.explanation: STIR suppresses tissues by T1 and can also suppress gadolinium enhanced tissue. Frequency selective fat suppression is preferred after gadolinium when enhancement must remain visible.

stems.label: A
stems.text: The signal from a voxel containing both fat and water varies with the echo time.
stems.explanation: In gradient echo the two species precess at different frequencies, so they cycle in and out of phase as TE changes.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Fat and water protons differ in resonant frequency by 3.5 ppm.
stems.explanation: Orbital electrons shield the nucleus differently in the two chemical environments: 220 Hz at 1.5 T, 440 Hz at 3 T.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Opposed-phase images show a dark outline at fat-water interfaces.
stems.explanation: The India-ink artefact - cancellation in voxels straddling the boundary.

stems.label: D
stems.text: In-phase and opposed-phase data can be combined to give separate fat-only and water-only images.
stems.explanation: SIP = Swater + Sfat and SOP = Swater - Sfat are two equations in two unknowns, which is exactly what Dixon solves.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Dixon reconstruction is free of artefact.
stems.explanation: It has its own failure mode, the Dixon swap artefact, where the fat and water assignments are exchanged.

stems.label: A
stems.text: MRI safe means an item with demonstrated safety in MRI environment within defined conditions.
stems.explanation: That wording defines MR Conditional. MR Safe means the item poses no known hazards in any MR environment.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Increases with slice thickness.
stems.explanation: Slice thickness and field of view are not simple primary determinants of SAR. SAR is dominated by RF pulse amplitude, flip angle, pulse number, duty cycle, patient loading and field strength.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Increases with flip angle.
stems.explanation: SAR rises approximately with the square of RF flip angle because larger excitation requires more RF power.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Microbubbles work by having a diameter equal to wavelength of ultrasound beam.
stems.explanation: Microbubbles are only a few micrometres in diameter, much smaller than the ultrasound wavelength; their nonlinear oscillation creates strong contrast echoes.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Lead is used as a protective agent because of its high atomic number.
stems.explanation: Lead's high atomic number and density provide strong attenuation, particularly through photoelectric absorption at lower photon energies.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Gadolinium cannot be used if eGFR <30.
stems.explanation: If absolute: gadolinium is avoided or used with caution in eGFR <30 depending on agent and indication.

stems.label: A
stems.text: 1g of bone will have more absorbed dose then 1g of soft tissue.
stems.explanation: For the same incident photon fluence, bone may absorb more energy than soft tissue because photoelectric absorption is greater, so absorbed dose can be higher. The exposure conditions must be the same.

stems.label: A
stems.text: The characteristic radiation energy is much lower than the initial electron energy.
stems.explanation: The recall key marks this true: characteristic x-ray energy is set by shell binding-energy differences, while the incident electron or photon energy used to create the vacancy is usually higher.

title: Regarding USS heating at the particular point will depend on

stems.label: A
stems.text: USS heating coefficient.
stems.explanation: Local temperature rise depends on absorbed acoustic energy and on heat transfer away by conduction and perfusion.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Blood flow in the tissue.
stems.explanation: Perfusion carries heat away, so local ultrasound heating depends on tissue blood flow as well as absorbed acoustic power.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Transfer of heat within the tissue.
stems.explanation: Local temperature rise depends on heat conduction/perfusion away from the exposed region.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Cryogen is a flammable hazard.
stems.explanation: Helium is inert and non flammable. Its major hazards are cold injury, pressure and oxygen displacement during a quench.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Distance of controlled area is 0.5mT.
stems.explanation: The MR controlled access boundary is conventionally associated with the 0.5 mT, or 5 gauss, fringe-field contour.

stems.label: C
stems.text: The magnet is the biggest hazard.
stems.explanation: The static field is always present and creates projectile/implant hazards; gradients, RF heating and cryogens add further risks.

stems.label: A
stems.text: 90 degree RF pulse is used.
stems.explanation: Conventional spin echo starts with a 90 degree excitation pulse.

stems.label: B
stems.text: 180 degree RF pulse is used.
stems.explanation: The 180 degree refocusing pulse rephases spins and produces the spin echo.

stems.label: C
stems.text: It is possible to get T2* effect.
stems.explanation: Spin echo produces true T2 weighting; T2* effects are characteristic of GRE.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Having more phase encoding steps improves signal due to longer TE.
stems.explanation: Longer TR. Spin echo uses 90 degree excitation and 180 degree refocusing, making it less sensitive to susceptibility than GRE.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Scatter to transmission ratio is 10:1.
stems.explanation: Scatter can greatly exceed transmitted primary radiation in large fields; a 10:1 scatter-to-primary/transmission ratio is a possible high-scatter situation, not a universal constant.

stems.label: A
stems.text: High Pulse Repetition Frequency (PRF) is limited by depth of tissue measured.
stems.explanation: The next pulse cannot be sent until echoes return from the selected depth, so maximum PRF is limited by imaging depth.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Sampling frequency must be twice the frequency to avoid aliasing.
stems.explanation: This is the Nyquist rule. Pulsed Doppler must sample at least twice the Doppler frequency shift to avoid aliasing.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Aliasing is more likely when the blood flow is 30cm per second.
stems.explanation: Aliasing can occur even at physiological velocities if PRF is too low, especially with deep sampling or high transmitted frequency.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Inversely proportional to density.
stems.explanation: Doppler shift depends on transmitted frequency, reflector velocity and cosine angle.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Inversely proportional to compressibility.
stems.explanation: Doppler shift depends on transmitted frequency, reflector velocity, insonation angle and sound speed, not tissue compressibility.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Speed in tissue is affected by temperature.
stems.explanation: Sound speed can vary with temperature because material stiffness and density change.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Speed in tissue is 1240ms-1.
stems.explanation: Diagnostic ultrasound systems assume an average soft-tissue speed of about 1540 m/s; 1240 m/s is too low for typical soft tissue.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Only radiologist can justify scans above 5mSV.
stems.explanation: Justification depends on employer entitlement and training, not on a 5 mSv threshold or the person being a radiologist.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Gaseous waste is not considered radioactive waste.
stems.explanation: Radioactive gases and patient excreta can constitute radioactive waste and must be managed under the applicable authorisation and local procedures.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Local Councils will inspect the premises to see if it adheres to the rules.
stems.explanation: Radioactive substances and waste regulation is handled by the relevant environmental regulator, not ordinary local council inspection.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Waste produced by patients is not considered radioactive waste.
stems.explanation: Patient excreta may contain radioactivity after nuclear medicine administration, but management depends on activity, isotope, route and local waste rules.

title: Regarding size of effective focal spot is affected by

stems.label: A
stems.text: Target angle.
stems.explanation: Smaller focal spots reduce penumbra and improve geometric sharpness.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Size of filament.
stems.explanation: Filament size and electron focusing help determine the effective focal spot size at the anode.

stems.label: C
stems.text: mA.
stems.explanation: Blooming. True: smaller focal spots reduce penumbra and improve geometric sharpness.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Grids improve spatial resolution.
stems.explanation: Grids mainly improve contrast by absorbing scatter; they do not improve intrinsic spatial resolution.

title: Regarding MRI signal to noise ratio is improved by

stems.label: A
stems.text: Size of field of view.
stems.explanation: Increasing voxel volume includes more spins in each voxel and increases signal. For fixed matrix size, a larger field of view or thicker slice therefore increases SNR.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Bigger slice selection.
stems.explanation: A thicker selected slice contains more excited spins, so signal and SNR increase, at the cost of slice resolution.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Narrower receiver bandwidth.
stems.explanation: Narrowing receiver bandwidth reduces noise per pixel and improves SNR, although it increases chemical shift and susceptibility-related distortions.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Bigger pixel size.
stems.explanation: Larger pixels/voxels contain more spins, increasing signal and SNR but reducing spatial resolution.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Bigger matrix size.
stems.explanation: For a fixed FOV, a bigger matrix gives smaller pixels, reducing voxel signal and SNR.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Signal to noise ratio is increased in DSA, after subtracting the mask image.
stems.explanation: Subtraction combines noise from the mask and live images, so image noise increases and SNR decreases unless dose or temporal averaging is increased.

title: Regarding spatial resolution in USS is affected by

stems.label: A
stems.text: Turning up TGC.
stems.explanation: Changing gain or monitor brightness changes displayed amplitude, not the intrinsic spatial resolution of the ultrasound system.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Turning up the brightness of the monitor.
stems.explanation: Monitor brightness changes display appearance, not the intrinsic axial or lateral resolution of the ultrasound beam.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Higher frequency.
stems.explanation: Higher frequency shortens wavelength and improves axial resolution, but penetration is reduced.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Dose to patient is increased if radionuclide has longer physical half life.
stems.explanation: When other factors are unchanged. A longer physical half life increases residence time and total nuclear transformations, raising absorbed dose.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Bone scan is 0.5mSV.
stems.explanation: A typical adult technetium bone scan effective dose is several mSv, commonly around 3 to 4 mSv, not 0.5 mSv.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Positron is detected by coincidence detectors.
stems.explanation: PET detects paired 511 keV annihilation photons in coincidence.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Cyclotrons are on hospital site.
stems.explanation: Some centres have onsite cyclotrons, but many receive short lived PET radionuclides from a regional production site.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Field of view of gamma camera is determined by size of collimator holes.
stems.explanation: Gamma camera field of view is mainly determined by the usable crystal and detector area, not by individual collimator hole size.

stems.label: B
stems.text: In Tc99m high sensitivity collimator is preferred to higher resolution collimator.
stems.explanation: Collimator choice depends on the examination. A high resolution collimator is often selected for technetium 99m when detail is important; high sensitivity is not universally preferred.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Molybdenum 68 is the parent of Tc99m. False. Parent is Mo99.
stems.explanation: Mo-99, not Mo-68, is the parent radionuclide in a Mo-99/Tc-99m generator.

title: Regarding desirable characteristics of radionuclide are

stems.label: A
stems.text: More than 500keV. False. Would prefer 150keV to 400keV.
stems.explanation: Diagnostic gamma photons above 500 keV are too penetrating and cause septal penetration; useful energies are typically much lower, around 100-250 keV.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Can be bound to a suitable pharmaceutical.
stems.explanation: The radionuclide must be attachable to a suitable pharmaceutical that localises in the target organ.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Half life more than 12 hours. False. Most used radionuclide is Tc99m which half life is 6 hours.
stems.explanation: For an ideal general diagnostic radionuclide: the half-life should be long enough for imaging but short enough to minimise dose; Tc-99m is about 6 hours.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Accumulates in the target organ.
stems.explanation: An ideal radiopharmaceutical should localise in the organ or process being imaged to maximise target-to-background contrast.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Produces Beta radiation. False. Gamma radiation is desired.
stems.explanation: Diagnostic nuclear medicine generally wants gamma emission for external detection; beta particles mainly increase local absorbed dose.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Film dosimeters can measure both Beta and gamma radiation.
stems.explanation: A film badge with appropriate filters can estimate exposure from beta, x ray and gamma radiation within its energy response.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Thermodosimeters can be used to measure finger doses.
stems.explanation: Thermoluminescent dosimeters/ring dosimeters can monitor extremity doses such as finger dose in radionuclide work.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Electronic dosimeters are not sensitive enough for IR.
stems.explanation: Electronic personal dosimeters can be sensitive enough for instantaneous/real-time monitoring in interventional radiology; TLDs/OSLs are used for official dose records.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Thermolumunicent dosimeters sensitivity is 0.1mSV.
stems.explanation: TLD sensitivity depends on design and readout; 0.1 mSv is not a safe universal sensitivity statement for all TLD dosimeters.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Effective dose requires knowledge of tissue weighting factor.
stems.explanation: Effective dose uses tissue weighting factors to estimate whole-body stochastic risk.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Is the same as the whole body equivalent dose for the same stochastic risk.
stems.explanation: Effective dose is defined as the uniform whole-body equivalent dose that would carry the same overall stochastic risk as the actual non-uniform exposure, via the tissue weighting factors.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Is relatively the same for most tissues in the diagnostic range of energies.
stems.explanation: Compton scatter involves a loosely bound outer-shell electron and is the dominant interaction in soft tissue at diagnostic energies.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Phosphor life is affected by radiation heat.
stems.explanation: CR phosphor plate life is limited mainly by handling damage, scratches, dirt and ageing, not by radiation heating.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Spatial resolution is better then film.
stems.explanation: For CR. Screen film historically had higher limiting spatial resolution, while CR offers wider dynamic range and processing flexibility.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Can be read after a 12 hours to a week.
stems.explanation: The latent image on a CR plate fades with time, so plates should be read promptly rather than left for many hours or days.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Comparing flat panel detectors with image intensifiers, FPD has lower geometric distortion.
stems.explanation: Flat panel detectors have much less pincushion and magnetic distortion than image intensifiers.

stems.label: A
stems.text: In beam hardening, lowers the CT number in the middle of the image.
stems.explanation: Beam hardening removes low-energy photons and can cause cupping or low central CT numbers.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Water HU number is 100.
stems.explanation: Water is defined as 0 HU; +100 HU is soft-tissue/blood range, not water.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Ring artefact can occur in multislice CT.
stems.explanation: Ring artefact can occur in multislice CT when a detector element is miscalibrated or faulty.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Increasing pitch, decreases dose.
stems.explanation: Pitch affects dose, scan time and noise; dose is inversely related to pitch if other factors are fixed.

stems.label: B
stems.text: In cone beam effect, the artefact is at the centre of the axis.
stems.explanation: Cone beam artefact is greatest away from the central plane, where the x ray beam is most oblique to the detector rows.

stems.label: A
stems.text: The RPS has to do prior risk assessment once pregnancy is notified.
stems.explanation: The employer must review the risk assessment and working conditions after pregnancy is declared; the RPS assists locally but is not the legal duty holder.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Dose limit of fetus is 1mSV from date it is informed in writing.
stems.explanation: Once pregnancy is declared in writing, working conditions must make it unlikely that the fetal dose exceeds 1 mSv during the remainder of pregnancy.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Must avoid fluoroscopy.
stems.explanation: Pregnant staff do not automatically have to avoid fluoroscopy or radiopharmaceutical work. Duties are modified according to risk assessment, monitoring, time, distance and shielding.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Must avoid working with radiopharmaceuticals.
stems.explanation: As an absolute statement: pregnant staff require risk assessment and dose restriction, but all work with radiopharmaceuticals is not automatically prohibited.

stems.label: A
stems.text: typical focal spot is between 0.5-1mm.
stems.explanation: A CT tube commonly uses focal spots in the approximate submillimetre to 1 mm range, depending on tube loading.

stems.label: B
stems.text: SSD suffer more from afterglow than sodium iodide photomultiplier tubes.
stems.explanation: Modern solid state CT detectors are designed for rapid response and low afterglow. They do not characteristically suffer more afterglow than sodium iodide based detectors.

stems.label: C
stems.text: modern SSD have a QDE of 80-90%.
stems.explanation: Modern solid state CT detectors have high detection efficiency, commonly in the region of 80 to 90 percent.

stems.label: D
stems.text: filter back projection is a common method of image construction.
stems.explanation: Filtered backprojection is a standard analytical CT reconstruction method.

stems.label: E
stems.text: for a 512 x 512 image with 12 bit accuracy, 400kb of storage is needed per image.
stems.explanation: A 512 x 512 image has 262,144 pixels. At 12 bits per pixel the raw data are about 393,216 bytes, approximately 384 KiB or conventionally rounded to 400 kB.

stems.label: A
stems.text: quantum mottle is a problem in obsese patient.
stems.explanation: Quantum mottle is random statistical fluctuation in the number of photons detected. Relative noise falls as the square root of detected photon number increases.

stems.label: B
stems.text: beam hardening from ribs can mimic hepatic abnormality.
stems.explanation: Beam hardening removes low-energy photons and can cause cupping or low central CT numbers.

stems.label: C
stems.text: scatter artifact can be corrected using post patient collimation.
stems.explanation: To an extent, post patient collimation reduces scatter reaching the CT detector, although software correction and detector geometry are also used.

stems.label: D
stems.text: unit of pitch is mms-1.
stems.explanation: No unit. False if saying higher pitch gives more dose: increasing pitch generally lowers dose for fixed mAs per rotation.

stems.label: E
stems.text: increasing slice width improves partial volume effects.
stems.explanation: Multislice or helical acquisition does not eliminate partial volume averaging. Thin reconstructed slices and near isotropic voxels reduce it.

title: Regarding SNR in MRI is directly proportional to

stems.label: A
stems.text: proton density.
stems.explanation: More mobile hydrogen nuclei contribute more transverse magnetisation and therefore more signal, increasing SNR.

stems.label: B
stems.text: slice width.
stems.explanation: Thicker slices contain more spins and therefore increase signal and SNR.

stems.label: C
stems.text: inhomogeneities in magnetic field.
stems.explanation: Magnetic field inhomogeneity causes dephasing, distortion and signal loss rather than improving SNR.

stems.label: D
stems.text: phase encoding steps.
stems.explanation: At fixed field of view and slice thickness, increasing the matrix reduces voxel size and therefore lowers SNR. More phase encoding steps also lengthen acquisition time rather than directly increasing signal.

title: Regarding chemical shift in spin echo MRI

stems.label: A
stems.text: increases with greater field strength.
stems.explanation: Spin echo uses 90 degree excitation and 180 degree refocusing, making it less sensitive to susceptibility than GRE.

stems.label: B
stems.text: occurs in frequency encodingnaxjs.
stems.explanation: Conventional chemical shift displacement occurs in the frequency-encoding direction because fat and water precess at different frequencies.

stems.label: C
stems.text: increases with gadolinium dtpa contrast.
stems.explanation: Gadolinium shortens T1 and can alter signal, but it is not the cause of fat-water chemical shift artefact.

stems.label: D
stems.text: occurs in phase encoding frequency.
stems.explanation: Classic chemical shift misregistration is along the frequency-encoding axis, not the phase-encoding axis.

stems.label: A
stems.text: is higher for pulsed Doppler compared to B Mode.
stems.explanation: Doppler shift depends on transmitted frequency, reflector velocity and cosine angle.

stems.label: B
stems.text: is limited by strict adherence by manufacturers of ISPTA.
stems.explanation: Manufacturers comply with output display and regulatory limits, but ISPTA alone is not the sole strict limit on ultrasound output.

stems.label: C
stems.text: is limited by practitioners under ALARA.
stems.explanation: ALARA is a radiation protection term; ultrasound output is controlled using ALARP/lowest output and shortest time principles, not ionising-radiation dose limits.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Keeping doses as low as reasonably practicable is a fundamental requirement of IRR17.
stems.explanation: The trap reads ALARP as an IR(ME)R-only slogan, but restriction of exposure so far as is reasonably practicable is the core duty in IRR17 too. ALARP belongs to both regulations; only dose limits are IRR-exclusive.

stems.label: E
stems.text: X-ray equipment must undergo a critical examination at installation.
stems.explanation: The installer's check of the safety features — warning lights, interlocks, emergency stops. Distinct from acceptance testing and from routine QA.

title: Regarding patient and staff dose in fluoroscopy

stems.label: A
stems.text: For abdominal screening the entrance skin dose rate is typically 10-20 mGy per minute.
stems.explanation: The beam is on continuously and abdominal penetration demands high kVp and mA. Note the unit: fluoroscopic skin dose must be expressed as a rate, since a cumulative figure means nothing without the screening time.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Pulsed fluoroscopy reduces the dose rate.
stems.explanation: 'Continuous' fluoroscopy is really 25-30 pulses per second, each 2-20 ms; the rate can be dropped to 15, 7.5 or 3.75 pulses per second. No flicker is seen because each image is held until the next arrives.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Staff dose comes mainly from the primary beam.
stems.explanation: Scatter off the patient is the dominant contribution, not the primary beam. Hence lead aprons, thyroid collars, leaded glasses, table drapes, ceiling-suspended screens, and distance.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Increasing the patient-to-detector distance reduces the entrance skin dose.
stems.explanation: It brings the patient closer to the tube and magnifies the image, so skin dose rises. It is increasing the tube-to-patient distance that lowers skin dose, by the inverse square law, with ABC holding detector dose constant.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Angling the beam and using several projections reduces peak skin dose.
stems.explanation: Dose spreading: the total dose is unchanged but no single patch of skin takes all of it. This is what prevents deterministic skin injury in long procedures.

title: Regarding IR(ME)R and the biological effects of radiation

stems.label: A
stems.text: Medico-legal exposures are included within IR(ME)R.
stems.explanation: IR(ME)R's scope catches every deliberate exposure of a person: diagnosis, therapy, health screening, occupational health surveillance, research, medico-legal, and non-medical imaging of asymptomatic individuals.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The referrer is responsible for justifying the exposure.
stems.explanation: The referrer supplies sufficient medical information to allow justification — information, not justification. The practitioner justifies and the operator optimises.

stems.label: C
stems.text: The risk of fatal childhood cancer from in-utero exposure is about 1 in 3,000 per mSv.
stems.explanation: 1 in 3,000 per mSv is the recycled wrong number. The in-utero figure is about 1 in 13,000 per mSv, so roughly 25 mSv doubles the natural childhood cancer incidence of about 1 in 500.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Stochastic effects have no threshold dose.
stems.explanation: The linear no-threshold model underlies the whole protection framework: probability scales with dose, severity does not, and the effects appear late.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The induction of malignancy is a deterministic effect.
stems.explanation: Malignancy is stochastic — no threshold, probability rather than severity rising with dose, late onset. Deterministic (tissue) reactions have a threshold above which the effect is certain and severity scales with dose.

title: Regarding dose limits and dose quantities under IRR17

stems.label: A
stems.text: The limit for the lens of the eye is expressed as an equivalent dose.
stems.explanation: The lens limit is an organ limit, quoted as an equivalent dose in mSv, alongside skin and extremities. Effective dose is the separate whole-body quantity used for stochastic risk.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The annual dose limit for the lens of the eye is 150 mSv.
stems.explanation: It is 20 mSv. The 150 mSv figure is out of date and survives only in older textbooks; 150 mSv is the skin figure at classification level, not the lens limit.

stems.label: C
stems.text: The annual effective dose limit for an employee is 20 mSv.
stems.explanation: Employee 20 mSv per year, member of the public 1 mSv, trainee under 18 years 6 mSv. Classification is required above 6 mSv effective.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The annual equivalent dose limit for the skin and extremities is 500 mSv.
stems.explanation: 500 mSv, the largest of the organ limits, because skin and extremities carry a low stochastic weighting and the concern is a deterministic tissue reaction.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Effective dose indicates the dose to the fetus in a pregnant patient.
stems.explanation: Fetal dose is the equivalent dose to the uterus. Effective dose expresses the mother's whole-body stochastic risk and says nothing directly about the fetus. One of the nine statements missed on both mock attempts.

stems.label: A
stems.text: ARSAC holder can prescribe in all the hospitals he/she works.
stems.explanation: An ARSAC practitioner licence and employer certificate are tied to specified practices and sites. Authority is not automatically transferable to every hospital where the practitioner works.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Dose to children is half of the adult dose.
stems.explanation: Paediatric administered activity is scaled using weight or validated paediatric dosage cards, not simply fixed at half the adult activity.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Breast feeding should be stopped for 24hrs.
stems.explanation: Mammography uses low-energy spectra, compression and high spatial resolution while minimising glandular dose.

stems.label: D
stems.text: NM examinations are contraindicated in a pregnant patient.
stems.explanation: Pregnancy is not an automatic absolute contraindication; the examination must be justified, optimised and usually deferred if not urgent.

stems.label: E
stems.text: All radioactive waste has to be disposed in sacks.
stems.explanation: Radioactive waste disposal route depends on waste form, isotope, activity and local/environmental permit conditions; it is not all disposed of in sacks.

title: Regarding quality assurance of X-ray and fluoroscopy equipment:

stems.label: A
stems.text: A step wedge is used to test kV.
stems.explanation: kVp accuracy is measured with a calibrated non-invasive kV meter. A step wedge assesses contrast and receptor response — a different question about a different part of the chain.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Total filtration may be estimated by measuring the half-value thickness of aluminium for the beam.
stems.explanation: HVL is the standard surrogate for total filtration — you cannot dismantle the tube, so you measure how much aluminium halves the beam and infer the filtration from it.

stems.label: C
stems.text: An ionisation chamber can be used to measure leakage radiation.
stems.explanation: It is the appropriate instrument for the job. In the same QA set: light-beam alignment is checked with a rectangular metal frame, and intensifying screens are checked with visible light — match the test object to the quantity being measured.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The image intensifier is affected by external magnetic fields, including the Earth's.
stems.explanation: The II works by accelerating and focusing electrons across the tube, and a magnetic field deflects them. This sits alongside its other geometric failings — pincushion and S-distortion from the curved input phosphor and the electron optics, and vignetting. A flat panel detector has none of these: lower geometric distortion, no vignetting, and the same resolution at every field of view.

stems.label: E
stems.text: X-ray tube output is measured annually.
stems.explanation: Too infrequent. IPEM Report 91 schedules output and consistency checks at roughly 1-3 monthly intervals; a formal annual physicist survey is additional to that, not the schedule. UK QA generally follows IPEM Report 91 (IPEM 89 for mammography), with tests graded Level 1/Level 2 and by expertise (Level A radiographer, Level B physicist), and action levels split into remedial and suspension.

title: Regarding quality assurance testing of X-ray equipment

stems.label: A
stems.text: Tube output is measured annually.
stems.explanation: IPEM Report 91 schedules output and consistency checks at roughly one to three monthly intervals. Annual is far too infrequent; the formal annual physicist survey is additional to that schedule, not a substitute for it.

stems.label: B
stems.text: A step wedge is used to test kV accuracy.
stems.explanation: kVp accuracy is measured with a calibrated non-invasive kV meter. A step wedge assesses contrast and receptor response.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Total filtration may be estimated by measuring the half-value thickness of aluminium for the beam.
stems.explanation: HVL is the standard surrogate for total filtration, which must exceed 2.5 mm Al equivalent above 70 kVp.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Light-beam alignment is checked with a rectangular metal frame.
stems.explanation: From the same QA set: an ionisation chamber measures leakage radiation, a metal frame checks light-beam alignment, and intensifying screens are checked with visible light.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Most UK medical equipment QA is based on IPEM Report 91, with IPEM Report 89 for mammography.
stems.explanation: Tests are graded Level 1 (good practice) and Level 2 (best practice), and by expertise: Level A radiographer-performed, quick and frequent; Level B physicist, complex. Action levels are remedial (fix, may still be used) or suspension (remove from clinical use immediately).

stems.label: A
stems.text: Can pass through unaffected.
stems.explanation: An x ray photon may traverse matter without interacting.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Can disappear completely.
stems.explanation: A photon may be completely absorbed in a photoelectric interaction, transferring its energy to an electron.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Divert from direction and gain energy.
stems.explanation: In Compton scatter the photon changes direction and loses energy to the recoil electron; it does not gain energy.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Back scattered photon of 180 gains more energy.
stems.explanation: At 180-degree backscatter the photon loses the greatest energy and the recoil electron gains the greatest energy.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Intensity dependent on kV.
stems.explanation: X ray output increases approximately with kVp squared when mAs is unchanged.

title: Regarding effective focal spot is affected by

stems.label: A
stems.text: Anode disc diameter.
stems.explanation: Effective focal spot is governed mainly by actual focal spot and target angle, not anode disc diameter.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Target material.
stems.explanation: Target material affects X-ray production/spectrum, not the geometric effective focal spot size.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Anode-cathode distance.
stems.explanation: Anode-cathode distance does not define effective focal spot; filament/focusing and target angle do.

title: Regarding focal spot size increases by

stems.label: A
stems.text: Target angle.
stems.explanation: Increasing the target angle increases the effective focal spot size, while reducing target angle reduces effective focal spot but worsens anode heat loading/coverage.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Target material.
stems.explanation: Target material affects X-ray production/spectrum, not the geometric effective focal spot size.

stems.label: A
stems.text: CS predominates.
stems.explanation: Compton scatter predominates in soft tissue at typical CT photon energies.

stems.label: B
stems.text: PEE predominates.
stems.explanation: Photoelectric absorption completely absorbs the photon and ejects a bound electron; characteristic radiation may follow.

stems.label: C
stems.text: HU of fat is typically -100.
stems.explanation: Fat is typically around -50 to -100 HU.

stems.label: D
stems.text: HU are given depending on the density of the material.
stems.explanation: CT number depends on linear attenuation, which is influenced by physical density, atomic number and photon energy.

stems.label: E
stems.text: If an object is smaller than the pixel size it is not seen.
stems.explanation: A subpixel object may still be visible through partial volume averaging if it produces sufficient contrast, although it cannot be spatially resolved at its true size.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Radioactive decay - emits radiation.
stems.explanation: Radioactive decay is spontaneous nuclear transformation accompanied by particulate or electromagnetic radiation.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Physical half life should be 24 hrs.
stems.explanation: An ideal diagnostic radionuclide should have a short practical half-life; 24 hours is unnecessarily long for many studies and increases dose.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Gamma ray energy should be 300KeV.
stems.explanation: As an ideal fixed value. Diagnostic gamma photons are preferably around 100 to 250 keV; 300 keV increases septal penetration and reduces collimator efficiency.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Parent should have shorter life than the daughter.
stems.explanation: Mo-99, not Mo-68, is the parent radionuclide for Tc-99m generators.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Can be produced in cyclotron.
stems.explanation: Several imaging radionuclides, including F-18 and I-123, are produced in cyclotrons.

stems.label: A
stems.text: PHA reduces noise.
stems.explanation: The pulse height analyser accepts events within an energy window around the photopeak, rejecting many scattered lower energy events and improving contrast.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Size of the crystal affects spatial resolution.
stems.explanation: Gamma camera crystal thickness/light spread affects intrinsic resolution; thicker crystals improve sensitivity but can worsen resolution.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Collimator holes affect spatial resolution.
stems.explanation: Hole diameter, length and septal thickness determine the collimator resolution and sensitivity trade off.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Photomultiplier does not affect the number of electrons.
stems.explanation: PMTs convert scintillation light to electrical pulses and help localise the event; they do not optically focus light.

stems.label: A
stems.text: If Transducer surface has high temperature it is due to increase in voltage.
stems.explanation: Probe surface heating mainly reflects electrical and mechanical losses within the transducer and poor acoustic coupling. It is not explained simply by increasing voltage.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Due to friction.
stems.explanation: Ultrasound heating is mainly from absorption of acoustic energy, not mechanical friction in the everyday sense.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Local heating mainly due to energy absorption.
stems.explanation: Tissue heating occurs when absorbed ultrasound energy is converted into heat.

stems.label: D
stems.text: TI is the increase in temp by 2 degrees.
stems.explanation: TI estimates tissue temperature rise and is affected by tissue attenuation, especially near bone.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Increases echoes from behind the fluid filled structures.
stems.explanation: TGC can amplify deeper echoes generally, but posterior acoustic enhancement behind fluid is a propagation effect caused by reduced attenuation, not a specific TGC function.

stems.label: B
stems.text: It can be altered to increase the echoes from structure behind the fluid filled structures.
stems.explanation: As a statement about the control, although it does not explain posterior acoustic enhancement. Time gain compensation can be adjusted for a selected depth range and therefore can increase the displayed amplitude of echoes from structures behind a fluid filled structure. Natural posterior enhancement is caused by reduced attenuation through fluid, and inappropriate TGC may either exaggerate or compensate for that appearance.

stems.label: C
stems.text: In Abdomen scanning 99% of time is utilised in receiving the echoes.
stems.explanation: Pulse echo ultrasound spends most of each pulse repetition period listening for returning echoes, commonly around 99 percent.

title: Regarding 21 operator can control - in US

stems.label: A
stems.text: PRF.
stems.explanation: The operator can alter pulse repetition frequency within limits imposed by imaging depth and mode.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Frame rate.
stems.explanation: The operator can alter frame rate indirectly through depth, sector width, line density and focal zones.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Focal zone.
stems.explanation: The operator can set focal zone position/number, which changes lateral resolution and frame rate.

title: Regarding MR safety zones and screening

stems.label: A
stems.text: The MR controlled access area is taken from the 0.5 mT (5 gauss) fringe-field contour.
stems.explanation: 0.5 mT = 5 gauss is the contour that matters and the conventional exam answer, so a stem giving 50 mT is false. Public access is permissible only below 0.5 mT.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The inner controlled area is defined at 3 mT.
stems.explanation: Exam-era UK guidance gives an inner controlled area at 3 mT - the projectile zone.

stems.label: C
stems.text: A person with a pacemaker should not enter the 0.5 mT stray field area.
stems.explanation: Excluding pacemaker wearers is the historical reason the 5-gauss contour delimits the MR environment. MR-conditional devices scanned under controlled conditions are a supervised exception, not a general permission. The verified source corrects the bank's key here.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The MR responsible person must be a medical physicist.
stems.explanation: The MR responsible person is a locally designated role for day-to-day safety and access control, often a senior radiographer. The MR safety expert is the one typically a physicist.

stems.label: E
stems.text: 'MR Safe' describes an item with demonstrated safety within defined conditions.
stems.explanation: That is MR Conditional. MR Safe means no known hazard in any MR environment - non-conductive, non-metallic, non-magnetic. The exam swaps these two.

title: Regarding exposure limits and bioeffects in MRI

stems.label: A
stems.text: Whole-body SAR limits are set to restrict the core temperature rise to about 1 degree Celsius.
stems.explanation: That figure belongs to first level (controlled) mode at 4 W/kg. Routine scanning runs in normal mode, which is stricter at 0.5 °C and 2 W/kg, so answer to whichever mode the stem names.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Rapid gradient switching can cause peripheral nerve stimulation.
stems.explanation: A rapidly changing field induces currents in the patient that stimulate nerve and muscle - more likely with the fast switching of cardiac and diffusion imaging.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Rapid gradient switching induces cardiac arrhythmias at clinical switching rates.
stems.explanation: The recognised effect is peripheral nerve stimulation and muscular contraction. Cardiac stimulation needs far higher dB/dt than the limits allow, which is why the limits exist.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Pregnancy in the first trimester is an absolute contraindication to MRI.
stems.explanation: It is a precaution, not an absolute bar. Unenhanced first-trimester MRI has shown no increased risk; scan where justified and avoid gadolinium.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Static field strengths of 5 T and above interfere with brain function.
stems.explanation: There is no evidence of permanent biological effects below 8 T. Vertigo, metallic taste and magnetophosphenes occur with rapid movement through the field but are transient.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Uses a bipolar gradient.
stems.explanation: Gradient echo forms the echo by reversing the readout gradient, using dephasing and rephasing gradients rather than a 180-degree RF refocusing pulse.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Small flip angles.
stems.explanation: GRE commonly uses small flip angles and short TR, making it fast and relatively low SAR.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Short repetition times (TR).
stems.explanation: GRE often uses short TR because the flip angle is usually less than 90 degrees and no 180-degree refocusing pulse is required.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Low SAR.
stems.explanation: GRE generally has lower SAR than spin echo because it avoids repeated 180-degree RF refocusing pulses.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Increases with increasing field strength.
stems.explanation: Chemical shift increases at higher B0 because the absolute frequency separation increases.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Decreased by increasing bandwidth.
stems.explanation: Increasing receiver bandwidth reduces the pixel displacement from chemical shift.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Affected by using gadolinium contrast.
stems.explanation: Gadolinium shortens T1 but does not remove the fat-water resonance frequency difference.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Occurs in frequency encoded direction.
stems.explanation: Fat-water frequency differences are mapped as displacement along the frequency-encoding axis.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Always occurs in pahse encoding direction.
stems.explanation: Chemical shift is due to the 3.5 ppm resonance difference between fat and water.

stems.label: A
stems.text: The nucleus contains equal numbers of protons and neutrons
stems.explanation: This is approximately true for atoms with Z<20, but the number of neutrons starts to increase for Z >20. Also, the hydrogen nucleus contains no neutrons at all.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The K-shell can hold up to 8 electrons
stems.explanation: The K-shell can only hold up to 2 electrons

stems.label: C
stems.text: All the electrons have negative energy in the atom
stems.explanation: Negative energy means they are 'bound' to the atom and can’t escape without receiving energy from an outside source, such as an x-ray.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The binding energy of the K-shell is proportional to the mass number of the nucleus
stems.explanation: The binding energy increases with the atomic number, Z, rather than the mass number. Even so, the increase in BE is not linear.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Chemical properties of the atom are determined by the number of electrons in the outermost shell
stems.explanation: Valence shell electrons participate in chemical bonding and determine the chemical properties of an element

title: Regarding the photoelectric effect in x-ray studies

stems.label: A
stems.text: Only occurs with K-shell electrons
stems.explanation: It can also occur in the L-shell or M-shell

stems.label: B
stems.text: Can produce characteristic radiation
stems.explanation: Characteristic radiation is emitted when an electron drops into the vacancy left behind by the photoelectron

stems.label: C
stems.text: Creates subject contrast in planar radiography
stems.explanation: The rate at which PE occurs is very sensitive to the differences in atomic number (Z) between adjacent tissues, resulting in large differences in x-ray beam attenuation (ie subject contrast)

stems.label: D
stems.text: Occurs less frequently at higher tube currents (mA)
stems.explanation: The likelihood of the photoelectric effect (PE) occurring depends on the energy of the xrays in the beam. Tube current (mA) only effects the number of x-rays emitted, not their energy.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Does not occur in the patient during CT scanning
stems.explanation: Although Compton scatter is the predominant interaction in the patient, PE does occur infrequently (eg an x-ray may undergo multiple scattering events which will reduce its energy, followed by a PE event)

stems.label: A
stems.text: Occurs between an x-ray and a free electron
stems.explanation: CS occurs when the binding energy of the electron is a negligible fraction of the x-ray energy. This is typically the case for outer shell electrons which are furthest from the nucleus and have very low BE.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The energy transferred to the electron increases with increasing scattering angle
stems.explanation: The x-ray loses more energy when scattered through a wide angle. This energy is transferred to the electron.

stems.label: C
stems.text: At higher incident x-ray energies, the energy of the scattered radiation also increases
stems.explanation: Scattered x-rays carry away a portion of the incident energy. As the energy of the incident photon increases so does the energy of the scattered photons.

stems.label: D
stems.text: It does not occur in bone for x-ray photons with energy below 45keV
stems.explanation: It is less prevalent than the photoelectric effect, but it still occurs.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Is the dominant interaction in soft tissue in nuclear medicine studies
stems.explanation: Photon energy in nuclear med studies is typically > 100keV & at this energy Compton scattering is the dominant interaction in soft tissue.

title: Regarding the effective focal spot of an x-ray tube

stems.label: A
stems.text: Is equal in size to the area of target from where x-rays are emitted
stems.explanation: The area of target from where x-rays are emitted is the 'real' focal spot size. The effective spot size is the projection of this onto the patient or image receptor. The effective focal spot size is smaller due to the target angle (line focus principle).

stems.label: B
stems.text: Decreases with increasing target angle
stems.explanation: Small target angles produce small effective focal spots

stems.label: C
stems.text: Depends on the size of the cathode filament
stems.explanation: Different filament sizes are used to create ‘broad’ & ‘fine’ focal spots

stems.label: D
stems.text: Is typically 1.0mm in conventional units
stems.explanation: Most units have a broad focal spot size of 1.2mm and a fine focal spot size of 0.6mm

stems.label: E
stems.text: Limits the contrast of the acquired image
stems.explanation: Focal spot size influences geometric unsharpness, but does not affect contrast. Contrast is determined by x-ray interactions in the patient and so depends on the kVp and the composition & thickness of the patients tissues.

title: Increasing the kVp of an x-ray tube from 60 to 80 will

stems.label: A
stems.text: Require the tube current (mA) to be reduced by approximately one-half to deliver the same dose to the image receptor
