stems.explanation: With a patient in the beam the receptor dose rises roughly as kV⁴, so the mAs must fall by about a factor of 3 — "one half" only holds free-in-air (kV²).

stems.label: B
stems.text: Reduce the relative number of photoelectric interactions that take place in the patient
stems.explanation: Probability of PE interaction decreases rapidly with increasing x-ray energy. Average x-ray energy in the beam is proportional to the tube voltage, kVp

stems.label: C
stems.text: Increase the image contrast
stems.explanation: Image contrast is created by photoelectric interactions in the patient. The relative number of these interactions will be lower at 80kVp

stems.label: D
stems.text: Reduce the amount of scattered radiation reaching the image receptor
stems.explanation: Relatively more scatter events will occur at 80kVp. This scatter will have more energy than it would at 60kVp and a greater proportion will be directed toward the receptor. Hence, more scatter is likely to reach the image receptor at 80kVp

stems.label: E
stems.text: Reduce the entrance surface dose to the patient for the same receptor dose
stems.explanation: At 80kVp a greater proportion of the beam will penetrate through the patient & reach the image receptor. Therefore, a lower entrance surface dose will be possible at 80kVp while still maintaining the same dose to the receptor.

stems.label: A
stems.text: The image plate is not sensitive to background radiation
stems.explanation: Any ionising radiation is capable of exposing the image plate.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Post-processing algorithms are selected according to the radiographic projection
stems.explanation: Digital images are produced in CR, which can be post-processed to promote visualisation of specific features in different studies.

stems.label: C
stems.text: The thickness of the phosphor layer is limited by the need to minimise read-out laser light spread
stems.explanation: A thicker phosphor will absorb more x-ray energy, making the plate more sensitive. However, the laser light used to read out the image plate will undergo greater amounts of scatter in a thick phosphor and this will degrade spatial resolution.

stems.label: D
stems.text: An inappropriately low exposure may result in increased image noise
stems.explanation: For low exposures, fewer x-rays will be used to form the image. This will increase image noise.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The image plate consists of a matrix of individual detector elements
stems.explanation: The image plate is a uniform phosphor coated onto a supporting plate. The discrete sampling of the signal during the read-out process produces a digital image.

stems.label: A
stems.text: The brightness gain is the product of the flux gain and the minification gain
stems.explanation: Brightness gain = flux gain x minification gain

stems.label: B
stems.text: The brightness gain is typically 5000-10000
stems.explanation: Brightness gain = flux gain x minification gain. Flux gain is typically 50-100 and the minification gain is typically ~100

stems.label: C
stems.text: The minification gain is numerically equal to the ratio of the diameters of the input and output screens
stems.explanation: Minification gain = area of the input screen / area of output screen. The area of each screen is proportional to square of its diameter.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The falloff in brightness towards the edge of the image intensifier is referred to as veiling glare
stems.explanation: The fall off in brightness towards the edge of the image intensifier is known as 'vignetting'

stems.label: E
stems.text: In magnification mode the limiting spatial resolution and contrast ratio both improve
stems.explanation: Spatial resolution and contrast are improved but at the expense of increased patient dose

title: Regarding gamma camera imaging with Tc99m

stems.label: A
stems.text: Tc99m decays by electron capture
stems.explanation: Tc99m decays via isomeric transition

stems.label: B
stems.text: Tc99m emits a gamma ray with energy of 0.14 MeV
stems.explanation: Tc99m emits gamma rays at 140keV (which is the same as 0.14MeV)

stems.label: C
stems.text: There is no associated β-particle emission
stems.explanation: Tc99m emits gamma rays, but not beta particles

stems.label: D
stems.text: The detection efficiency of the scintillator crystal is of the order of 40%
stems.explanation: The NaI crystal in a gamma camera absorbs ~90% of any Tc99m gamma rays

stems.label: E
stems.text: The effective half-life of the tracer is dependent upon the radiopharmaceutical used
stems.explanation: The effective half-life depends on both the physical half-life of the radionuclide and the biological half-life of the radiopharmaceutical

title: The contrast in a planar nuclear medicine scan is dependent

stems.label: A
stems.text: The type of collimator fitted to the gamma camera
stems.explanation: Collimators determine sensitivity & spatial resolution, but have no effect on contrast.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The separation between the patient & collimator
stems.explanation: Changing the separation between the patient & collimator will affect spatial resolution only. (The air gap technique does not work in nuclear medicine because both the primary & scattered radiation is emitted in all directions).

stems.label: C
stems.text: The width of the pulse height analyser window
stems.explanation: The width of the pulse height analyser window will control the amount of scatter being recorded in the image. Wider PHA windows allow more scatter into the image. Scatter always reduces contrast.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The delay between injection and scan
stems.explanation: Contrast in nuclear medicine depends on the relative uptake of the radioactive tracer in different organs. A delay between injection and scanning allows for greater biological clearance of the tracer from background tissues.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The radiochemical purity of the radiopharmaceutical
stems.explanation: Contrast in nuclear medicine depends on the relative uptake of the radioactive tracer in different organs. Radiochemical purity of the radiopharmaceutical refers to the % of total radioactivity that is bound to the pharmaceutical. So a radiochemical purity of 90% means 10% of the administered activity is 'unbound' and will be taken up by different organs than the administered radiopharmaceutical. Hence, the radiochemical purity (or labelling efficiency) will affect the relative distribution of the tracer within the patient, and therefore the contrast.

title: Regarding planar bone scanning in nuclear medicine

stems.label: A
stems.text: Spatial resolution deteriorates with increasing distance from the collimator
stems.explanation: Gamma camera collimators are very 'short-sighted'. Spatial resolution deteriorates with increasing distance from the collimator.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The spatial resolution of the images is typically 10mm FWHM
stems.explanation: This is a typical value for planar whole-body bone scans

stems.label: C
stems.text: The activity can only be administered by a practitioner with an ARSAC license
stems.explanation: Administration can be performed by a trained IRMER operator (eg a radiographer) following a written protocol.

stems.label: D
stems.text: There is a legal limit of 600MBq on the injected activity
stems.explanation: 600MBq is the national DRL for planar bone scanning. The DRL can be exceeded in individual circumstances provided the additional exposure is justified by the IRMER practitioner.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The effective dose to the patient is typically 3mSv
stems.explanation: This is the calculated effective dose to an average sized patient following the administration of 600MBq Tc99m-phosphonates

title: Regarding SPECT scans in nuclear medicine

stems.label: A
stems.text: Typically require the administration of larger activities than planar studies
stems.explanation: The administered activity is increased to improve image quality (SPECT reconstruction amplifies random noise)

stems.label: B
stems.text: Are acquired using high resolution collimators for studies involving Tc99m
stems.explanation: High resolution collimation is needed to compensate for the increased separation between camera & patient in a SPECT study (which deteriorates spatial resolution).

stems.label: C
stems.text: Are degraded by photon attenuation in the patient
stems.explanation: Photon attenuation causes an apparent reduction in the intensity of deeper structures compared to more superficial ones and must be corrected for.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Are degraded by gamma camera non-uniformity
stems.explanation: Gamma camera non-uniformity can cause ring artefacts in SPECT images

stems.label: E
stems.text: Have poorer spatial resolution than planar studies
stems.explanation: SPECT studies are acquired at greater collimator-patient separations than planar studies, leading to degraded spatial resolution. Also SPECT reconstruction results in additional smoothing/blurring of the images. However, SPECT images have much better contrast than planar images.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Sodium iodide is typically used as the detector crystal
stems.explanation: Sodium iodide is not very efficient at detecting the 511keV gamma rays in PET. Instead, BGO, LSO or GSO are frequently used as scintillators in PET scanners.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The sensitivity of the scanner for detecting radiation is much higher than for SPECT cameras
stems.explanation: The sensitivity is higher in PET because collimators (which absorb most of the radiation) are not used

stems.label: C
stems.text: Both positrons & gamma radiation are detected
stems.explanation: PET scanners do not detect positrons; they detect annihilation radiation (511keV gamma rays)

stems.label: D
stems.text: The spatial resolution is optimum at the centre of the detector ring
stems.explanation: Towards the edges of the detector ring, resolution is degraded by gamma ray absorption at different depths in the crystals

stems.label: E
stems.text: Each line of response requires the detection of two events in separate crystals
stems.explanation: This is known as "coincidence detection" of annihilation radiation

title: Regarding the biological effects of ionising radiation

stems.label: A
stems.text: Induction of malignancy is a deterministic effect
stems.explanation: Deterministic effects (or tissue reactions) only occur above a relatively high threshold dose. The severity of the effect increases with dose (above the threshold). They also appear very quickly after exposure. Cancer induction does not meet these criteria and is a stochastic effect.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The cornea is more radiosensitive than the lens
stems.explanation: The lens is a radiosensitive structure. Exposure of the lens can result in cataract formation. The dose limit specified in IRR17 applies to the lens of the eye.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Medical exposures in the first trimester of pregnancy increases the likelihood of the foetus having Down's syndrome
stems.explanation: Diagnostic radiology exposures typically result in a foetal dose < 50mGy. In the first trimester, the only known health effect associated with such an exposure is increased risk of paediatric cancer.

stems.label: D
stems.text: A single dose of 2 Gy to the eye may cause point opacities in the lens
stems.explanation: Cataract formation is a deterministic effect (or tissue reaction) with a threshold dose of ~0.5Gy

stems.label: E
stems.text: Gamma-rays have a higher radiation weighting factor than x-rays
stems.explanation: X-rays and gamma-rays both have a radiation weighting factor of 1

title: According to the Ionising Radiations Regulations 2017, a

stems.label: A
stems.text: Is any area where the annual effective dose to staff will exceed 1mSv
stems.explanation: An area only needs to be controlled if the annual effective dose is expected to exceed 6mSv.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Cannot be entered by pregnant members of staff
stems.explanation: Pregnant staff can enter a controlled area, but may need to follow specific work instructions while working there.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Must have a radiation warning sign at the entrance
stems.explanation: The sign must indicate the nature of the hazard (eg x-rays or unsealed radioactive sources etc)

stems.label: D
stems.text: Must have up to date local rules
stems.explanation: Local rules describe safe work practices for a controlled area.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Must have at least one appointed radiation protection supervisor (RPS)
stems.explanation: The RPS ensures that the Local Rules are followed by other staff. More than one RPS may be needed to cover all work shifts.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Are typical dose quantities for standard sized patients undergoing a specific medical exposure
stems.explanation: DRLs are recorded dose quantities for standard patients undergoing a specific examination on a particular piece of equipment.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Should be reviewed annually
stems.explanation: Annual review is not a legal requirement under IRMER17. However, annual audit of DRLs is good practice & will detect changes in technique.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Must be recorded as the dose to the patient in mSv
stems.explanation: Any convenient exposure parameter that relates to patient dose can be used (eg kVp, mAs, KAP, CTDIvol, administered activity in MBq etc)

stems.label: D
stems.text: Can never be exceeded during routine procedures
stems.explanation: They can be exceeded in individual cases. DRLs are guidance values for the exposure of 'standard size' patients.

stems.label: E
stems.text: National DRLs should be achievable in most radiology departments
stems.explanation: National DRLs should be achievable, however, local DRLs will depend on the type of equipment available.

stems.label: A
stems.text: The activity of each patient dose must be measured prior to administration
stems.explanation: This is a requirement under IRMER17

stems.label: B
stems.text: National DRLs for common procedures are published by the Care Quality Commission
stems.explanation: National DRLs are published by ARSAC

stems.label: C
stems.text: They may only be administered intravenously
stems.explanation: Inhalation & oral administrations are also allowed

stems.label: D
stems.text: A fraction of the administered activity is assumed to be excreted as liquid radioactive waste
stems.explanation: Typically 40% of all Tc99m administrations are assumed to go down the toilet as waste.

stems.label: E
stems.text: All administrations must be performed in a controlled area
stems.explanation: This is not necessarily true it depends on the findings of the radiation risk assessment

stems.label: A
stems.text: The primary function of a bow tie filter is to reduce the appearance of streak artifacts from metal implants
stems.explanation: The bow tie filter is used to control peripheral patient dose

stems.label: B
stems.text: Beam hardening artifacts commonly occur at bone-soft tissue junctions
stems.explanation: Bone preferentially absorbs low energy x-rays due to its high atomic number (Z) and mass density. As low energy ("soft") photons are removed form the beam, the average photon energy will increase, making it more penetrating ("harder").

stems.label: C
stems.text: Partial volume artifacts can be reduced by increasing the pitch
stems.explanation: The partial volume artifact refers to the averaging of signals from multiple different tissues within pixels. Measured signals are averaged during spiral CT. As the pitch increases more averaging occurs, making partial volume effects more likely.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The calculated CT number of any tissue is independent of the X-ray tube voltage (kVp)
stems.explanation: The CT number is a measure of the attenuation properties of a tissue relative to that for water. The attenuation coefficients of water & human tissues change to different extents with increasing x-ray energy (kVp), hence, CT numbers are dependent on kVp.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The calculated CT number of any tissue is independent of the X-ray tube current (mA)
stems.explanation: The CT number is a measure of the attenuating properties of a tissue relative to that for water. The attenuation coefficients of water & human tissues are not affected by mA (mA changes the total number of x-ray photons in the beam, but not their energy).

title: Spatial resolution in CT imaging can be improved by

stems.label: A
stems.text: Using a smaller focal spot size
stems.explanation: Using a smaller focal spot size reduces geometric unsharpness

stems.label: B
stems.text: Sampling the transmitted x-ray signal using smaller x-ray detectors
stems.explanation: Smaller detectors offer improved spatial sampling of the transmitted x-ray beam, which will improve the spatial resolution

stems.label: C
stems.text: Decreasing the scan time
stems.explanation: Decreasing the scan time reduces the possibility of patient motion artifacts

stems.label: D
stems.text: Interpolating the final image from a 512x512 matrix to a 1024x1024 matrix
stems.explanation: Interpolation occurs after the data has been acquired. The spatial resolution cannot be improved beyond the detector size used to sample the transmitted x-ray beam during acquisition. Interpolation reduces the apparent size of pixels in the image (to make them less noticeable), but because it occurs after the acquisition, it does not improve spatial resolution.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Increasing the slice thickness
stems.explanation: Increasing the slice thickness will reduce spatial resolution along the axial direction, leading to greater partial volume artifacts (blurring of signal).

title: Regarding the noise recorded in a CT study is increased

stems.label: A
stems.text: By increasing the matrix size
stems.explanation: Increasing the matrix size (eg from 256x256 to 512x512) will make the pixels smaller. The number of photons recorded in each pixel will therefore decrease, hence random/Poisson noise will increase.

stems.label: B
stems.text: When imaging obese patients
stems.explanation: There will be greater attenuation of the beam, which will reduce the number of x-rays reaching the detectors hence, random noise will increase.

stems.label: C
stems.text: By decreasing the gantry rotation speed
stems.explanation: Decreasing the gantry rotation speed (fewer rotations per second) will increase the the number of x-rays emitted per slice of the study and therefore decrease the noise.

stems.label: D
stems.text: By increasing the tube current (mA)
stems.explanation: Increasing the tube current will increase the number of x-rays emitted per rotation and therefore decrease the noise (because more x-rays are detected per CT slice).

stems.label: E
stems.text: By decreasing the display window width
stems.explanation: Decreasing the display window width will enhance the visualisation of small differences in image intensity. Noise may become more apparent, but the actual level of noise recorded in the image will not change.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Is measured in units of mGy/cm
stems.explanation: CTDI is measured in mGy

stems.label: B
stems.text: Is the dose delivered to the organs of the patient
stems.explanation: CTDI is the average dose in a standard-sized Perspex phantom. It can be used to compare radiation doses for different imaging protocols.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Increases with tube current (mA)
stems.explanation: CTDI is directly proportional to tube current (mA)

stems.label: D
stems.text: Increases with the pitch of the scan
stems.explanation: Both CTDI and patient dose decrease with increasing pitch for spiral CT scans (CTDIvol= CTDI/pitch)

stems.label: E
stems.text: Is higher for head scans than for body scans when using the same scan parameters
stems.explanation: A 32cm diameter phantom is used to measure CTDI for body imaging. A 16cm diameter phantom is used to measure CTDI for head imaging. Due to the smaller phantom size for head scans, there is less attenuation causing the dose along the central axis of the phantom to increase.

title: Regarding Patient doses delivered during CT imaging

stems.label: A
stems.text: Are proportional to the tube current (mA)
stems.explanation: Increasing the mA will increase the mAs, which is proportional to the number of x-rays interacting with (& delivering a dose to) the patient.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Are proportional to the gantry rotation speed
stems.explanation: Patient dose is directly proportional to the mAs. Increasing the gantry speed will reduce the acquisition time per slice and therefore the mAs. Hence patient dose will decrease.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Increase with the pitch of the scan
stems.explanation: As pitch increases, there are increasing gaps between consecutive CT slices. Hence, the x-ray beam passes through a smaller volume of tissue. The patient dose therefore decreases.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Can be reduced using iterative reconstruction techniques
stems.explanation: Iterative reconstruction (IR) can reduce the noise in a reconstructed image. Therefore, IR permits lower exposure parameters to be used (which would normally increase noise), without any overall increase in noise. Using lower exposure parameters will reduce patient dose.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Are typically 4mSv effective dose for a study of the abdomen & pelvis
stems.explanation: 8mSv would be more typical for a CT study of the abdomen & pelvis

title: In MR imaging, the Larmor frequency is

stems.label: A
stems.text: The rate at which protons precess in a magnetic field
stems.explanation: Protons will precess at the Larmor frequency in a magnetic field.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Proportional to the field strength, Bo
stems.explanation: A proton will precess twice as fast in a 2T field compared to a 1T field

stems.label: C
stems.text: Proportional to the T1 relaxation time
stems.explanation: T1 is a measure of how quickly the longitudinal magnetisation recovers after a 90 degree pulse. It does not affect the Larmor frequency.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Inversely proportional to the gyromagnetic ratio
stems.explanation: Larmor frequency is proportional to the gyromagnetic ratio. Different nuclei have different gyromagnetic ratios.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Decreases with time due to relaxation processes
stems.explanation: Relaxation processes govern the behaviour of the MR signal, not the Larmor frequency of individual protons.

stems.label: A
stems.text: The bulk magnetisation vector, Mo represents a single proton precessing about the axis of the main magnetic field, Bo
stems.explanation: Mo represents the collective behaviour of the proton spin population.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The magnitude of Mo is independent of the strength of Bo
stems.explanation: Mo is directly proportional to Bo

stems.label: C
stems.text: After a 90 degree RF pulse the longitudinal and transverse magnetisation vectors are equal in size
stems.explanation: After a 90 degree pulse the longitudinal magnetisation vector, Mz=0, while the transverse magnetisation vector, Mxy=Mo

stems.label: D
stems.text: After a 180 degree RF pulse the nuclear spin population will be inverted
stems.explanation: A 180 degree pulse will invert the spin population. Note that the protons themselves are not physically relocated just the phase of their spin.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Rotation of the magnetisation vector in the x-y plane gives rise to the MR signal
stems.explanation: A rotating magnetisation vector will induce a voltage in a receiver coil

title: Regarding the spin echo pulse sequence

stems.label: A
stems.text: After the 90 degree RF pulse, magnetic field inhomogeneities cause the protons to lose phase coherence
stems.explanation: This is true, but dephasing also occurs due to intermolecular spin-spin interactions

stems.label: B
stems.text: The 180 degree RF pulse rephases the spins
stems.explanation: Rephasing the spins creates an echo signal at a time TE/2 after the 180 degree pulse

stems.label: C
stems.text: The spin echo signal appears at a time TE after the 180 degree pulse
stems.explanation: The MR signal (echo) appears at time TE after the 90 degree pulse

stems.label: D
stems.text: It can be used to generate either T1 or T2 weighted images
stems.explanation: T1 or T2 weighted images can be generated by choosing appropriate values for TR (pulse repetition time) & TE (time to echo).

stems.label: E
stems.text: Multiple sequential 180 degree pulses can be applied after the 90 degree pulse to improve the contrast in T1-weighted images
stems.explanation: Multiple 180 degree pulses are used in FSE (Fast Spin Echo) sequences where contrast is compromised for faster imaging

title: Regarding Gradient recalled echo pulse sequences

stems.label: A
stems.text: Frequently use flip angles < 90 degrees
stems.explanation: A small flip angle allows greater recovery of the longitudinal magnetisation vector, Mz between repeated pulse excitations. This allows shorter pulse repetition intervals (TR) and faster scans.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Apply a 180 degree RF pulse to generate the MR signal
stems.explanation: A bipolar gradient field is used to dephase & subsequently rephase the spin population to generate an “echo” signal.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Can be used to generate T2-weighted images
stems.explanation: GRE sequences produce T2* weighted images (ie as well as the T2 relaxation time of the tissues, the inhomogeneity of the main magnetic field also contributes to the decay of the MR signal).

stems.label: D
stems.text: Are often used for MR angiography
stems.explanation: GRE is a fast imaging procedure that can be used to generate blood flow studies

stems.label: E
stems.text: Are affected by main field inhomogeneities
stems.explanation: The bipolar gradient used to generate the echo signal cannot compensate for inhomogeneities of the main magnetic field

stems.label: A
stems.text: Travel at a speed of 1540m/s in soft tissue
stems.explanation: US waves travel at slightly different speeds through different tissues. However, they have an average velocity of 1540m/s through soft tissue.

stems.label: B
stems.text: In bone, travel at greater than twice the speed compared to soft tissue
stems.explanation: The speed of US wave propagation depends on the stiffness and density of the medium. Bone has a higher density & is much stiffer than soft tissue, hence the wave speed is much higher (4,000m/s)

stems.label: C
stems.text: Deposit more energy in bone & ligaments than soft tissue
stems.explanation: Tissues with a high collagen content are strong absorbers of US radiation

stems.label: D
stems.text: Can ionise molecules
stems.explanation: US is regarded as being safe because the radiation is non-ionising

stems.label: E
stems.text: Have a wavelength of 1-5mm in soft tissue
stems.explanation: The wavelength of US waves in soft tissue is typically 0.3-1mm

title: Regarding the interaction of US beams with human tissue

stems.label: A
stems.text: The intensity of a beam decreases exponentially with depth
stems.explanation: US radiation undergoes exponential attenuation in tissue. This means a fixed fraction of the beam energy is removed per cm travelled

stems.label: B
stems.text: Both reflection & refraction can occur at the junction of two tissues with differing acoustic impedances
stems.explanation: Both processes can occur when there is a change in acoustic impedance, but refraction will only occur if the beam strikes the interface at an oblique angle

stems.label: C
stems.text: Most of the beam energy is converted to heat in the patient
stems.explanation: Only a small amount of US energy is detected to form an image, the rest is converted into heat

stems.label: D
stems.text: US radiation does not interact with structures that are smaller than the wavelength of the US pulse
stems.explanation: US radiation is scattered by objects that are smaller than the wavelength

stems.label: E
stems.text: The attenuation coefficient of soft tissue is typically 0.8dB/cm at 1MHz
stems.explanation: Quoted values range from 0.5 1.0 dB/cm/MHz

title: The axial resolution of an ultrasound image depends on

stems.label: A
stems.text: The diameter of the transducer crystal
stems.explanation: This will change the width of the beam line & so will affect lateral resolution, rather than axial resolution.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The pulse repetition frequency (PRF)
stems.explanation: PRF is the number of pulses emitted per second. This will not affect axial resolution.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Focusing of the US beam
stems.explanation: Beam focusing will change the width of the beam line & so will affect lateral resolution, rather than axial resolution.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The spatial pulse length (SPL)
stems.explanation: Spatial pulse length (number of waves in each pulse x wavelength) directly affects axial resolution. Axial resolution = SPL/2

stems.label: E
stems.text: The depth of the target in the patient
stems.explanation: Axial resolution = Spatial pulse length (SPL) / 2. The SPL does not change with depth, so axial resolution is independent of depth.

title: Regarding the Doppler Effect in US imaging

stems.label: A
stems.text: The frequency of reflected US waves decreases for objects moving towards the transducer
stems.explanation: The frequency increases for objects moving towards the receiver

stems.label: B
stems.text: The effect is greatest for structures moving at right angles to the direction of the US beam
stems.explanation: The effect is most noticeable when the beam is in the same direction as the motion

stems.label: C
stems.text: It requires a higher frequency than B-mode studies
stems.explanation: The same range of frequencies are used for both B-mode & Doppler

stems.label: D
stems.text: The maximum detectable frequency shift is one-half of the pulse repetition frequency (PRF)
stems.explanation: This is true for pulsed Doppler

stems.label: E
stems.text: Aliasing does not occur during continuous wave Doppler
stems.explanation: Aliasing only occurs with pulsed Doppler

title: Regarding the biological effects of ultrasound radiation

stems.label: A
stems.text: Thermal effects are more prevalent in bone than soft tissue
stems.explanation: Bone is a stronger absorber of US than soft tissue, so thermal effects will be greater

stems.label: B
stems.text: B-mode scans are potentially more dangerous than Doppler mode
stems.explanation: Doppler uses higher power, longer pulses & must radiate along the same scan line multiple times. These factors can potentially result in higher temperature rises in tissues.

stems.label: C
stems.text: The exposure time of a foetal examination should be restricted for a thermal index of 0.5
stems.explanation: Restricted imaging times are recommended only if TI > 0.7

stems.label: D
stems.text: Neonatal lung damage can occur if the mechanical index > 0.3
stems.explanation: There is increased risk of mechanical damage (cavitation ) in lung tissue for MI > 0.3

stems.label: E
stems.text: Cavitation occurs more readily when contrast agents are used
stems.explanation: US contrast agents contain gas-filled micro-bubbles. When exposed to US radiation these bubbles are more likely to undergo cavitation than soft tissue.

stems.label: A
stems.text: The energy of each photon is proportional to its frequency
stems.explanation: Higher frequency EM radiation is more energetic

stems.label: B
stems.text: Photon energy is usually expressed in joules
stems.explanation: The electron-volt (eV) is typically used to express photon energy

stems.label: C
stems.text: The speed with which a photon travels depends on its energy
stems.explanation: All photons travel at the speed of light in a vacuum

stems.label: D
stems.text: Microwaves and ultraviolet radiation are examples
stems.explanation: Microwaves have a longer wavelength than visible light, whereas UV has a shorter wavelength

stems.label: E
stems.text: Gamma and x-ray photons of the same energy have different wavelengths
stems.explanation: They are identical in every way (energy, frequency, wavelength). The only difference is the manner in which the photons were produced.

stems.label: A
stems.text: The photoelectric effect can only occur when the energy of the incident x-ray exceeds the binding energy of the electron
stems.explanation: When the photon energy < BE the electron cannot be liberated from the atom

stems.label: B
stems.text: Compton scattering cannot involve K-shell electrons
stems.explanation: CS occurs in hydrogen where the single atomic electron resides in the K-shell. The main requirement for CS is that the BE of the electron is negligible in comparison with the energy of the photon.

stems.label: C
stems.text: The probability of occurrence of both photoelectric & Compton scattering events decreases with increasing x-ray energy
stems.explanation: This is why x-ray beams are more penetrating at at higher energies (at higher tube voltages)

stems.label: D
stems.text: The photoelectric event is the predominant mode of x-ray interaction with iodinebased contrast media
stems.explanation: Iodine has a high atomic number (Z=54) which encourages more PE events to occur. Remember the probability of PE events is proportional to Z^3

stems.label: E
stems.text: Compton scattering is the predominant mode of x-ray interaction in soft tissue during CT exposures
stems.explanation: CT operates at 120-140kVp with heavy beam filtration. The average photon energy in the beam is 50-60keV and CS predominates at these energies in soft tissue.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Bremsstrahlung x-rays are emitted when an electron interacts with the nucleus of an atom in the target
stems.explanation: The electron undergoes a sudden deceleration and the change in kinetic energy is released as an x-ray photon

stems.label: B
stems.text: The efficiency of bremsstrahlung emission is typically 10% in diagnostic x-ray tubes
stems.explanation: In diagnostic radiology only about 1% of the electron energy striking the target is emitted as bremsstrahlung x-rays

stems.label: C
stems.text: Bremsstrahlung production is more efficient at higher tube voltages
stems.explanation: The probability of bremsstrahlung interactions is proportional to: atomic number of the target atoms (Z) x x-ray tube voltage (kVp). Hence, more bremsstrahlung x-rays are emitted at higher kVp

stems.label: D
stems.text: For a tungsten x-ray target both L-shell and K-shell characteristic x-rays can reach the image receptor
stems.explanation: Characteristic x-rays from the L-shell are very low energy & easily absorbed in the patient

stems.label: E
stems.text: The energy of K-shell characteristic x-rays is always just less than the K-shell binding energy
stems.explanation: Characteristic x-ray energy is the difference in binding energy (BE) of 2 electron shells. So for an electron transition between the M-shell and the K-shell, the energy of the characteristic x-ray will be: X-ray energy = BE K-shell BE M-shell So the characteristic x-ray will always have slightly lower energy than the BE of the electron shell it was emitted from

title: The following actions will improve the spatial resolution of an

stems.label: A
stems.text: Decreasing the focal spot size from 1.6mm to 0.6mm
stems.explanation: A smaller focal spot will reduce the penumbra around structures, which improves spatial resolution

stems.label: B
stems.text: Increasing the tube current (mA)
stems.explanation: Increasing the mA (in isolation) will not improve resolution. Increasing the mA may allow for a shorter exposure time (which would reduce patient motion blur), however, the question didn't mention any change in exposure time.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Using an anti-scatter grid with a higher grid ratio
stems.explanation: Using a higher grid ratio will improve contrast (by removing scatter) but will affect not spatial resolution.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Increasing the amount of added filtration in the beam
stems.explanation: Filtration changes the energy spectrum of the beam by preferentially removing low energy x-rays (which will affect contrast & patient dose), but will have no effect on spatial resolution.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Decreasing the patient-to-image receptor distance
stems.explanation: Decreasing the patient-to-image receptor distance will reduce geometric unsharpness (ie reduce the size of the penumbra around structures). In routine radiography the image receptor is positioned as close as possible to the patient.

title: Increasing the tube voltage of a diagnostic x-ray set will

stems.label: A
stems.text: Increase the half value layer (HVL) of the beam
stems.explanation: The beam is more penetrating at higher kVp, so a greater thickness of attenuating material will be needed to reduce the intensity by 50% (ie the HVL will increase).

stems.label: B
stems.text: Increase the entrance skin dose (ESD) in direct proportion
stems.explanation: The ESD will increase, but not in direct proportion. ESD will increase according to the square of the kV

stems.label: C
stems.text: Reduce the effective dose to the patient if the image receptor dose is kept constant
stems.explanation: The beam is more penetrating, so there is less absorption in the patient for the same dose to the image receptor

stems.label: D
stems.text: Increase the exposure time if the image receptor dose is kept constant
stems.explanation: The exposure time (mAs) can be REDUCED — the higher-kV beam is both more intense and more penetrating, so the same receptor dose arrives in a shorter time.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Decrease the level of quantum mottle in the image
stems.explanation: Increasing kVp (in isolation) will mean that more x-rays are emitted. Their energy is also increased so a greater proportion reach the image receptor, so image noise will decrease

stems.label: A
stems.text: Spatial resolution increases with pixel depth
stems.explanation: Pixel depth determines the number of x-rays that can be recorded by each pixel. However, pixel size (its physical dimensions) is the only factor that affects spatial resolution.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Objects smaller than the pixel size cannot be visualised
stems.explanation: Objects smaller than the pixel size will occupy a single pixel in the image. The contrast of the object will be reduced by the partial volume effect. So, visualisation is possible for small structures with high contrast.

stems.label: C
stems.text: High pass filtering can improve spatial resolution
stems.explanation: High pass filters are edge enhancement filters that improve resolution, but also increase image noise

stems.label: D
stems.text: They have typical dynamic range of 10,000:1
stems.explanation: The dynamic range is the ratio of the largest to the smallest measurable signal by the detector. Digital detectors have a broad dynamic range, which allows for the visualization of both subtle and extreme variations in tissue density within the same image

stems.label: E
stems.text: They reduce the need for repeat exposures
stems.explanation: Because they have a wide dynamic range, digital detectors are less likely to be overexposed or underexposed which would require a repeat exposure (this was a problem with conventional film-screen systems).

stems.label: A
stems.text: Images with contrast media are subtracted from a mask image
stems.explanation: The mask image is subtracted from the post-contrast (“Live”) image

stems.label: B
stems.text: Logarithmic subtraction eliminates the effects of over& underlying tissues
stems.explanation: Attenuation in the surrounding tissues is exponential with depth, rather than linear. Logarithmic subtraction (rather than linear subtraction) takes this into account to provide a more accurate removal of background.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Live images cannot be produced
stems.explanation: Subtraction can be performed very rapidly to generate subtracted images in real time

stems.label: D
stems.text: The subtraction process increases the random noise content of the images
stems.explanation: The subtraction process removes detected x-rays from the final images. Subtracted images will therefore contain fewer detected events, thus increasing the random (Poisson) noise level.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The subtraction process improves spatial resolution
stems.explanation: The subtraction process enhances image contrast, but does not affect spatial resolution

stems.label: A
stems.text: The tube voltage is typically 25-35kVp
stems.explanation: Low tube voltages are used in mammography to promote photoelectric absorption in the patient (which will maximize image contrast)

stems.label: B
stems.text: The focal spot size is typically 1mm
stems.explanation: 0.3mm focal spot sizes are routinely used to improve spatial resolution

stems.label: C
stems.text: The source-to-image distance is typically 100cm
stems.explanation: The source-to-image distance is typically 65cm. The x-ray output from a mammographic unit is lower than for conventional radiographic units (due to low kVp and lower Z targets). Using a longer source-image distance would reduce the beam intensity further (due to the inverse-square law) and require longer exposure times.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Characteristic x-rays must be filtered out of the beam
stems.explanation: High & low energy bremsstrahlung x-rays are filtered out of the beam using K-edge filtration. The energy of the characteristic x-rays is just right to maximise image contrast and these are preferentially transmitted by the k-edge filter.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Screening is justified because breast tissue has a low radiosensitivity
stems.explanation: The breast is radiosensitive, but screening is justified because asymptomatic lesions can be detected (and treated) at fairly low radiation doses, ie there is a net benefit to the exposure.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Tc99m is supplied by eluting a molybdenum generator each morning
stems.explanation: The Mo99-Tc99m generator is eluted each morning to provide a fresh supply of Tc99m

stems.label: B
stems.text: Tc99m gamma rays have a HVL of approximately 5cm in soft tissue
stems.explanation: This means that radiation emitted from a depth of 10cm will be attenuated by a factor of ~75%

stems.label: C
stems.text: Tc99m gamma rays predominantly interact with soft tissue via Compton scattering
stems.explanation: Tc99m gamma rays have an energy of 140keV which favours Compton scattering interactions in low Z materials (soft tissue).

stems.label: D
stems.text: The thickness of the scintillation crystal in a gamma camera affects both its spatial resolution & sensitivity
stems.explanation: Thicker crystals have better sensitivity (ie detect more radiation) but poorer spatial resolution

stems.label: E
stems.text: The width of the pulse height analyser window will affect both the contrast resolution & sensitivity of the gamma camera
stems.explanation: The PHA window controls the amount of scatter reaching the image. A wide PHA window allows more scattered radiation to be detected (so sensitivity will increase), however increased scatter will reduce image contrast.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Longer acquisition times will reduce image noise
stems.explanation: Longer acquisition times will allow more gamma rays to be detected, which reduces random (Poisson) noise

stems.label: B
stems.text: Dynamic studies are seldom performed
stems.explanation: Dynamic imaging is frequently used in renal, lymphatic and gastrointestinal studies.

stems.label: C
stems.text: The injected activity for thyroid imaging using Tc99m is typically 80MBq
stems.explanation: 80MBq is the national DRL specified by ARSAC. In a normal patient 1-4% of this activity will localise in the thyroid gland.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Using a high resolution collimator will allow shorter acquisition times
stems.explanation: High resolution collimators have reduced sensitivity and so allow fewer gamma rays to be detected each second. Hence, longer acquisition times are needed to acquire a pre-defined number of counts.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The spatial resolution in a bone scan image changes with increasing delay between administration of the radiopharmaceutical & scan acquisition
stems.explanation: Increasing the delay will allow greater clearance of tracer from background tissues. This will affect image contrast, not spatial resolution.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Reducing the angular sampling interval will improve the spatial resolution of SPECT images
stems.explanation: Decreasing the angular sampling interval form say 6-degrees to 3-degrees will increase the number of projections recorded in the SPECT study. Spatial resolution improves with increasing number of angular samples (projections).

stems.label: B
stems.text: Increasing the matrix size from 128x128 to 256x256 will improve the spatial resolution of SPECT images
stems.explanation: Changing the matrix size would improve resolution if pixel size was the limiting factor. In SPECT studies, the spatial resolution of the camera is very poor, so making the pixels smaller will not alter the sharpness of the images.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Spatial resolution is uniform throughout transaxial PET images
stems.explanation: Spatial resolution is optimum at the centre of transaxial images (ie along the central axis of the detector rings) and degrades slightly towards the periphery.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Spatial resolution in PET is better than that in SPECT
stems.explanation: Spatial resolution in PET is typically 4mm FWHM, while SPECT is ~10mm FWHM

stems.label: E
stems.text: In PET studies, the bed positions must be overlapped by at least 33% to compensate for axial variations in sensitivity
stems.explanation: This is done to compensate for the triangular axial sensitivity profile in 3D PET (sensitivity is largest in the centre of the axial FoV and decreases linearly towards the boundary of the FoV)

stems.label: A
stems.text: Random coincidences do not affect image quality
stems.explanation: Random coincidences are mis-positioned events and therefore reduce image contrast and must be corrected for.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The CT dose is much larger than that delivered by the 18FDG
stems.explanation: The effective dose from CT is typically 4-5mSv, which is lower than the dose from FDG (typically 5-6mSv)

stems.label: C
stems.text: The injected activity of 18FDG for adults is typically 100MBq
stems.explanation: Most adults will be injected with 250-350MBq FDG (the actual dose is based on patient weight, typically 3.0 4.0 MBq per kg are administered)

stems.label: D
stems.text: The effective dose to adult patients from 18FDG administration is typically 6mSv
stems.explanation: For administered activities in the range 250-350MBq the effective dose will be 5-7mSv

stems.label: E
stems.text: An uptake time of 30 minutes is used to prevent excessive decay of 18F
stems.explanation: Uptake periods of 60min are used for to permit optimum uptake in lesions

stems.label: A
stems.text: Require employers to be registered prior to starting diagnostic x-ray work
stems.explanation: The employer must register with the HSE prior to starting x-ray imaging work

stems.label: B
stems.text: Specify dose limits for occupational & medical exposures
stems.explanation: Medical exposures are not subjected to dose limits

stems.label: C
stems.text: Do not apply to procedures involving unsealed radionuclides
stems.explanation: The regulations apply to occupational exposure to any type of ionising radiation

stems.label: D
stems.text: Place responsibility for providing protection on the radiation protection adviser (RPA)
stems.explanation: The employer is responsible for providing protection. The RPA advises the employer on matters of radiation safety & compliance with IRR17.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Require all doses to be kept as low as reasonably practicable (ALARP)
stems.explanation: Doses being ALARP refers to dose optimisation, which is a fundamental requirement of the regulations

stems.label: A
stems.text: Any person performing QC tests on medical radiation equipment is acting as an operator
stems.explanation: An operator is someone who carries out practical aspects of a patient exposure. The outcome of equipment testing could significantly affect patient exposures

stems.label: B
stems.text: The practitioner is legally responsible for all aspects of the exposure
stems.explanation: Each professional is individually responsible for their own role in any patient exposure. The practitioner's responsibility is to justify the exposure.

stems.label: C
stems.text: The patient must be informed when an unintended or accidental exposure has occurred
stems.explanation: This will depend on the Employer's duty of candour policy. IRMER17 doesn't specify that the patient must be informed of any unintended exposure.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The regulations do not permit the exposure of a person unless they will benefit from it directly
stems.explanation: Normal volunteers can be exposed as part of a research trial and may not benefit from the exposure (society as a whole may benefit though).

stems.label: E
stems.text: Nuclear medicine studies may only be performed if both the practitioner and the employer possess a valid licence
stems.explanation: The licensing scheme under IRMER requires both the practitioner and the nuclear medicine department (ie the Employer) to hold a valid licence.

title: Regarding the management of radioactive waste in diagnostic

stems.label: A
stems.text: Patients administered with Tc99m-labelled tracers are expected to excrete 40% of the administered activity in their urine
stems.explanation: Excretion factors are used to estimate radioactive discharges. It is assumed that 40% of all Tc99m administrations enter the hospital sewer

stems.label: B
stems.text: Radioactive urine from injected patients must be stored in delay tanks for up to 1 week before entering the sewer
stems.explanation: Radioactive urine is discharged directly to the sewer, where it is diluted with non-radioactive waste

stems.label: C
stems.text: Solid radioactive waste containing Tc99m is typically stored on-site for up to 1 week
stems.explanation: Storage for 1 week will allow the radioactivity to decay to background levels

stems.label: D
stems.text: Injected in-patients can only return to another hospital or nursing home if that organisation has a permit for the disposal of radioactive waste
stems.explanation: Hospitals are exempt from needing a permit if they receive small numbers of injected patients each year

stems.label: E
stems.text: The MPE is responsible for ensuring that hospitals comply with the conditions of their radioactive waste permit
stems.explanation: The Radioactive Waste Advisor (RWA) is responsible for ensuring compliance with the regulations

title: Regarding radiation risks from medical exposures

stems.label: A
stems.text: The average effective dose to the UK population from all sources of radiation is approximately 0.3mSv
stems.explanation: It is approximately 2.7mSv per year

stems.label: B
stems.text: Approximately 15-20% of the annual dose is due to medical exposures
stems.explanation: On average, about 0.4mSv per year is due to medical irradiation. This is 0.4/2.7 = 15% of the total

stems.label: C
stems.text: An effective dose of 10mSv carries with it a risk of cancer induction of 1 in 2000
stems.explanation: The risk factor for cancer induction is 1 in 20,000 per mSv (averaged over the whole population). A dose of 10mSv will carry a risk of 1 in 20,000/10 or 1 in 2,000.

stems.label: D
stems.text: A dose of 25mSv delivered to a foetus will double the risk of cancer in childhood
stems.explanation: The risk factor for cancer induction for in-utero irradiation is 1 in 13,000 per mSv. A dose of 25mSv carries a risk of 1 in 13000/25, or 1 in 520. This is similar to the natural incidence of childhood cancer (currently this is 1 in 500 in the UK)

stems.label: E
stems.text: Five CT exposures of the head within a 3 month interval can result in cataract formation in a patient
stems.explanation: The maximum dose to the eyes would be ~40mGy from a single CT scan of the head. Hence at least 12 studies would be needed to reach the dose threshold for cataract induction (500mGy).

title: Regarding the effective dose to a patient for a radiographic examination

stems.label: A
stems.text: Is the sum of the equivalent dose to each organ multiplied by their respective weighting factors
stems.explanation: Effective dose = sum of (organ dose x tissue weighting factor)

stems.label: B
stems.text: Is measured in mGy
stems.explanation: Effective dose is measured in units of mSv

stems.label: C
stems.text: Is calculated by averaging the entrance and exit doses
stems.explanation: Effective dose depends on doses to individual tissues and the corresponding tissue weighting factors. The entrance & exit dose are the dose in air at the points where the beam enters & leaves the patient's body respectively.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Is indicative of the radiation dose to a foetus for a pregnant patient
stems.explanation: Effective dose is a measure of the overall risk to the patient. The equivalent dose to the uterus would be indicative of foetal dose.

stems.label: E
stems.text: It is used to determine the risk from both stochastic and deterministic effects
stems.explanation: Effective dose is a measure of risk for stochastic effects only. (Deterministic effects always occur if the threshold dose is exceeded).

stems.label: A
stems.text: Pre-patient collimation is employed to remove scattered radiation
stems.explanation: Pre-patient collimators limit the volume of tissue irradiated along the z-axis of the patient. A thin antiscatter grid sits permanently on top of the bank of detectors to remove scatter.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The focal spot size is typically 1mm
stems.explanation: CT tubes generally have a large focal spot of 1.2mm and a fine focal spot of 0.6mm

stems.label: C
stems.text: The primary function of the bow tie filter is used to harden the beam
stems.explanation: The bow-tie filter is used to modulate beam intensity across the patient & reduce patient dose

stems.label: D
stems.text: Transaxial images are reconstructed using filtered backprojection
stems.explanation: FBP is still widely used to reconstruct transaxial slices

stems.label: E
stems.text: Image contrast is largely determined by tissue density
stems.explanation: Compton scatter is the predominant mode of interaction in the patient, which is dependent on the (mass) density of the patient's tissues

title: Regarding Signal-to-Noise ratio (SNR) in CT scanning

stems.label: A
stems.text: Is proportional to the tube current (mA)
stems.explanation: Increased mA will reduce noise, but SNR is proportional to √mAs (ie the square root of the mAs)

stems.label: B
stems.text: Is inversely proportional to gantry rotation speed
stems.explanation: A slower gantry rotation speed will increase the number of x-rays emitted and detected per slice. This will reduce noise, but not in a linear manner.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Increases with the pitch of the scan
stems.explanation: Increasing the pitch will increase the 'gaps' between successive slices. The patient is exposed to less radiation. This will increase image noise but reduce dose to the patient.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Is unaffected by the reconstruction filter
stems.explanation: The reconstruction filter smooths the image, which will affect SNR

stems.label: E
stems.text: Is unaffected by the CT display window width
stems.explanation: The SNR of data recorded in the image does not depend on the way it is displayed

title: Regarding the effective dose to the patient in CT

stems.label: A
stems.text: It is unaffected by pixel size
stems.explanation: Changing pixel size in isolation will not affect patient dose.

stems.label: B
stems.text: It is unaffected by slice thickness
stems.explanation: Changing slice thickness in isolation will not affect patient dose

stems.label: C
stems.text: The CT dose index (CTDI) is the organ dose delivered per slice
stems.explanation: It is the dose to a standard size phantom and is used to compare imaging protocols

stems.label: D
stems.text: It increases with the number of slices acquired
stems.explanation: More tissue will be irradiated, so the DLP will increase

stems.label: E
stems.text: It is typically 1-2mSv for a routine brain scan
stems.explanation: This is the effective dose for a standard sized patient

title: Regarding CT studies of the thorax-abdomen-pelvis in adults

stems.label: A
stems.text: CT data are acquired as a spiral scan
stems.explanation: Spiral (helical) acquisitions allow a large section to be imaged in a short period of time.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The tube voltage is typically 80-100kVp
stems.explanation: Higher tube voltages are typically used for adults, usually 120kVp or above

stems.label: C
stems.text: The in-plane spatial resolution is typically 0.7lp/mm
stems.explanation: This is typical of modern scanners

stems.label: D
stems.text: The CT acquisition is started simultaneously with IV contrast administration
stems.explanation: There must be a delay between the administration of the contrast and the start of CT acquisition to allow the contrast to reach the organs of interest in either the arterial or venous phase.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The minimum slice thickness attainable is equal to the z-axis beam collimation
stems.explanation: Beam collimation refers to the width of the beam along the z-axis, which must cover all the detectors in the array. Slice thickness is determined by the detector thickness in the z-axis.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Is produced following any RF pulse
stems.explanation: No signal will be produced after a single 180 degree pulse, or if the spin population is saturated (this can happen when 90 degree pulses are repeated at short TR intervals)

stems.label: B
stems.text: Increases with main field strength (Bo)
stems.explanation: Signal size increases because the bulk magnetisation vector, Mo, increases with Bo

stems.label: C
stems.text: Decreases in size with time
stems.explanation: The signal decays due to spin-spin (T2) relaxation

stems.label: D
stems.text: Is created by spinning hydrogen nuclei
stems.explanation: The rotation of billions of tiny magnetic nuclei creates a signal in a receiver coil

stems.label: E
stems.text: Consists of a voltage induced in a coil of wire
stems.explanation: A rotating magnetisation vector will induce a voltage in a receiver coil

title: Regarding relaxation times in MR imaging

stems.label: A
stems.text: T1 is typically 20-200ms for most tissues
stems.explanation: The typical range for T1 is 200-2000ms

stems.label: B
stems.text: T1 decreases with increasing magnetic field strength
stems.explanation: For the majority of biological tissues, the T1 relaxation time lengthens as the magnetic field strength (Bo) increases.

stems.label: C
stems.text: For any tissue, T1 is always longer than T2
stems.explanation: The MR signal (Mxy) decays away long before Mz recovers. The decay of Mxy is determined by T2 relaxation. The recovery of Mz is determined by T1 relaxation. So T2 < T1

stems.label: D
stems.text: The T2 relaxation time is a measure of how fast the MR signal decays
stems.explanation: The T2 of any tissue is the time taken (in msec) for the MR signal to decay to 37% of its full value

stems.label: E
stems.text: The T1 relaxation time influences the repetition rate of a spin echo pulse sequence
stems.explanation: TR is chosen to allow Mz to recover to a particular level before the pulse sequence is repeated. The recovery of Mz is dependent on T1 so the choice of TR also depends on T1

title: Spatial resolution of MR images is improved by

stems.label: A
stems.text: Decreasing the slice thickness
stems.explanation: Reducing the slice thickness will reduce the voxel size, which results in finer spatial sampling of the patient

stems.label: B
stems.text: Increasing the image matrix size
stems.explanation: A larger matrix size (eg going from 128x128 to 192x192) means there are more pixels covering the same field of view. Hence, pixel size will be smaller and spatial resolution will improve due to finer digital sampling of the MR signal.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Decreasing the field of view
stems.explanation: A smaller field view means the same number of pixels are used to sample a smaller region of the patient. Hence, pixel size will be smaller and spatial resolution will improve due to finer digital sampling of the MR signal.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Increasing the main magnetic field strength
stems.explanation: Increasing Bo will increase the SNR, but will not have a direct effect on spatial resolution

stems.label: E
stems.text: Increasing the time to echo (TE)
stems.explanation: Increasing TE will reduce the SNR, but will not affect spatial resolution

stems.label: A
stems.text: Occurs for tissues containing fat and water
stems.explanation: Because of the local magnetic effects of orbiting electrons, protons in water and fat have slightly different Larmor frequencies when placed in a strong magnetic field. This is the basis of the chemical shift artefact

stems.label: B
stems.text: Is more prominent at high field strengths
stems.explanation: The difference in Larmor frequency between water & fat is enhanced at higher field strengths

stems.label: C
stems.text: Is minimised by the STIR pulse sequence
stems.explanation: The signal from fat is eliminated by STIR

stems.label: D
stems.text: Is visible along the frequency encode axis of the image
stems.explanation: Changes in frequency are related to linear position along the frequency encode axis. Hence, the chemical shift artefact causes fat and water to be placed in different positions along this direction.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Is caused by inhomogeneities in the main field
stems.explanation: The artefact occurs because of differences in the intrinsic magnetic properties of protons in water and fat molecules

title: Regarding biological effects in MR imaging

stems.label: A
stems.text: Static magnetic field strengths of 5T and above can interfere with brain function
stems.explanation: There is no evidence of permanent biological effects < 8 T

stems.label: B
stems.text: Any metal object presents a projectile hazard in the fringe field of the scanner
stems.explanation: Only ferromagnetic objects (ie those containing iron, nickel or cobalt) will be strongly attracted towards the scanner bore and present a missile hazard.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Rapid gradient switching can cause peripheral nerve stimulation
stems.explanation: During the acquisition of an image slice, the three gradient fields are switched on and off very rapidly. A rapidly changing magnetic field can induce a rapidly changing electric current that is capable of nerve stimulation in patients.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The specific absorption rate (SAR) is a measure of tissue heating
stems.explanation: RF energy absorbed in the body causes an increase in temperature & this is quantified by the SAR

stems.label: E
stems.text: Metal implants may be affected by the magnetic fields of both the main field & the RF pulses
stems.explanation: A ferromagnetic implant can be made to move or rotate in the presence of the Bo field, while the selective absorption of the RF field in the metal can cause elevated temperatures and increase the risk of burning adjacent tissues

title: In ultrasound examinations, the acoustic impedance of a

stems.label: A
stems.text: Increases with the mass density of the tissue
stems.explanation: Acoustic impedance measures how much a medium resists the transmission of sound waves. Denser tissues, like bone, have molecules packed closely together and this contributes to higher acoustic impedance.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Increases with the speed of propagation of the beam in the tissue
stems.explanation: Sound travels faster through stiffer, less compressible materials. This 'stiffness' also increases the acoustic impedance of the medium. Hence, acoustic impedance increases with the speed of sound.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Depends on whether the tissue is stationary or moving
stems.explanation: Acoustic impedance is an intrinsic property of the tissue regardless of its state of motion

stems.label: D
stems.text: Is measured in units of decibels (dB)
stems.explanation: dB are used to compare the relative intensity of waves (for instance for quantifying attenuation). Acoustic impedance is measured in units called Rayls

stems.label: E
stems.text: Muscle has a greater acoustic impedance than fat
stems.explanation: Muscle has a slightly higher density than fat, so its acoustic impedance will be slightly greater.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Multiple pulses are sent down a single scan line
stems.explanation: This is true for A-mode & M-mode scans, but not for B-mode

stems.label: B
stems.text: Real time images are produced
stems.explanation: Images are built up in real time and refreshed each second

stems.label: C
stems.text: The selected pulse repetition frequency (PRF) depends on the imaging depth
stems.explanation: It takes 13 microseconds for a pulse to travel to & from a structure 1cm from the transducer. Deeper structures require longer intervals between successive pulses, so the PRF must decrease to prevent pulses overlapping

stems.label: D
stems.text: Image brightness is dependent on the angle of the transducer relative to the organ surface
stems.explanation: This will effect the angle of incidence of the beam on a tissue boundary. The maximum echo strength is received from normal incidence/reflection

stems.label: E
stems.text: Image brightness is proportional to the acoustic impedance of the tissues
stems.explanation: Image brightness in B-mode scans is proportional to the echo intensity. This depends on the difference in acoustic impedance between adjacent tissues

title: Regarding Axial resolution in a B-mode scan

stems.label: A
stems.text: Is dependent on the spatial pulse length (SPL)
stems.explanation: SPL = US wavelength x No of waves in a pulse. Axial resolution = SPL/2

stems.label: B
stems.text: Varies with depth in the patient
stems.explanation: Axial resolution depends only on the spatial pulse length (SPL) which in turn, depends on the wavelength of the US wave. Wavelength doesn't change with depth.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Improves with increasing frequency
stems.explanation: The wavelength of the US waves (and therefore the SPL) is shorter at higher frequencies. Hence axial resolution improves with increasing frequency.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Is dependent on the diameter of the transducer
stems.explanation: The diameter of the transducer does not influence the SPL and therefore does not affect axial resolution.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Is typically 0.5-1mm
stems.explanation: Wavelengths in US are 0.3-1.0mm, which produce Spatial Pulse Lengths of 0.9-3mm. Remember, Axial resolution = SPL/2

title: Regarding the frequency shift in Doppler ultrasound

stems.label: A
stems.text: Increases with Doppler angle
stems.explanation: Doppler shift is greatest for angle=0 degrees and drops to zero as the angle approaches 90 degrees

stems.label: B
stems.text: Increases with operating frequency
stems.explanation: Increasing the operating frequency of the US waves causes a larger frequency shift in the reflected signal

stems.label: C
stems.text: Increases with the velocity of blood flow
stems.explanation: The Doppler frequency shift increases in proportion to the velocity of blood flow

stems.label: D
stems.text: Increases with the propagation velocity of the ultrasound beam
stems.explanation: The Doppler shift is inversely proportional to propagation velocity

stems.label: E
stems.text: Increases with pulse repetition frequency (PRF)
stems.explanation: The PRF determines the maximum frequency shift that can be detected before aliasing occurs. It does affect not the size of the frequency shift though.

title: Regarding Electron binding energy in atoms

stems.label: A
stems.text: Is the energy needed to move an electron up to the next shell
stems.explanation: It is the energy needed to remove the electron from the atom

stems.label: B
stems.text: Is greatest for K-shell electrons
stems.explanation: They are closest to the nucleus and & experience a strong attractive force

stems.label: C

title: Regarding beam filtration in conventional x-ray machines

stems.label: A
stems.text: Its primary purpose is to remove characteristic radiation emitted from the x-ray target

stems.text: Inherent filtration is typically equivalent to 2mm Al

title: Quantum noise in fluoroscopy can be reduced by

stems.label: A
stems.text: Increasing the tube voltage (kVp)
stems.explanation: Quantum/random/Poisson noise is decreased when more x-rays are detected. An increase in kVp will increase the intensity & penetration of the beam so more x-rays will reach the image intensifier thus decreasing the quantum noise

stems.label: B
stems.text: Increasing the tube current (mA)
stems.explanation: An increase in mA will increase the intensity of the beam. More x-rays will therefore be detected, thus decreasing the quantum noise.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Removing the anti-scatter grid
stems.explanation: Removing the anti-scatter grid will increase the number of x-rays reaching the image intensifier & so will reduce quantum noise, (a lot of these x-rays will be scattered so contrast will be degraded)

stems.label: D
stems.text: Increasing the source-to-skin distance
stems.explanation: Increasing the source-skin distance will move the image intensifier further from the x-ray tube & so will reduce the intensity of the beam. This will mean that fewer x-rays will be detected and so quantum/random noise will increase.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Selecting a different dose control curve for the automatic brightness control (ABC)

stems.label: B

stems.explanation: Changing the mA will have no effect on the energy of the x-rays. Contrast is created by differential attenuation between different tissues. stems.label: C

title: Regarding radiation protection in the Radiology Department

title: The calculated CT number of a pixel in a transaxial CT slice is

stems.label: A
stems.text: Tube voltage (kVp)
stems.explanation: The CT number (HU) is a measure of the attenuating properties of the tissue (relative to water) in the corresponding voxel in the patient. Attenuation properties change with x-ray energy, which is affected by the kVp

stems.label: B
stems.text: Tube current (mA)
stems.explanation: There is no change in attenuation with changes in tube current (changing the mA does not change the energy of the x-rays in the beam)

stems.label: C
stems.text: Slice thickness
stems.explanation: Increased slice thickness will result in more partial volume effects. The calculated CT number of the pixel is an average across the tissues contained within the voxel

stems.label: D
stems.text: Surrounding patient anatomy
stems.explanation: Beam hardening occurs when the x-rays pass through dense bone. This increases the average energy of the transmitted beam and makes it more penetrating so any other tissues the beam passes through appear to be less attenuating (the CT number decreases)

stems.label: E
stems.text: Reconstruction algorithm used
stems.explanation: The reconstruction algorithm affects the resolution and noise proerties of the CT slices, which in turn can affect the CT numbers

title: Increasing the pitch of a MDCT scan from 1.0 to 1.5 will have

stems.label: A
stems.text: Reduced image noise
stems.explanation: Increasing the pitch actually increases image noise. This is because a higher pitch acquires fewer projections, resulting in less data used to reconstruct the image and a lower signal-to-noise ratio.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Reduced patient dose
stems.explanation: For a pitch > 1 the table moves further than the beam width during one rotation, leading to a smaller volume of tissue being irradiated. This reduces the radiation dose to the patient

stems.label: C
stems.text: Reduced scan time
stems.explanation: A higher pitch allows the table to move faster, covering more anatomy in the same amount of time. This results in shorter scan times.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Reduced partial volume artifacts
stems.explanation: Z-plane resolution is degraded resulting in greater averaging between gantry rotations

stems.label: E
stems.text: Reduced patient motion artifacts
stems.explanation: A shorter duration scan means less chance of patient motion

title: Regarding Comparing reconstruction techniques in CT imaging

stems.label: A
stems.text: Filtered back projection (FBP) is generally faster at reconstructing images compared to statistical iterative reconstruction (SIR).
stems.explanation: FBP is a simpler and computationally less demanding technique, resulting in faster reconstruction times. SIR involves iterative calculations and more complex processing, which can take longer.

stems.label: B
stems.text: SIR methods are more effective at suppressing image noise, particularly in lowdose CT scans.
stems.explanation: SIR excels at noise reduction by incorporating statistical models and iterative refinement to estimate the image. This makes it particularly valuable for low-dose CT, where noise is more prominent.

stems.label: C
stems.text: FBP typically produces images with sharper edges and finer details compared to SIR.
stems.explanation: FBP often prioritizes edge enhancement and fine detail preservation, resulting in sharper images. However, this can come at the cost of increased noise. SIR may sometimes produce slightly less sharp images due to its focus on noise reduction.

stems.label: D
stems.text: FBP is better at handling artifacts caused by metal implants or beam hardening compared to SIR.
stems.explanation: SIR techniques are generally more robust in handling artifacts like metal streaks and beam hardening. They can incorporate corrections for these effects into the reconstruction process, leading to improved image quality.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Both FBP and SIR are equally susceptible to motion artifacts.
stems.explanation: Both techniques are vulnerable to motion artifacts, as patient movement during the scan can introduce blurring and distortions regardless of the reconstruction method. Minimizing patient motion is crucial for optimal image quality with either technique.

title: Decreasing each of the following parameters will reduce the

stems.text: Gantry rotation speed
stems.explanation: A slower rotation speed means a longer acquisition time per rotation, which means more x-rays are detected per rotation. This will reduce statistical noise.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Slice thickness
stems.explanation: Thinner slices result in fewer photons being used per voxel, which will increase statistical (random) noise.

stems.label: C

stems.explanation: Lower kVp results in fewer X-ray photons being produced, which will increase noise.

stems.label: D

stems.explanation: A smaller matrix size (going from 512x512 to 256x256) means larger pixels, hence more x-rays per voxel will be recorded and this will reduce statistical noise and increasing noise.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Tube current (mA)
stems.explanation: Lower mA results in fewer X-ray photons being emitted each second and therefore, fewer x-rays being detected. This will increase statistical (random) noise.

stems.explanation: As FoV increases the pixel size will also increase (the same number of pixels are sampling a larger area). Therefore, voxels get bigger and generate larger signals.

stems.explanation: This will improve spatial resolution along the phase encoding axis, but will not improve the SNR
