stems.explanation: TGC can be varied by the operator to amplify signals from depth at different rates

stems.label: E
stems.text: Refraction occurs at interfaces between tissues with different acoustic velocities
stems.explanation: Refraction is the change in direction of the transmitted beam when it strikes the boundary of 2 media at an oblique angle.

title: Regarding Lateral resolution in a B-mode scan

stems.label: A
stems.text: Improves with increasing frequency
stems.explanation: Each beam line is narrower at higher frequencies. Spatial resolution in US improves with increasing frequency

stems.label: B
stems.text: Varies with depth
stems.explanation: The beam width diverges at depth and this will diminish the lateral resolution.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Is dependent on the number of scan lines in each frame
stems.explanation: A higher line density improves the sampling rate which will improve the lateral resolution.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Is dependent on the frame rate
stems.explanation: The frame rate will affect the number of scan lines available per frame. A fast frame rate will necessitate a lower number of scan lines for each frame.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Is typically 2-3mm in clinical imaging studies
stems.explanation: Lateral resolution is usually larger (ie worse) than axial resolution

title: The purpose of time gain compensation is to

stems.label: A
stems.text: Improve axial resolution
stems.explanation: TGC has no effect on axial resolution

stems.label: B
stems.text: Compensate for differences in echo signal strength from different tissue boundaries
stems.explanation: If it did we would lose all contrast in the image

stems.label: C
stems.text: Compensate for attenuation of echo signals from different depths
stems.explanation: Echoes from the same boundaries at different depths will have different sizes without TGC

stems.label: D
stems.text: Produce similar signals from similar tissue boundaries
stems.explanation: Boosting signals from greater depths compensates for attenuation of the echoes from greater depths

stems.label: E
stems.text: Increase the dynamic range of the signals
stems.explanation: TGC will produce a narrower range of signal intensities (by amplifying weaker ones)

stems.label: A
stems.text: Variations in the speed of the US pulse can cause displacement of structures along the axis of the US beam
stems.explanation: The depth of the reflecting surface is determined using an assumed speed of 1540m/s. If the actual speed is different from this the depth is incorrectly calculated.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Comet tail artifact is caused by reverberation of the US beam
stems.explanation: The artifact is caused by multiple closely spaced reverberations

stems.label: C
stems.text: Acoustic shadowing can be caused by both cysts & gallstones
stems.explanation: The fluid within cysts is less attenuating than surrounding soft tissue and will cause distal enhancement.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Side lobes in the US beam can result in the lateral displacement of structures in the image
stems.explanation: Side lobes are weak off-axis beams emitted by the transducer. They can cause signals from off-axis structures to be detected and falsely placed along the central beam axis in the image.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Refraction artifacts can be reduced by reducing the transmit frequency
stems.explanation: Refraction is the change in direction of the transmitted beam when it strikes the boudary of 2 media at an oblique angle. The amount of refraction that occurs depends only on the angle of incidence & the speed of US in the two media not on the frequency of the US waves.

title: Regarding the temperature rise in an ultrasound examination

stems.label: A
stems.text: It increases with pulse repetition frequency, PRF
stems.explanation: As the PRF increases more US pulses are emitted per second. Each pulse transfer energy to the patient & will contribute to an increase in temperature.

stems.label: B
stems.text: It is greatest in the superficial layers of the patient
stems.explanation: US beams are attenuated as they travel through a patient. The attenuation is least near the surface and so the energy carried by the beam is greatest. at shallow depths.

stems.label: C
stems.text: It is greater in bone than soft tissue
stems.explanation: Bone is much more highly absorbing than soft tissue.

stems.label: D
stems.text: It increases with operating frequency of the probe
stems.explanation: Beam attenuation increases strongly with increasing operating frequency. So more US energy will; be absorbed per cm travelled, which manifests as a temperature rise.

stems.label: E
stems.text: It is greater in highly perfused tissues
stems.explanation: Blood flow will carry heat energy away from the tissue.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Is the predominant mode of x-ray interaction in the patient during mammography
stems.explanation: The likelihood of a PE event is energy dependent. The average photon energy in mammography is typically ~20keV, which promotes PE interaction

stems.label: B
stems.text: Occurs more frequently at higher x-ray energies
stems.explanation: The occurrence of PE decreases rapidly at higher x-ray energies. The probability of occurrence is proportional to 1/E^3

stems.label: C
stems.text: Occurs more frequently in tissues with a high mass density
stems.explanation: As density increases there are more atoms to interact with in the path of the x-rays

stems.label: D
stems.text: Results in a higher radiation dose to bone than soft tissue
stems.explanation: PE interactions occur more frequently in high atomic number (Z) material. Bone has a higher Z than soft tissue.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Results in the complete absorption of the x-ray
stems.explanation: The initial x-ray is completely absorbed (even if there is some low energy characteristic radiation emitted afterwards)

stems.label: A
stems.text: Predominantly involves K-shell electrons
stems.explanation: Compton scattering occurs when the binding energy of the electron is much, much lower than the energy of the x-ray photon. Hence, it usually involves outer shell electrons that are weakly attached to the atom.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Occurs more frequently with increasing tube voltage (kVp)
stems.explanation: The probability of Compton scattering decreases slowly with increasing photon energy (or kVp)

stems.label: C
stems.text: Degrades image contrast in x-ray and nuclear medicine studies
stems.explanation: Scattered x-rays (or gamma-rays) are redirected from their original path and always degrade image contrast.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Is the predominant mode of interaction in patients during CT procedures
stems.explanation: The average photon energy in CT beams is ~70keV, making Compton scattering much more likely than the photoelectric effect in soft tissue

stems.label: E
stems.text: Is the predominant mode of interaction in the input screen of an image intensifier
stems.explanation: The input screen utilises a CsI phosphor. CsI has a high atomic number which favours photoelectric interactions

stems.label: A
stems.text: It is equal to the fractional reduction in x-ray intensity per unit area of an attenuator
stems.explanation: The linear attenuation coefficient = the fractional reduction in x-ray intensity per unit thickness of an attenuator

stems.label: B
stems.text: The linear attenuation coefficient of bone > the linear attenuation coefficient of water for photon energies up to 200keV
stems.explanation: Good absorbers have a high linear attenuation coefficient. Bone is more dense and has a higher atomic number (Z) than water. This makes bone better at absorbing x-rays.

stems.label: C
stems.text: The linear attenuation coefficients of soft tissue and water vary in the same way with increasing photon energy
stems.explanation: The densities and the effective atomic numbers of water & soft tissue are very similar.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The linear attenuation coefficient of any material is proportional its the half-value layer (HVL)
stems.explanation: Linear attenuation coefficient = 0.693 / HVL. So it is inversely proportional to the HVL

stems.label: E
stems.text: Linear attenuation coefficient of compact bone in diagnostic radiography depends on the product of tube current & exposure time (mAs)
stems.explanation: The linear attenuation coefficient is energy dependent. Changing the mAs will alter the total number of x-rays emitted, but not their energy.

title: Regarding Scattered radiation in abdominal radiography can be reduced

stems.label: A
stems.text: Increasing the tube current (mA)
stems.explanation: Increasing the mA will increase the number of x-rays in the incident beam & also the number of scattered x-rays in the transmitted beam (ie the scatter fraction remains constant).

stems.label: B
stems.text: Making the x-ray beam more collimated
stems.explanation: Increasing the collimation will reduce the x-ray field size (area of the beam). In turn, this will reduce the volume of tissue which can generate scatter.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Compressing the abdomen
stems.explanation: Tissue compression (also used in mammography) reduces the volume of tissue which can generate scatter

stems.label: D
stems.text: Reducing the tube voltage (kVp)
stems.explanation: Reducing the kVp will promote more photoelectric interactions to take place. Also at lower kVp, when scatter occurs, the radiation will tend to be scattered through larger angles (ie more backscatter) & so will not reach the image receptor

stems.label: E
stems.text: Increasing the patient-to-image receptor distance
stems.explanation: Increasing the patient-to-image receptor distance will introduce an air gap between the patient and image receptor. This allows scatter to be directed away from the image receptor & go undetected (but this will produce a magnified image).

title: In planar radiography, image sharpness is improved by

stems.label: A
stems.text: Increasing the tube voltage (kVp)
stems.explanation: Tube voltage affects the energy of the x-rays emitted by the tube. This will affect the type of interactions taking place in the patient (ie contrast is affected), but not the spatial resolution.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Increasing the focus to patient distance
stems.explanation: Increasing the FSD will reduce the amount of geometric unsharpness (size of the penumbra).

stems.label: C
stems.text: Increasing the patient to image receptor distance
stems.explanation: Increasing the PIR distance will allow the x-ray beam to diverge more as it travels towards the image receptor. This will increase the geometric unsharpness (size of the penumbra).

stems.label: D
stems.text: Inserting a grid between the patient and the image receptor
stems.explanation: Grids reduce the amount of scatter reaching the image receptor, and so will affect image contrast, but won't affect spatial resolution

stems.label: E
stems.text: Increasing the focal spot size
stems.explanation: The penumbra is the projection of the finite focal spot size onto the image receptor. Increasing the focal spot size will therefore increase the size of the penumbra.

stems.label: A
stems.text: The image plate must be read-out within 3min of the exposure to prevent signal loss
stems.explanation: The stored signal in the plate will gradually dissipate with time, causing the image to fade. It is best to readout the plate as soon as possible after exposure, but delays of 1520min can be tolerated.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The spatial resolution is typically 4lp/mm
stems.explanation: The typical spatial resolution achievable in computed radiography (CR) ranges from 3.5 to 5.5lp/mm. the highest resolution is obtained for smaller imaging plates as these will have smaller pixels.

stems.label: C
stems.text: The size of the laser spot on the imaging plate does not affect spatial resolution
stems.explanation: The laser light stimulates the release of the stored signal in the plate. For larger laser spot sizes there is greater averaging (blurring) of signal from adjacent areas.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The images must be corrected for variations in non-uniformity of the storage phosphor
stems.explanation: DR systems consist of many individual detectors, whose response can vary across the detector, and this must be corrected. CR plates, on the other hand, are a single continuous detector they do not require correction for phosphor variations.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The perceived image contrast is controlled by image acquisition parameters
stems.explanation: These are digital images which can be post-processed to improve the appearance of the image.

title: Regarding fluoroscopy with an image intensifier

stems.label: A
stems.text: The input phosphor is typically made of sodium iodide
stems.explanation: CsI is used as the input phosphor in an image intensifier. NaI is used as a scintillation crystal in a gamma camera

stems.label: B
stems.text: Light from the output screen can be used to control the exposure
stems.explanation: Light from the output screen can be measured and used to control the x-ray tube operating parameters in a feedback loop

stems.label: C
stems.text: For abdominal studies, the dose rate at the surface of a patient is typically 10-20 mGy/min
stems.explanation: Because the beam is on continuously and relatively high KVp and mA are required to penetrate the abdomen

stems.label: D
stems.text: Veiling glare can be removed by an anti-scatter grid
stems.explanation: A grid will remove x-rays that have been scattered by the patient. However, veiling glare is caused by scattered light and electrons within the image intensifier itself.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The brightness gain of an image intensifier decreases with time
stems.explanation: As the phosphor ages it becomes less efficient and this leads to a decrease in brightness gain.

stems.label: A
stems.text: The focus-receptor distance is typically 65cm
stems.explanation: A shorter FSD is needed than for traditional radiography due to the low radiation output of mammographic units.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Breast compression improves both contrast & spatial resolution
stems.explanation: Compression brings the lesions closer to the image receptor (improving geometric unsharpness) and reduces the thickness of tissue irradiated (less scatter is produced)

stems.label: C
stems.text: K-edge filtration is employed to improve image contrast
stems.explanation: K-edge filtration removes higher energy x-rays from the beam & promotes greater photoelectric absorption

stems.label: D
stems.text: Exposure times are typically > 1 second
stems.explanation: X-ray tube outputs are low in mammography, so exposure times are long

stems.label: E
stems.text: The effect of quantum mottle is increased in magnification studies
stems.explanation: Quantum mottle increases because the receptor is moved further from the x-ray tube, which reduces beam intensity according to the inverse square law. A smaller focal spot size must be used in magnification studies to prevent excessive penumbra and this also limits the available x-ray output. The combined effect is reduced detected intensity of the beam (which increases quantum mottle).

title: The ideal properties of a radionuclide for imaging with a

stems.label: A
stems.text: A physical half-life less than or equal to 1 hour
stems.explanation: A short half-life will limit the shelf life of a radiopharmaceutical and require constant replenishment. The ideal half-life is 4-6 hours.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Gamma ray emission in an energy range 0.1-0.2MeV
stems.explanation: Photons below this energy range are primarily absorbed in the patient leading to a higher dose. Photons above this range are harder to collimate and detect in the gamma camera.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Does not decay via electron capture
stems.explanation: Electron capture can result in the formation of an excited daughter nucleus which subsequently emits a gamma ray. I123 and In111 both decay via electron capture and are used in radionuclide imaging.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Decays to a non-radioactive daughter
stems.explanation: A radioactive daughter would lead to further irradiation of the patient, increasing their radiation dose

stems.label: E
stems.text: Is cyclotron produced
stems.explanation: Cylcotron production is expensive and not available all the time. Radionuclide generators provide a cheaper, readily available supply.

stems.label: A
stems.text: The NaI crystal has a detection efficiency of about 90% for 140keV gamma rays
stems.explanation: NaI has a high atomic number and high density. This leads to a high detection efficiency for 140keV gamma rays.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The spatial resolution of the camera is largely controlled by the thickness of the NaI scintillation crystal
stems.explanation: The collimator has the largest influence on resolution

stems.label: C
stems.text: The detected count rate is proportional to the activity administered to the patient for activities up 1GBq
stems.explanation: This is only true for low levels of activity in the FoV. At higher activities the camera cannot accurately detect all gamma rays reaching the detector (known as "dead-time" effects).

stems.label: D
stems.text: Septal penetration may occur when imaging radionuclides which emit gamma rays with energy >200keV
stems.explanation: There is always a small amount of septal penetration in all studies, but this becomes more likely for higher energy gamma rays

stems.label: E
stems.text: Less than 0.1% of the gamma rays emitted from a patient are utilized to form an image
stems.explanation: Most of the emitted gamma rays are either directed away from the camera, absorbed in the collimator, or rejected as scatter by the PHA window.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Up to 120 images are acquired at different angles around the patient
stems.explanation: Images are typically acquired at angular steps of 3 degrees

stems.label: B
stems.text: Spatial resolution is improved by using patient-contoured, rather than circular orbits
stems.explanation: Patient-contoured orbits reduce the separation between the patient and the camera. The spatial resolution of a gamma camera deteriorates with distance.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Iterative reconstruction algorithms are used exclusively
stems.explanation: The datasets are relatively small, which means iterative reconstruction can be performed in a reasonable time with improved image quality.

stems.label: D
stems.text: CT data can be used to correct for non-uniform attenuation in the patient
stems.explanation: CT images map the regional attenuation coefficients of tissues in the patient.

stems.label: E
stems.text: CT data can be used to correct for non-uniform response of the gamma camera
stems.explanation: CT images contain no information about the performance of the camera, so cannot be used to correct it.

stems.label: A
stems.text: The axial field of view of the PET detectors is typically 15-25cm
stems.explanation: The limited axial FoV requires PET studies to be performed via sequential positioning & data collection along the length of the patient

stems.label: B
stems.text: PET and CT data are always acquired sequentially
stems.explanation: CT data are usually acquired first

stems.label: C
stems.text: Time-of-flight acquisitions can only be acquired using bismuth germanate (BGO) detectors
stems.explanation: ToF requires detectors with very good temporal resolution. However, BGO detectors emit light from each scintillation relatively slowly.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Time-of-flight information can be used to eliminate scatter
stems.explanation: ToF improves effective SNR by constraining each event’s position along its line of response — it does not improve spatial resolution and cannot eliminate scatter.

stems.label: E
stems.text: All PET radionuclides have an atomic number < 20
stems.explanation: Rb82 (Z=37) and Ga68 ( Z=31) are two PET radionuclides which are in clinical use. They are produced via radionuclide generators.

title: Regarding the Ionising Radiations Regulations 2017 stipulate

stems.label: A
stems.text: The role of the RPA is to advise an employer on compliance with all radiation protection legislation
stems.explanation: The RPA must advise on compliance with IRR17 only

stems.label: B
stems.text: Local Rules must specify dose investigation levels for staff working in that area
stems.explanation: A dose investigation level (DIL) can be set by the employer to match the type of work carried out in that area. The DIL is not a legal dose limit, but must be included in the Local Rules.

stems.label: C
stems.text: X-ray equipment must undergo a critical examination at installation
stems.explanation: A 'critical exam' refers to an assessment of the safety features of radiation equipment (emergency stop, warning lights etc).

stems.label: D
stems.text: Dose records of classified staff must be maintained for at least 30 years
stems.explanation: Employers must keep dose records of classified staff for 30 years. For unclassified staff, the doses only need to be kept for 2 years.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Staff must not receive a whole body dose > 1mSv when pregnant
stems.explanation: The dose to the foetus must not exceed 1mSv from the declaration of pregnancy until birth. The dose to the mother can still exceed this level provided the limit for the foetus is observed.

stems.label: A
stems.text: The RPA is responsible for establishing dose limits for common medical procedures at each hospital
stems.explanation: There are no dose limits for medical exposures and the MPE is the 'qualified expert' for these regulations, not the RPA.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Exposures that are in excess of twice the diagnostic reference level must be reported
stems.explanation: The criteria for reporting incidents depends on the intended dose. The multiplication factor for low dose studies can be as high as x10 or x20.

stems.label: C
stems.text: The CQC must be notified of any significant accidental or unintended exposures within 2 weeks of the incident
stems.explanation: This is the deadline for initial reports. A more detailed investigation report can be submitted later.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The Medical Physics Expert is responsible for reporting all over exposures
stems.explanation: The Employer must report all incidents.

stems.label: E
stems.text: A significant overexposure caused by a faulty contrast injector is reportable
stems.explanation: Incidents caused by equipment as well as human and procedural errors are all reportable.

stems.label: A
stems.text: The absorbed dose is the energy deposited per unit volume
stems.explanation: Absorbed dose is defined as radiation energy absorbed per unit mass (energy/mass)

stems.label: B
stems.text: Effective dose takes into account both acute and late biological effects
stems.explanation: Effective dose only considers the risk of stochastic effects. Acute reactions are predictable & only occur above a high threshold dose.

stems.label: C
stems.text: In diagnostic radiology equivalent dose always equals the absorbed dose
stems.explanation: The radiation weighting factors (which modify the absorbed dose) are all the same for xrays, gamma rays & electrons.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The effective dose provides a means of comparing the risk from x-ray investigations of different parts of the body
stems.explanation: Effective dose is a measure of the risk to an average person following a medical exposure

stems.label: E
stems.text: Effective doses from different imaging modalities cannot be combined
stems.explanation: Effective dose is a measure of risk. The risks from different exposures can be combined or compared.

title: Regarding the radiation dose to a patient from injected

stems.label: A
stems.text: Increases in direct proportion to the biological half-life
stems.explanation: The biological half-life determines how quickly the radioactivity is removed from the body. The longer the residence time the greater the dose, but the dose is not directly proportional to the biological half-life.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Depends on the properties of both the radionuclide and the pharmaceutical
stems.explanation: The physical properties of the radionuclide (half-life, type of radiation emitted) and the biochemical properties of the pharmaceutical (ie distribution and residence time within the body) both effect the dose to the patient.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Is delivered at a much lower dose rate than in CT studies
stems.explanation: The radiation dose from a radiopharmaceutical is delivered to the patient over several hours, whereas in CT the dose is delivered in a few seconds.

stems.label: D
stems.text: May be measured using a gamma camera
stems.explanation: The gamma camera can only measure activity distributions in the patient, not radiation dose

stems.label: E
stems.text: Is a factor which limits the quality of radionuclide images
stems.explanation: Low activities must be administered to minimise patient doses, but this results in noisy images

title: Regarding Radiation protection in nuclear medicine

stems.label: A
stems.text: Breastfeeding must be interrupted for 24hr following any diagnostic administration of Tc99m
stems.explanation: Not all radiopharmaceuticals are excreted in breast milk, in which case, there is no need to interrupt breastfeeding

stems.label: B
stems.text: The activity administered to children is usually half the adult dose
stems.explanation: Paediatric doses are scaled down from adult doses according to patient weight and body surface area.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Nuclear medicine exposures must be authorised by a licensed practitioner
stems.explanation: Authorisation can be performed by an IRMER operator following a written protocol issued by a licensed practitioner. Justification, on the other hand, can only be performed by a licensed practitioner.

stems.label: D
stems.text: All radioactive waste must be stored on the hospital premises until it has decayed
stems.explanation: This is true for solid waste, however, most radioactive waste is in the form of patient excreta & is discharged immediately

stems.label: E
stems.text: All administered patient activities must be measured in a dose calibrator beforehand
stems.explanation: A dose calibrator measures the activity in syringes & vials.

stems.label: A
stems.text: The transmitted x-ray intensity is measured by an array of scintillation detectors
stems.explanation: The detectors are typically made of gadolinium oxysuphide

stems.label: B
stems.text: The x-ray beam is heavily filtered using copper or tin filters
stems.explanation: The beam is 'pre-hardened' using heavy beam filtration to remove low energy bremsstrahlung x-rays.

stems.label: C
stems.text: The x-ray beam is pulsed during acquisition to reduce patient dose
stems.explanation: The x-ray tube is continuously energised as it rotates around the patient.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Focal spot sizes of 0.6mm and 1.2mm are typically used
stems.explanation: Broad and fine focal spot sizes are available

stems.label: E
stems.text: The pitch is the distance moved by the imaging table in a single rotation divided by the slice thickness
stems.explanation: Pitch = distance moved by the table / collimated beam width

title: Regarding the following actions will increase the noise in a CT slice

stems.label: A
stems.text: Decreasing the gantry rotation speed
stems.explanation: A slower rotation speed means a longer acquisition time per rotation resulting in more xrays being detected this will reduce random noise

stems.label: B
stems.text: Decreasing the slice thickness
stems.explanation: Thinner slices result in fewer photons passing through each voxel (and being detected), thus increasing random noise levels.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Decreasing the tube voltage (kVp)
stems.explanation: Lowering the kVp causes a significant reduction in beam intensity. Fewer x-ray photons will be detected for each voxel, so random noise will increase.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Decreasing the matrix size
stems.explanation: Matrix size refers to the number of pixels the image is divided into along the vertical and horizontal axes. A smaller matrix size means fewer but larger pixels along each axis. Larger pixels collate detected x-rays from a wider area so the random noise level will decrease.

stems.label: E
stems.text: Using a bone filter during image reconstruction
stems.explanation: Different filers are available for image reconstruction with FBP. A bone filter will optimise spatial resolution at the expense of increased image noise.

stems.label: A
stems.text: Slice thickness is determined by the collimator width
stems.explanation: Slice thickness in MSCT is determined by the size of the detector elements used to record the transmitted x-ray intensity

stems.label: B
stems.text: Quarter detector offset is used to increase transaxial resolution
stems.explanation: The centre of the detector array is offset from the location of the focal spot by 1/4 of the detector size. This improves the sampling frequency in projections which are 180deg apart (ie opposing projections)

stems.label: C
stems.text: Ring artifacts do not occur when acquiring data in helical mode
stems.explanation: Ring artifacts are caused by faulty detector elements which map out a circular defect during gantry rotation.

stems.label: D
stems.text: The reconstruction filter can significantly influence transaxial resolution
stems.explanation: Different filers are available for image reconstruction with FBP. These will transmit different ranges of spatial frequencies. Soft tissue filters suppress image noise, but 'smooth' (ie introduce blur to) the image.

stems.label: E
stems.text: CT numbers are based on the attenuation coefficient of a tissue relative to that of water
stems.explanation: The CT number of water = 0

title: Regarding patient safety in CT studies

stems.label: A
stems.text: The effective dose to the patient is proportional to the dose length product (DLP)
stems.explanation: The effective dose can be estimated by multiplying the DLP by a conversion factor. There are different conversion factors for different CT examinations.

stems.label: B
stems.text: National diagnostic reference levels for the DLP must not be exceeded
stems.explanation: CTDI and/or DLP can be used as a DRL in CT imaging. National DRLs are guidance values only. They are not legal limits.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Iodinated contrast agents must not be given if the patient's eGFR < 50 ml/min/1.73m2
stems.explanation: The cut-off is usually taken as 30 ml/min/1.73m2

stems.label: D
stems.text: The effective dose for a chest-abdomen-pelvis study is typically 12-15mSv
stems.explanation: Generally true in the UK, but will depend on the acquisition parameters used.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The foetal dose in a pelvic CT study is typically 20-30mGy
stems.explanation: Generally true in the UK, but will depend on the acquisition parameters used.

stems.text: T1 relaxation involves the transfer of energy from the protons to the surrounding atoms

stems.label: B
stems.text: T1 is the time taken for the longitudinal magnetisation vector to recover to 63% of its original value
stems.explanation: This is how T1 is defined

stems.label: C
stems.text: The T1 relaxation of all tissues increases with magnetic field strength
stems.explanation: T1 relaxation requires molecular motion/rotation at frequencies close to the Larmor frequency. As the Larmor frequency increases with Bo, the molecular motions no longer match the Larmor frequency causing T1 to increase.

stems.text: T2 relaxation involves the loss of spin coherence due to magnetic field inhomogeneities
stems.explanation: T2 relaxation refers to random interactions between the spin population at a molecular level. T2* relaxation includes signal loss due to field inhomogeneities.

stems.label: E
stems.text: T2 is typically 300-800 msec for most tissues

stems.text: Hydrogen protons precess at the same frequency in a fixed magnetic field, regardless of tissue composition.
stems.explanation: Protons in water and fat have different resonant frequencies due to electronic shielding in the surrounding molecules.

stems.text: Inversion recovery pulse sequences using a short inversion time (TI) can be used to null the signal from CSF
stems.explanation: STIR pulse sequences use a short TI to eliminate the signal from fat. Nulling the signal from CSF would require a long TI

stems.label: C
stems.text: Both fat and water appear hyper-intense on T2-weighted FSE pulse sequences
stems.explanation: Within lipid molecules a spin-spin coupling (called 'J-coupling') occurs between the atomic nuclei. This coupling shortens T2 relaxation time for fat relative to water (hence fat should be darker in the image). However, fast repetition of 180° pulses in FSE disrupts Jcoupling, causing T2 of fat to lengthen. So both fat & water appear bright in a FSE image.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Flowing blood appears dark in spin-echo pulse sequences
stems.explanation: Blood flowing into a slice of tissue will not have been exposed to the 90deg pulse and will generate no echo after the 180deg pulse is applied.

stems.label: E
stems.text: In gradient recalled echo pulse sequences the refocussing gradient is applied along the frequency encode axis
stems.explanation: A bi-polar gradient is used to deliberately dephase and then rephase the MR signal to create an echo. This gradient is applied along the 'frequency-encode' or 'readout' axis.

title: Regarding the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) in MR imaging

stems.label: A
stems.text: SNR of T1-weighted images is higher than that for T2-weighted images
stems.explanation: T1 weighting uses a shorter TE so the signal is stronger, because there is less decay of the signal before the echo is detected.

stems.label: B
stems.text: Increasing the receiver bandwidth will increase the SNR
stems.explanation: Receiver bandwidth refers to the range of frequencies detected in the receiver coils. The 'signal' has a much narrower range of frequencies than the noise, so increasing the receiver bandwidth will allow more noise to be recorded, so SNR will decrease.

stems.label: C
stems.text: Increasing the matrix size from 128x128 to 256x256 will halve the SNR
stems.explanation: The voxels in a 256x256 image are 4 times smaller than those in a 128x128 image. The signal size depends on the voxel size (which is 4x smaller), whereas the noise signal is generated from the patient as a whole (an so doesn't change). Hence the SNR will be 4 times smaller.

stems.label: D
stems.text: SNR is inversely proportional to the TE of the pulse sequence
stems.explanation: The MR signal decays exponentially with time, so the signal strength will not be proportional to TE.

stems.label: E
stems.text: SNR is proportional to the proton density
stems.explanation: The MR signal comes from protons, so the higher the proton density, the higher the signal.

stems.explanation: Wraparound artifacts occur when body parts outside the field of view (FoV) are incorrectly displayed within the image, often overlapping anatomy. By making the FoV larger than the object, all signals are correctly mapped within the image, thus eliminating the artifact.

title: Regarding With respect to radioactive decay processes

stems.label: A
stems.text: the activity of a radionuclide is 1 MBq if there are 1000 nuclear disintegrations per second
stems.explanation: 1 MBq equals 1,000,000 disintegrations per second, not 1000.

stems.label: B

stems.explanation: Half-life equals 0.693 divided by the decay constant.

stems.label: C
stems.text: after 10 half-lives the activity of a radionuclide will have decreased by a little more than 1000fold
stems.explanation: Ten half-lives means halving ten times: 2^10 = 1024. The activity is left at 1/1024 of what it started as, which is a reduction of a little more than 1000-fold — so the statement is true as written. This is the practical rule behind decay storage: hold a Tc-99m source (6 hour half-life) for ten half-lives, about 60 hours, and you are down to a thousandth of the starting activity. The useful shorthand is that 10 half-lives is roughly a factor of 1000, and 20 half-lives roughly a factor of a million.

stems.label: D

stems.explanation: Different radioisotopes have different nuclear configurations and therefore different physical half-lives.

stems.label: E

stems.explanation: Physical half-life is a nuclear property and is independent of biological clearance.

title: Regarding the following are true of electromagnetic radiation

stems.label: A
stems.text: It travels in straight lines unless attenuated
stems.explanation: Electromagnetic radiation travels in straight lines unless scattered, absorbed, or refracted.

stems.label: B
stems.text: The intensity of radiaton emitted from a point source will reduce in inverse proportion to the square of the distance from that point source
stems.explanation: This is the inverse square law stated exactly: intensity falls in inverse proportion to the SQUARE of the distance (I ∝ 1/d²).

stems.label: C
stems.text: The frequency of electromagnetic radiation is inversely proportional to its wavelength
stems.explanation: Frequency and wavelength are inversely related for a given propagation speed.

stems.label: D
stems.text: Doubling the distance from a point source will reduce the radiation intensity by 50%
stems.explanation: Doubling distance reduces intensity to one quarter, not by 50%.

stems.label: E
stems.text: The inverse square law will predict the reduction in intensity of a beam of radiation from a point source passing through lead
stems.explanation: The inverse square law does not account for attenuation through lead.

stems.text: The main source of radiation to staff is due to scatter from the patient

stems.text: The risk of developing fatal childhood cancer from radiation exposure in utero is around 1 in 13,000 per mGy

stems.label: C
stems.text: Thermoluminescent detectors can directly measure entrance surface dose
stems.explanation: TLDs measure absorbed dose at their position; entrance surface dose is usually derived/estimated with appropriate placement and backscatter correction.

stems.text: Deterministic effects are best measured by DAP
stems.explanation: Deterministic skin effects are better related to peak skin dose, not DAP.

stems.explanation: Entrance skin dose is approximately proportional to kV squared when other factors are fixed.

stems.explanation: Fast-flowing blood often appears as a signal void on spin echo sequences.

stems.explanation: Short TE minimises T2 weighting in proton-density sequences.

stems.explanation: Ringing/truncation is reduced by increasing matrix or filtering, not reducing matrix.

stems.explanation: NHSBSP standard breast mean glandular dose should be below about 2.5 mGy per image.

stems.explanation: PET radionuclides generally have short half-lives.

stems.explanation: Increasing mA or rotation time increases photons and improves SNR.

stems.explanation: Bow-tie filters compensate for patient shape and reduce beam-hardening/non-uniformity.

title: Regarding the effective dose to a patient from a single radiograph under Automatic exposure control is as follows:

stems.label: C
stems.text: Decreased by using a faster detector
